stories.Headline: This election’s biggest AI story isn’t about data centers
stories.Summary:
Democrats swept the midterms this week, and Vox's Sigal Samuel argues the bigger AI story is not data centers but the new crop of leaders who want to regulate the technology itself. Candidates in several races made data centers a campaign issue, 40 ballot measures to slow or stop them passed, and an exit poll found 56 percent of respondents called AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote. A separate episode summary from the All-In podcast says the Democrats won both chambers, took at least 29 governorships and will hold 54 to 56 Senate seats, with at least 250 House seats. The same summary says markets saw a roughly $4 trillion one-day wipeout in market value around the data center backlash, though it does not detail the cause.

Samuel says several winners have been vocal about AI risk since major AI hacks this summer. Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Michigan Senate race, wants a "full-on pause" on frontier AI research, a treaty with China to avoid an arms race, a ban on recursive self-improvement, and a new federal agency that could inspect companies and block releases. Jon Ossoff won in Georgia after attacking AI developers and calling for inspectors in frontier labs and an AI treaty. Scott Wiener, behind California's SB 1047, which was vetoed, and SB 53, which was signed, won Nancy Pelosi's seat and says he will push strict federal safety standards. Manny Rutinel won in Colorado and cited a 10 percent risk of wiping out human civilization, while Sam Forstag in Montana and Troy Jackson in Maine also spoke of existential risk.

Samuel names two levers for Democrats, hearings and lawmaking. Sen. Ed Markey, reelected in Massachusetts, posted that they would need to plant new forests for all the subpoenas to be printed. Sen. Maria Cantwell, slated to chair the Senate Commerce Committee, has released a framework calling for mandatory safety standards for cutting-edge models, independent testing and audits before release, and prompt reporting of safety incidents. Brad Carson, a former congressman who leads Americans for Responsible AI, said every Democrat supports it and only five or six Republicans are needed to beat the filibuster, and he thinks they can be found.

Mackenzie Arnold of the Institute for Law & AI said policymakers once discussed AI at a high level of abstraction, but that has shifted, and he expects public pressure from hearings to improve company practices. Carson said President Trump could still sign safety rules, though he holds veto power and has let tech companies move with few guardrails. Alex Bores, a New York Assembly member, called for a unified Democratic baseline on AI safety ahead of 2028, and Rep. Greg Casar, who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus, called the data center revolt an early tremor of a much bigger shake-up. Samuel notes that blocking data centers one by one would slow, but not stop, the buildout, since AI companies can find other places to build.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's Eldest Daughter Madison Huang Cancels South Korea Trip One Day Before Arrival; Nvidia AI Day to Proceed as Planned
stories.Summary:
Madison Huang, senior director of product marketing for Omniverse and Robotics at Nvidia and the eldest daughter of CEO Jensen Huang, canceled her trip to South Korea one day before she was due to arrive. She had planned to enter the country on Nov. 8, attend Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX in Seoul on Nov. 9 and 10, and hold talks with relevant government ministries. According to the South Korean government and the IT industry on Nov. 7, she pulled out for family reasons, and no further detail was given. Her planned Nov. 8 meeting with Deputy Prime Minister and Science and ICT Minister Bae Kyung-hoon was also scrapped, and the two sides had meant to discuss high-level cooperation there.

The trip would have been her fourth to South Korea this year. In April she visited Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, LG Electronics, Hyundai Motor and Doosan Robotics, in June she accompanied her father and met SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, and in August she visited LG Electronics' robot data factory construction site. The conference itself will go ahead as scheduled, with about 2,000 attendees and 20 partner companies expected. Deepu Talla, vice president of Robotics and Edge AI, and Jonathan Cohen, vice president of Applied Research, will give the Nov. 9 morning keynotes, followed by 15 afternoon sessions across three tracks. Nov. 10 will include a hands-on workshop in Korean, an AI for Science Forum and a Physical AI Startup Connect event, and Samsung, SK hynix, LG Electronics, Naver Cloud, Doosan Robotics and Coupang are among those taking part.

No official explanation beyond family reasons has been given, and no link has been confirmed between the cancellation and recent foreign media reports. Some industry observers suggest those reports, which allege a Chinese spy connection involving someone close to Jensen Huang, may have played a part. The New York Times reported on Oct. 29 that U.S. intelligence authorities concluded Alice Huang, a Chinese national and businesswoman, passed information to Beijing and had grown close to the Nvidia chief. She was formerly an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that is both an Nvidia customer and cloud partner. The Times said no evidence showed Jensen Huang knew of any espionage, and that President Trump took no action after being briefed on the intelligence about a year ago.

Nvidia responded that the CEO's dealings with Alice Huang were neither unusual nor unexpected, since meeting customer executives is part of the job, and Jensen Huang separately called the interactions entirely normal. The Financial Times reported on Nov. 7 that the U.S. government assessed the relationship as romantic and wrote an internal memo on it, and Nvidia declined to comment. The chairs of three U.S. House committees, the Select Committee on China, the Foreign Affairs Committee and the Intelligence Committee, wrote to Jensen Huang on Nov. 4 asking him to attend a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18, citing concerns about Chinese technology infiltration and espionage risks. Meanwhile, Intel will hold AI Summit Seoul 2026 at the same venue on Nov. 12, with an SK hynix vice president giving a keynote.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Is Winding Down Oracle Deal to Rent AI Cloud Capacity
stories.Summary:
Only one article was provided, and it covers a different deal from the one named in the headline. It reports that Oracle has ended a $7 billion contract to lease artificial intelligence chips to Tencent, according to a report from the Financial Times that other outlets repeated. The deal, which was revealed in September, would have given Tencent access to about 100,000 high-end AI processors through Oracle data centers in Southeast Asia. The article says Oracle dropped the arrangement after U.S. officials raised concerns about it.

The contract ran for five years and was billed as the largest foreign chip leasing deal Tencent had signed. It was said to include an upfront payment of around 30% of its estimated value. The article says U.S. officials were worried about Chinese access to sophisticated computer technologies, and that Oracle backed out after being asked about the pact. It does not say whether Oracle will keep any advance payments, or how the cancellation will affect the company's financial forecast.

The articles supplied contain nothing about Microsoft winding down an Oracle deal to rent AI cloud capacity, so that part of the story cannot be confirmed from this material. Neither Oracle nor Tencent is quoted directly in the piece, and the account rests on the Financial Times report as relayed by GuruFocus. The cancellation is described as cutting off a significant source of contract revenue just as Oracle is investing heavily in more AI computing power. The article adds that it raises questions about whether other overseas customers could face similar limits.

The article describes the episode as evidence of regulatory uncertainty facing cloud providers that use offshore facilities to serve Chinese technology companies. The next development to watch, it says, is whether Oracle discloses the financial impact and whether it can replace the lost capacity with commitments from other customers. Beyond that, no further steps are laid out, and the Microsoft connection in the headline is not addressed. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Meta introduces specialized versions of its existing models, trained using Muse Wonder, bringing Active Memory and Active Focus to all Muse and Meta AI users (Frederic Lardinois/The New Stack)
stories.Summary:
The articles give little detail on what Meta announced, so this account covers only what they say. Meta has introduced specialized versions of its existing AI models, and these versions were trained using a more capable model called Muse Wonder. The report by Frederic Lardinois of The New Stack, which Techmeme also carried, describes it as Meta's best model now training the one that most of its users actually get. The announcement came to light on November 6, 2026, according to the publication date on the original report.

What changes for users is the addition of two features, Active Memory and Active Focus. Meta is bringing both to all users of Muse and Meta AI, not only a select group. The available text names no further numbers, prices, dates or model sizes. It also does not explain how either feature works or how the specialized versions differ from the models they are built on, so those details remain unclear from what has been published.

Responsibility for the release rests with Meta, which developed and trained the models. The New Stack's report is credited to Lardinois, and Techmeme summarized it on November 7, 2026. The text provided to me does not include any statement from Meta executives or spokespeople, so there is no company comment to paraphrase beyond the announcement itself. The same is true of any outside reaction, since the available excerpts contain none.

For context, a separate report from TechGig, dated November 9, 2026, discusses a related trend in AI, though it does not mention Meta's announcement. It explains that world models, unlike large language models, use visual inputs to generate digital environments that simulate real-world physics. That technology is described as important for home robotics and driverless cars, because it lets AI systems practice in a digital setting. It adds that a company called Niantic Spatial uses world data to build 3D replicas for robot simulation, and that such models must grasp physics and cause and effect to make AI react accurately. The articles do not say what comes next for Meta's new features, including when users will see them or how the specialized models will be extended.

stories.Headline: Roundup: China passes law against cross-border corruption, ratifies agreement on establishing World AI Cooperation Organization-Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Chinese lawmakers on Friday, November 6, 2026, voted to adopt a law against cross-border corruption and a law on procuratorial public-interest litigation. They also ratified an agreement on establishing the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization. The votes took place at the closing meeting of the 25th session of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People's Congress (NPC) in Beijing. Zhao Leji, chairman of the NPC Standing Committee, presided over the meeting at the Great Hall of the People.

The same meeting adopted a law on Antarctic activities and environmental protection and a revised Water Law. Lawmakers also approved a decision amending 15 laws, among them the Emergency Response Law. In a personnel move, they voted to remove Li Lecheng from his post as minister of industry and information technology. President Xi Jinping signed five presidential orders to promulgate the laws and the amendment decision, and a sixth order to announce the personnel change.

Zhao spoke at the closing meeting and called for higher standards and more concrete measures to make Party building within the people's congress system more effective. He also urged further improvements to the legal framework for combating corruption. Before the closing meeting, he chaired a meeting of the Council of Chairpersons of the NPC Standing Committee, and afterward he presided over a lecture for lawmakers. The session further adopted reports on the examination of deputies' proposals and on the qualification of certain deputies, along with other personnel-related bills.

The official announcement left many questions open, according to one outlet's account of the session. It did not describe the provisions, enforcement mechanisms or specific offenses covered by the cross-border corruption law or the public-interest litigation law. Nor did it explain the membership, governance structure or timetable of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, or give a reason for Li Lecheng's removal or name a successor. The articles do not say when the new laws will take effect, and they offer no detail on what changes the amendments to the 15 laws will bring.

stories.Headline: American billionaire Sam Altman’s OpenAI raises $11 billion at $1.25 trillion valuation as AI stocks tumble
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has raised $11 billion in new funding at a valuation of $1.25 trillion, according to a report from billionaires.africa citing Bloomberg. The money was wired on Friday and marks the first close of a larger round that could reach about $20 billion, with the remaining commitments expected in the coming weeks. Coatue Management and T. Rowe Price led this first close. Other investors in the broader round include SoftBank Group, Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund and Andreessen Horowitz, and a group of investors from the United Arab Emirates has also joined.

The new valuation is a 46.7% rise from the $852 billion at which OpenAI was valued in March, when it raised $122 billion. It still falls short of the company's original plan, since Bloomberg reported in late September that OpenAI wanted at least $30 billion at a valuation of about $1.4 trillion. The company later cut its target to between $15 billion and $20 billion as investors grew uneasy about the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending. OpenAI is also working with investment banks to raise money from wealthy individuals and retail investors, and it has pushed back its own stock market listing, which is now expected at some point in 2027, according to TechCrunch.

The raise came during a sharp selloff in AI stocks. On Thursday the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% and entered correction territory, while the Nasdaq-100 lost about $2.3 trillion in market value. Investors fled AI-linked stocks after Democrats won control of Congress and many pledged tighter restrictions on data centers. Rival Anthropic faces similar pressure, as Bloomberg reported that potential buyers of its planned listing are discussing a valuation as low as $1.1 trillion, down from about $2 trillion floated in early October.

The round follows a string of large deals this year. In February, OpenAI raised $110 billion at a $730 billion pre-money valuation, with Amazon committing $50 billion and Nvidia and SoftBank each pledging $30 billion. Sam Altman, who co-founded OpenAI in 2015, has said he holds no direct equity in the company, and his fortune comes largely from early investments in startups such as Stripe, Reddit and the nuclear energy company Helion. Separately, the Times of India reported that Altman told Vanity Fair, in an interview published on October 5, 2026, that he had not decided at what age his own children should use ChatGPT. At a US Senate hearing in May 2025, he said he did not want his son's best friend to be an AI bot, and he argued that children need stronger protections than adult users.

stories.Headline: Cloudflare Soars 20%, IREN Surges 15% as Earnings Beats Spark AI Cloud Rebound; CoreWeave Jumps 10%
stories.Summary:
Two strong earnings reports on November 5 pulled battered AI cloud stocks into a relief rally the next morning. Cloudflare shares traded at $293.43, up 20%, after the security and developer platform had fallen 17% over the prior month. IREN, a GPU cloud provider, rose 15% to $20.81, bouncing after a steep drop the session before during broad tech selling and a 50% slide over the past month. CoreWeave, which did not report this week, climbed 10% to $48.07, suggesting the company results fed a sector-wide rebound.

Cloudflare's third quarter revenue rose 39% from a year earlier to $782.5 million, ahead of the $738.3 million analysts expected. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.38 against a consensus of $0.34. For the full year, the company now expects revenue of $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion and adjusted EPS of $1.35, with fourth-quarter sales guided to $845 million to $846 million, above expectations. IREN's quarterly revenue reached $228 million, up from $137 million in the prior quarter, and its adjusted EBITDA of $66 million topped forecasts. Its AI Cloud sales jumped to $200 million from $71 million, and its net loss narrowed to $263 million from $684 million.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince called the quarter the company's best ever, and he now markets the business as the first agentic cloud. Even so, Cloudflare's GAAP net loss widened to $34.1 million from $1.3 million a year earlier, weighed down by $174.1 million in stock-based compensation. IREN said it has signed a five-year contract at $22 million per megawatt since quarter-end, with the customer prepaying 90% of the related GPU capital costs. A separate short-duration contract carries a rate of $40 million per megawatt. IREN's management says owning its land, power and data centers, much of it converted from crypto mining, lets it pace spending to funding conditions.

Risk appetite also got a lift from the October jobs report, which showed the U.S. adding 165,000 jobs, far above what economists surveyed by Bloomberg expected. Unemployment ticked down to 4.1%, September was revised up to 60,000 from 29,000, and monthly wage growth came in at 0.4% against a forecast of 0.3%. CoreWeave had dropped 48% over the past month on worries about its debt load, which pressured its bonds, and investors are also watching Nebius and Akamai. Cloudflare is aiming for GAAP profitability in the fourth quarter, while IREN must show whether more than $4 billion in annualized revenue run rate comes online by January 31, 2027, a target that could slip to the end of February. Bears point to IREN's $6 billion in planned spending that is still unfunded, CoreWeave's heavy debt and Cloudflare's lower free cash flow margin, while bulls cite rising contract prices, prepayments and Cloudflare's fastest revenue growth in nearly four years.

stories.Headline: IREN Sinks 9% After Report Links It to Microsoft's AI Spending Delay; Nebius Tumbles 11%, CoreWeave Slides 7%
stories.Summary:
On November 4, a report from The Information, citing unnamed sources, said delays at IREN's Childress campus in Texas led Microsoft to push back capital spending it had planned for the September quarter. Microsoft spent $5 billion less on capex than planned, though it is not clear how much of that gap came from IREN's delays. IREN stock fell about 9% to $19.70 on the news, while Nebius dropped 11% to $125.88 and CoreWeave slid 7% to $44.89. Cipher Digital also traded lower, and the moves came on top of losses in the prior session, when AI data center stocks sold off after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections.

The report matters because Childress sits at the center of IREN's shift from crypto mining to AI cloud services. IREN delivered Horizon 1, the first of four 50-megawatt liquid-cooled deployments for Microsoft, in August, and it has said it aims to have $4 billion of contracted annualized recurring revenue running by December 31. Its multiyear contract calls for Microsoft to spend $9.7 billion leasing GPU servers at Childress. IREN was due to report first-quarter fiscal 2027 results after the market close on November 5, which will test whether Horizons 2 through 4 stay on track for December.

Microsoft's own explanation came last week, when CFO Amy Hood said capital expenditures were $45.2 billion because some third-party capacity deliveries expected in the first quarter were delayed. She did not name IREN. Politics added a second layer of worry, since Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants an immediate moratorium on data centers in Texas, defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. Lawmakers could slow the build-out with a longer, costlier approval process, though an outright stop looks less likely. On Bloomberg Businessweek, Eric Weiner said hyperscale growth plans were built around Texas and Ohio, where new governors are there to block them, and that expectations have shifted from astronomical growth to incremental.

The wider selloff has been steep. From October 6 to November 6, CoreWeave fell 49.9% to $45.89 and Nebius fell 47.7% to $130.78, with both rebounding on November 6. CoreWeave carries heavy debt, with interest costs guided at $860 million to $940 million for the third quarter, and it reports on November 10. Nebius, which holds about $8 billion in cash, needs roughly $2.02 billion in second-half revenue to reach the low end of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion guidance and reports on November 12.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania may require lawyers, other court filers to verify AI-generated citations
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania's Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence, which advises the state Supreme Court, is considering a rule that would require lawyers and other court filers to certify that they checked the accuracy of citations and information in documents that used artificial intelligence. The proposal was published last month in the Pennsylvania Bulletin, the state's weekly gazette for proposed rules. Under it, filers who fail to comply could face sanctions ranging from a reprimand to fines to dismissal of a case. The committee's concern is that generative AI can produce inaccurate, misleading, or fabricated material, such as made-up legal citations or quotations.

The rule would apply to all court filers, including lawyers and people representing themselves. Filers would have to thoroughly review any AI-generated content before submitting it and certify that they did so. That review would cover summaries of legal principles as well as every legal citation and quote. In effect, the accuracy burden would fall on people rather than on the technology.

The public has until Nov. 24 to comment, after which the committee can revise the proposal or submit it as is to the court's seven justices for a vote. The Pennsylvania Bar Association has not yet taken a position on the proposal, a spokesperson said. The association and the Philadelphia Bar Association had already issued a joint opinion in 2024 offering guidance on using AI, including that lawyers should verify all AI-generated content. The Supreme Court created the advisory committee in 2024 to monitor AI use, and the following year the justices adopted an interim policy allowing judges and court staff to use AI for legal research, initial drafting, and readability editing.

That policy does not cover lawyers or others outside government, which is why the new proposal would extend oversight to all filers. The effort reflects a broader national problem. Courts across the country have dealt with filings containing false information, often called hallucinations, and over the summer a federal judge in Mississippi sanctioned lawyers on both sides of a civil case for filing fake citations, barring two of them from practicing in that district's federal court for two years. Spotlight PA reported that at least 13 Pennsylvania court cases in 2025 contained confirmed or implied AI hallucinations, including a high-profile gender discrimination case before an appellate court.

stories.Headline: AI-assisted learning platform helps robots reason beyond literal commands
stories.Summary:
MIT and New York University researchers have developed FLEX, an AI-assisted learning platform that lets robots read more into natural language commands than the literal words. The study, led by MIT assistant professor Andreea Bobu with co-authors Audrey Lee and Ilia Sucholutsky of New York University, is set to be presented at the annual Conference on Robot Learning this month. FLEX is a flexible feature-editing pipeline for robot motion planning, and the researchers tested it in simulations. The team describes the work as a way for people to talk to robots in everyday conversational language. In the simulated scenarios, a person types a command to a robotic arm, such as "Don't spill on the laptop!"

while the robot carries a coffee cup across a cluttered table. FLEX uses a large language model, an AI system trained on large amounts of text from the internet, to find broader patterns behind such instructions. Study author Nathan Dennler, a postdoc at MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, explains that the model has seen many accounts of liquids damaging devices, so it infers that electronics should be avoided. As a result, the robot changes its path to avoid both the laptop and a nearby phone without being told to. The platform works in three steps: "Add" a feature from the user's command, "Generalize" it with the language model, and "Mask" out objects no longer present, a process that takes about five seconds.

The researchers tested FLEX on three tasks: serving a cup of coffee, moving a candle, and carrying a bowling ball. Volunteers typed commands such as "Stay away from the stack of paper" and "Don't drop on the mug," and the robot followed them literally while also avoiding flammable objects and fragile items. Bobu, who heads the Collaborative Learning and Autonomy Research Lab at MIT, says the researchers are aiming for household and assistive robots that can adapt in real time to a person's preferences. Dennler notes that earlier methods required users to name every feature to avoid, which becomes tiresome and can leave outdated items on the list as environments change. The authors position FLEX as a way to avoid that burden by letting robots infer preferences from a sentence or two.

stories.Headline: 4 cheating cases using AI glasses caught at middle, high schools this year
stories.Summary:
The South Korean education ministry reported on Monday, November 9, 2026, that four students have been caught cheating with AI glasses at middle and high schools this year. The ministry collected data from all 5,679 middle and high schools nationwide between October 27 and the previous Tuesday, and found one middle school student and three high school students had used the glasses during midterm or final exams. Three of the students were caught repeatedly touching their glasses, while the fourth switched to AI glasses after the exam had started, and a proctor was watching him closely after another student tipped off the staff. Two of the high schools are in Seoul and North Jeolla Province, and the third is on Jeju Island, while the middle school is in Seoul.

All four students received zero scores on the affected exams, in line with the relevant rules. The three high school students also faced separate discipline, including three days of special education, four hours of community service, and a five-day suspension. The middle school student received no formal disciplinary action but was asked to do volunteer work on campus. The ministry plans to distribute educational materials that describe these cases to students and to issue guidelines that help schools prevent the misuse of AI glasses. It will also discuss further preventive steps with regional education offices and the Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation.

The ministry has already set a tougher line for the national college entrance exam. Anyone caught cheating on the College Scholastic Ability Test using AI glasses will face criminal charges and a three-year ban from the test, up from the current one-year ban. This year's test is scheduled for November 19. The ministry's announcement comes amid broader concern over how easily AI-enabled devices can be used to get around exam rules, and the articles do not describe any further steps beyond those already listed.

stories.Headline: AI Deepfakes of CEOs and Lawyers Stole $129 Million, Prosecutors Say
stories.Summary:
Three men are charged in a federal indictment unsealed November 5 in Manhattan with using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate chief executives and attorneys at large law firms. Prosecutors say the group persuaded employees at hospitals, a bank and other companies to wire more than $129 million into accounts it controlled between 2024 and early 2026. The defendants are Jacob Soall, 41, of Marbella, Spain, Sharon Hazan, 54, of Israel, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, of Israel and the United Arab Emirates. Spanish police arrested Soall in June and Hazan in August, Britain's National Crime Agency detained Sheetrit in September, and U.S. extradition requests for all three are pending.

The scheme typically began with an email that appeared to come from a company's chief executive, asking for help with a confidential deal. Employees then received calls in which the group allegedly used AI to copy the executive's voice and, in some cases, face, before handing them to a fake lawyer who borrowed the name of a real attorney at a major firm. The indictment says a handwritten script titled "Lawyer Call" was used to discourage employees from discussing the transaction with colleagues. Victims named by their losses include a British financial technology company, which lost about $11.6 million, a Florida pet food maker, a Massachusetts mutual fund company, a Missouri hospital system and a Rhode Island bank. The money moved through accounts in several countries before being converted into cryptocurrency and divided among the conspirators.

Each defendant faces seven counts, including wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering, with a combined maximum of 104 years in prison. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald urged businesses to consider how to guard against what he called the emerging threat of AI-enabled crime. Prosecutors say Hazan, who was convicted of bank fraud conspiracy in the same court in 2008, boasted of laundering more than $400 million in three years. These are allegations, and none of the three has been convicted. The FBI has asked anyone who believes they were targeted to contact the bureau through its online tips page.

The case is a reminder of how much the scheme depended on trust in a familiar voice rather than on hacking. The losses are roughly five times the $25.6 million that British engineering firm Arup lost in 2024 after an employee joined a video call with a deepfake of its finance chief. The indictment also reports that one attempted transfer of about $2.85 million from a major New York investment bank was stopped by the bank's back office before it left. Prosecutors have not said how much of the money has been recovered, and the extradition process for all three defendants is still pending.

stories.Headline: Democrat shaping AI policy bought chip stocks despite backing congressional trading ban
stories.Summary:
Rep. Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat who helps write his party's artificial intelligence agenda, has disclosed new purchases of AI-linked stocks, CNBC reported on Nov. 7. A filing received by the House Clerk on Nov. 4 shows a purchase of Benchmark Electronics stock on Oct. 12 and Applied Materials stock on Oct. 26, each worth between $1,001 and $15,000. Both were made in a jointly owned Morgan Stanley account, which had earlier bought three lots of Advanced Micro Devices shares. The same filing lists a sale of PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia stock. The purchases came just months after he voted to bar lawmakers and their families from buying individual stocks.

The Stop Insider Trading Act, which would prohibit members and their families from buying most individual stocks, passed the House on July 22, but it has not become law. Gottheimer was one of only 13 Democrats to vote for it, while some Democrats objected to a voter-ID provision attached to it. Four years earlier, he backed legislation requiring lawmakers to use blind trusts and pledged to set one up himself. The five AI-linked trades CNBC counted were worth between $5,005 and $75,000 in total, which is small beside the household's disclosed assets of $15.1 million to $59 million, including up to $44.5 million in stocks.

Filings show the AMD buys were made in April and May, before the vote, and that an Applied Materials position was bought in August and sold in September before the October repurchase. Gottheimer's spokesman, Haraden Bottomley, said the congressman handed control of his investments to a third party with full investment discretion before taking office in 2017. He added that Gottheimer is awaiting congressional approval of a blind trust and has meanwhile set up an independent trust. Gottheimer, a former Microsoft executive, sits on the House Financial Services subcommittee that oversees AI in finance, has introduced AI regulation legislation, and co-chairs a commission developing Democrats' broader AI agenda.

CNBC noted there is no evidence of wrongdoing. His household has reported more than 1,100 securities transactions over three years. The disclosures draw fresh attention because Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January, which will give them new power to investigate and regulate the AI industry. Reps.

Maxine Waters and Greg Casar have introduced a resolution opposing taxpayer bailouts for AI companies, referred in part to Gottheimer's committee, and Casar has called for AI executives to testify under oath. The purchases came shortly before a sharp selloff, in which the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on Thursday, with Nvidia down more than 9% and AMD down about 17%. Benchmark fell nearly 17% over Wednesday and Thursday to close at $59.34, roughly 25% below its price on the day of Gottheimer's purchase, before recovering somewhat on Friday. Applied Materials was Benchmark's largest disclosed customer in 2025, making up 14% of its revenue.

stories.Headline: China reiterates support for live-action micro-dramas, vows to regulate AI productions as actors seek new opportunities amid industry shifts
stories.Summary:
China's National Radio and Television Administration (NRTA) has recently reiterated its support for live-action micro-dramas while promising tighter oversight of AI-generated productions. The regulator has called on platforms to ensure that all content is reviewed before release and undergoes full human review. It has also pledged to step up efforts against AI-assisted plagiarism, unauthorized remakes, and the unauthorized use of people's likenesses and voices. The announcement came at the 2026 Conference on Creation of High-Quality Product in Radio and Television of China, where an NRTA official spoke about the changes under way.

The official said AI is doing more than cutting production costs and speeding up work in micro-dramas. It is reshaping production methods, industry structures and development models across the whole chain, from scriptwriting and filming to distribution and overseas operations. The official stressed that AI should serve as a tool for high-quality creation, with people remaining at the center of the creative process. The official also said AI can generate images but cannot generate lived experience, so human actors' emotional expression remains essential. Technology, the official argued, should not replace human thought and creativity.

For actors, the shift is already changing job prospects and career choices. Yin Jiaxuan, 25, entered the micro-drama industry in mid-2024 after working as a theme park character, and he now takes more work at tourist attractions and live performances as filming opportunities decline. He told the Global Times that some experienced screen actors are moving into cultural tourism and commercial live performances, and that some attractions prefer them for handling spontaneous interactions with visitors. Yin said the drop in acting work cannot be blamed on AI alone, since shrinking film and television investment, fewer productions entering filming and changing platform policies have also played a part. Cultural researcher Zhang Peng of Nanjing Normal University told the Global Times that AI's impact on live-action actors is likely to be structural rather than a direct replacement of human performance.

Zhang attributed the rapid growth of AI-generated micro-dramas mainly to lower costs for filming, post-production and special effects, along with audience demand for fast-paced, plot-dense storytelling on short-video platforms. He said the technology could open new niches such as customized advertising, interactive dramas and IP spin-offs, while encouraging human-AI collaboration. He also warned that without clear rules on the use of celebrities' likenesses, including the scope of authorization, the duration of use and revenue sharing, control over likenesses and fair distribution of revenue could become contested, with ordinary actors facing added pressure. The NRTA official reiterated the regulator's commitment to continuing its crackdown on unauthorized use of likenesses and voices and related abuses.

stories.Headline: SRA AI Guidance for Law Firms: What the Regulator Says in 2026
stories.Summary:
Solicitors in England and Wales received a formal warning from the Solicitors Regulation Authority on 17 August 2026 about the misuse of artificial intelligence. The "Misuse of AI" warning notice was prompted by 42 reports of possible AI misuse received between July 2025 and July 2026, with open investigations covering inaccurate citations, weak supervision and confidentiality lapses. The regulator has not written new AI rules. Instead it says existing duties apply whatever tool a solicitor uses, and it has tied those duties to two specific risks: fictitious cases or citations reaching a court, and client information being entered into AI tools without safeguards.

The notice makes clear that the solicitor stays fully accountable for any AI output, since the technology has no separate legal personality. Before any named case goes to a court, the solicitor must confirm it is genuine, relevant and has a verifiable citation, and reliance on an AI output is not a defence. Public AI tools used with client information will likely breach confidentiality and may waive legal professional privilege permanently. Client data should remain in a secure environment, should not train models without authority, and should not be kept longer than necessary. Solicitors who ignore the notice face the risk of disciplinary action.

The SRA's June 2026 update to its effective supervision guidance added a section on AI, stating that AI-assisted work needs appropriate human review, scrutiny and professional judgement, and that an authorised individual keeps ultimate responsibility for it. The regulator, whose Executive Director of Strategy and Policy is Aileen Armstrong, has said that the use of AI does not change the professional standards expected of solicitors and firms. Its current chief executive, Sarah Rapson, has also said that innovation has an important role in improving legal services. The regulator supports AI use: it authorised Garfield.Law, an AI-driven litigation assistant, in May 2025 under strict conditions, and joined the government-backed Advisory AI Growth Lab in 2026.

The position sits alongside a wider set of rulings and guidance. In the Divisional Court's June 2025 judgment in Ayinde and Al-Haroun, the court referred lawyers who cited non-existent cases to the SRA and the Bar Standards Board and said reliance on generative tools does not excuse checking authorities. The Law Society and the Bar Council have issued their own AI guidance, and the Civil Justice Council's October 2026 final report recommends declarations from witnesses and experts where AI has shaped their evidence, though those proposals are not yet in force. Comparable US guidance from the American Bar Association reaches similar conclusions on checking and supervision but goes further on client consent and billing.

stories.Headline: Province-wide protests call for moratorium on AI data centre proposals in N.S.
stories.Summary:
Nearly 1,000 Nova Scotians marched through downtown Halifax on Saturday, November 7, 2026, to protest a proposed artificial intelligence data centre in southern Cape Breton. The crowd gathered in front of the provincial legislature at noon and filled an entire block of Hollis Street before moving through the city's core. Organizers said it was one of at least seven protests held across the province that day. The demonstrators called for a moratorium on all large-scale AI data centre proposals in Nova Scotia.

The protest followed an announcement last month by Everwind Fuels that it plans to lease a data centre in Point Tupper to the U.S. AI company Anthropic. Everwind describes the project as a $10-billion investment, the largest private investment in provincial history. Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for the 18,600-square-metre facility, which will power its Claude assistant. The centre is expected to come online in 2027 and draw 95 megawatts in its first phase, with a 325-megawatt expansion scheduled for mid-2028 that would raise total demand to 420 megawatts. Water from Landrie Lake will cool the servers, averaging 100,000 litres a day at first and 500,000 litres a day later.

Ned Zimmerman, a tech worker from Dartmouth and one of the rally's organizers, argued that large-scale AI data centres are socially destructive and environmentally irresponsible. He said the community was not consulted until the project was announced, and that the provincial guidelines are not enough for a project of this size. Everwind says it will cover the cost of all electricity infrastructure and that the project will not raise power rates. A statement from Premier Tim Houston's office said the centre will proceed only if it meets provincial and federal guidelines. Everwind did not respond to a request for comment about the protest.

The protesters are also concerned about the absence of an environmental impact assessment, and Nova Scotia's Environment Minister, Timothy Halman, said an industrial approval is the more appropriate tool for this type of project. Houston has said he does not know whether new legislation is needed, but his office said the province would consider changes if necessary. A petition on Change.org against AI data centres in the province had garnered nearly 28,000 signatures. Rebecca Lawrence, who attended the Halifax rally, said the government should listen to Nova Scotians, many of whom oppose these facilities.

stories.Headline: SoftBank to face scrutiny of AI strategy at second-quarter earnings after selloff
stories.Summary:
The technology selloff of the past week put pressure on the companies financing artificial intelligence's expansion, though their latest spending plans show little sign of an immediate pullback. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% on Thursday, Nov. 5, as higher borrowing costs and the prospect of restrictions on data center construction fed worries about an AI bubble. Stocks recovered some ground on Friday. The turbulence has left open how quickly AI investments will pay off. These market losses reduce stock values rather than directly draining corporate cash, though a prolonged decline could make raising equity more costly and push companies to conserve cash.

A selloff does not automatically cancel chip orders or construction contracts. For now, the clearest guide is the spending commitments companies laid out before the drop. Alphabet kept its 2026 capital expenditure forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion in its October earnings call, and its CFO, Anat Ashkenazi, said spending would increase significantly in 2027. Alphabet also reported negative quarterly free cash flow of $9.1 billion.

Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in quarterly capital expenditures, which its CFO, Amy Hood, said came in below expectations because of delayed capacity deliveries. The company still generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow. CEO Satya Nadella told analysts, "We are building against a growing book of business." Microsoft also priced a $25 billion debt offering on Oct. 29, with closing set for Nov. 4, and the article notes that financing came before Thursday's decline.

Meta forecast $135 billion to $145 billion in annual capital expenditures and reported negative quarterly free cash flow of $2.1 billion, and its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, said the investments were paying off. SpaceX announced on Oct. 26 a roughly $40 billion lease commitment covering Nvidia chips and related equipment, with closing subject to conditions and deliveries expected in the first half of 2027. Investment professionals see room between continued acceleration and a sharp collapse in spending. Tim Nyland of Synergy Asset Management anticipated a gradual slowdown in the growth of AI capital commitments and actual spending, while Schwab Asset Management's Omar Aguilar stressed the strength of major AI investors but voiced concern about their growing reliance on debt.

The article frames three possible paths: sustained customer demand despite weaker share prices, phased projects that favor revenue-generating products, or costlier financing and construction limits that force longer delays. The article presents these as scenarios rather than announced responses to Thursday's trading, and it notes they need not affect every company equally. For banks, payments companies and retailers buying AI services, the practical question is whether providers deliver promised capacity at workable prices. The next spending forecasts, the article suggests, will show whether market pressure changes deployment schedules, investment priorities or only the explanations executives give investors.

stories.Headline: NAVER's $9 Billion AI Factory Is Built on a Fee Contract Banks Can Lend Against
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA paid $1 billion for a 4.13% stake in NAVER on November 6, completing the final step of a deal that began with a condition. The chipmaker would invest only after NAVER secured at least $9 billion in separate committed financing for computing infrastructure. Brookfield signed that infrastructure agreement with NAVER on October 27. The headline frames this as an equity story, but the articles describe a credit structure underneath it.

Under that structure, a Brookfield-funded company will buy the GPUs and data center assets and lease computing to NAVER Cloud. NAVER Cloud will run the facilities and pay usage fees, which NAVER says are tied to its business revenue. Korean banks plan to lend against those fees, with KB Kookmin Bank announcing on November 1 a mandate to arrange about KRW 10.7 trillion of loans for a KRW 12.6 trillion project. Hana Bank, Shinhan Bank, Woori Bank and NH Investment & Securities are reported as participants, though final commitments have not been disclosed. NAVER also guarantees NAVER Cloud's fee obligations for up to eight years, with a nominal amount of KRW 18.74 trillion, but the guarantee does not cover the syndicated loan itself.

The articles also set out the capacity plan and what remains unsettled. At the GAK Sejong data center, capacity is staged at 55 MW in the first half of 2027, 100 MW by the end of 2027 and 200 MW in 2028, within a wider project NAVER describes as a 1-gigawatt-scale global AI factory. NAVER issued a little over 6.5 million new shares on November 6, raising about KRW 1.3 trillion. The articles say the fee formula, including any minimum payment and how fees move when sales are slow, is not disclosed. NAVER is expected to consolidate the Brookfield-owned company as a subsidiary under K-IFRS, so its borrowings and assets would appear in NAVER's own accounts.

NAVER has not named customers for the capacity, though it targets enterprise and government clients in Asia, Europe and the Middle East. In October, NAVER Cloud and Vietnam's FPT announced cooperation on AI factories and GPU-as-a-service across Asia-Pacific. The articles say no purchase commitment for this capacity has been disclosed. Separately, NVIDIA and NAVER are expanding their AI model work, with NAVER Cloud taking part in NVIDIA's Nemotron Alliance and using related technology for its HyperCLOVA X model, according to a November 9 report.

stories.Headline: How AI is transforming customer experience
stories.Summary:
Customer experience at contact centers is being reshaped by artificial intelligence, according to a May 2026 NTT DATA perspective by Sashen Naidu, who heads the firm's global CX practice. The piece argues that contact centers, long treated as a fixed cost to be trimmed, can instead act as real-time intelligence hubs that inform business decisions. In a typical scenario, a customer calling about a delayed delivery would be routed directly to the right system, sometimes without any human involvement, and agents who do take the call would receive context and suggested actions. The article presents this as a shift away from fragmented systems and manual processes.

The article describes several specific effects. NTT DATA's own observations suggest that 60% to 70% of routine interactions, such as checking balances or tracking orders, can be handled by conversational AI without a human. Beyond that, the "agent-assist" model is said to cut query handling time and make responses more consistent, since agents spend less time switching between systems. Customer interactions can also be analyzed at scale to spot sentiment and recurring problems in real time, and the technology can move service from reactive to proactive, such as warning customers about network outages or flagging unusual account activity before fraud occurs. The author adds that continuous learning requires cloud platforms, consolidated data and strong governance, and that human oversight remains essential for compliance, fairness and trust.

Separately, a Microsoft customer story from November 2026 describes how Banco Hipotecario, an Argentine mortgage lender, moved its Dynamics 365 customer relationship system from on-premises servers to the cloud. The migration ran from 2023 to 2025 and was carried out in-house with support from Microsoft FastTrack and Unified Support. The bank previously could not connect its CRM to cloud services, faced delayed incident detection, and had customers who had to email, call or visit a branch to file complaints. After the move, it built two Copilot Studio agents, an internal assistant called MAIA that answers employee questions and an external agent called DynaBot, which was still preparing for launch and will take complaints and account requests through WhatsApp and Microsoft Teams.

The bank's Head of CRM, Rodrigo Espinosa, credits the cloud foundation with enabling faster answers and a more agile bank, while Technical Lead Pablo Ruggieri says the tools bring employee tasks together in one channel and should improve customer satisfaction scores. The story reports that Net Promoter Score rose 114% between June and September 2025, that database storage fell 92%, and that internal tests showed DynaBot cut average case creation time by 80%. It also says incident resolution improved by at least 24 hours. The two accounts describe the same trend from different angles: AI agents handling routine work while human staff focus on complex cases, with the main outcomes still being reported internally by the companies involved.

stories.Headline: Anthropic secures $3.4 billion generator deal for AI data centers, FT reports - CNA
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI startup, has reportedly agreed to a deal worth about $3.4 billion to secure gas-fired power generators for its data centers. The Financial Times reported the arrangement on Sunday, November 8, 2026, and the account was echoed by Reuters and CNBC. According to the report, Anthropic bought commitments in late September for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty generators from OnePWR Solutions, an equipment supplier based in San Antonio, Texas. The deal gives the company access to the generating capacity it needs to run its computing operations.

The report says Anthropic did not acquire OnePWR itself, and none of the supplier's employees moved over to the AI company. The agreement did, however, include the engineering and construction capabilities needed to install the generators, according to a person familiar with the matter, whom the report cited. That detail matters because it means the startup secured not only the equipment but also the know-how to get it running. The arrangement fits a broader pattern in which companies building large AI systems are seeking reliable power as well as chips and servers. The articles do not say how the power will be delivered beyond the generators themselves.

Reuters said it could not immediately verify the report, and neither Anthropic nor OnePWR responded to requests for comment. As a result, the terms and figures come from the Financial Times account and the unnamed source it relied on, not from an official statement by either company. The articles offer no direct remarks from the companies on the deal's purpose or timing. Their silence leaves the details open to confirmation as more information emerges.

The context offered in the coverage centers on demand for Anthropic's Claude family of AI models, which has pushed the company to secure additional computing and power capacity. stories.Headline: How to get started with AI agents, which are best for specific tasks
stories.Summary:
The Associated Press published a guide on November 8, 2026, by technology writer Kaitlyn Huamani, aimed at people new to AI agents, which it described as tools designed to work proactively on a user's behalf for tasks such as buying groceries or managing to-do lists. The guide says these agents have taken off in 2026, with companies including Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic competing in the consumer market. It notes that the leading AI labs have offered agentic tools for years, but the new consumer-facing agents only recently gained wide popularity. The article's purpose is to help readers sort out the differences among the offerings and decide which agents suit particular jobs.

The guide recommends that beginners not rely on a single agent but instead build a "stack" of several tools from different companies, since, as business consultant Jose Artigas put it, no single agent does everything. Clara Gigling, founder of Oudae Labs, described a system in which one agent does the work and another critiques it, so the mistakes get caught. The article points out that agents differ in price, with some free, some requiring a monthly subscription, and some still in testing or unavailable outside the United States. It also says each company markets its agent differently, with Anthropic's Claude Duet aimed at professionals and small business owners, and Meta's Muse aimed at everyday tasks like saving money and shopping. Artigas suggested Muse as a starting point for novices because it is user-friendly.

Experts quoted in the article advise readers to test agents through trial and error, starting with a specific, repeated online chore that they have been putting off, such as a long email or a flight booking. The article notes that agents work best when given a detailed goal along with the context and tools to reach it, and that they cannot handle physical chores. It also warns that agents typically need access to a great deal of personal data, including email, calendars, identification details and financial information, which has raised privacy concerns. Gigling urged users to be mindful when sharing such information, while noting that many companies now publish privacy policies explaining how their agents run on dedicated cloud computers and how users can control memory retention.

stories.Headline: From Fake CEO Calls To Garland Police Briefings: Texas And Federal Moves Against AI Impersonation
stories.Summary:
Federal prosecutors in New York unsealed charges on November 5 against Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42. The Justice Department alleges that the three and their co-conspirators targeted companies around the world between 2024 and 2026, using artificial intelligence to imitate corporate executives and lawyers. According to the indictment, the scheme stole more than $129 million from businesses, including hospital systems and financial firms. Conspirators allegedly posed as chief executives, used synthetic voices or images on calls, and sent employees to supposed attorneys who directed large wire transfers into accounts they controlled.

Authorities arrested the defendants in Spain and the United Kingdom between June and September, and extradition requests were still pending when the charges were announced. President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14390 on March 6, directing agencies to develop measures against international scam centers and cyber-enabled financial fraud. The order calls for stronger coordination, prosecution priorities, and recommendations for returning money to victims from recovered criminal proceeds. On November 5, the Justice Department also announced a Super Intelligence Task Force to address malicious uses of emerging technology by foreign actors and transnational criminal groups.

The FBI warned in July that criminals had used AI-generated videos resembling FBI personnel to lure earlier fraud victims toward fake Internet Crime Complaint Center websites, where impostors promised to recover lost money while collecting more personal information. The Justice Department has not said the task force has already stopped any such fraud. Texas has taken its own legal steps. Senate Bill 2373 took effect September 1, 2025, criminalizing specified financial abuse carried out with artificially generated media or phishing, and it creates a civil route for certain victims to seek damages.

House Bill 149, the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, took effect January 1, 2026, setting rules for specified AI uses, including certain government and health care disclosures, and giving the attorney general enforcement authority. Neither law bans every synthetic voice or image. Closer to home, Garland police scheduled a November 5 presentation at the West Garland Library on deceptive calls, messages, and AI voice cloning. The FBI advises people to verify unexpected requests through a previously trusted phone number, to use multi-factor authentication, and to be cautious with unsolicited links.

stories.Headline: Voters Pull the Plug on Big Tech's AI Data Center Boom
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 3, 2026, voters across the United States turned down data center development in nearly every local ballot contest on the subject. Ballotpedia tallied 41 local measures in 10 states that would limit data center construction in various ways, and the New York Times counted 40 of the 41 going against the industry. The Detroit News reported that voters in at least 29 jurisdictions passed bans or restrictions. The lone exception was in Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected a charter amendment that would have required extra review before the city approved industrial developments, including data centers.

The measures took different forms, from outright bans to a 180-day moratorium to limits on a site's electricity or water use. In Maine, voters approved a retroactive moratorium, in Florida they approved a charter ban on new data centers within the city, and in Ohio they rejected a development and supply agreement with EdgeConneX, all of which count as votes to restrict. Restrictions won an average of more than 70% support. The strongest result came in Morgan County, Illinois, where 88.3% of the 10,663 votes cast went against data center development, while the narrowest was in Sprigg Township, Adams County, Ohio, at 52.6%. In Ohio, 21 municipalities used local ballot measures or referendums to try to block proposed facilities.

Polling pointed the same way. An NBC News exit poll found that 76% of voters opposed building a new data center in their community, a figure the Associated Press also reported at roughly three-quarters. The same poll found 23% calling data centers crucial to their vote for Congress and 33% calling them a major factor, which adds up to 56%. The AP described the narrower finding as about one-quarter of voters calling them crucial. Voters in both Republican and Democratic areas cited electricity costs, water use, noise, pollution, and the conversion of farmland and open space.

The projects at issue were proposed by technology companies building facilities to power their artificial intelligence platforms, and the articles do not quote any company responding to the results. One article, from Legal Insurrection via Watts Up With That, argued that China was the biggest winner of the election, noting that X said it had removed a suspected network of roughly 200,000 inauthentic Chinese accounts, about 200 of which amplified coordinated anti-AI messaging aimed at US audiences. That article also said the concerns should be met with better engineering and more attention to local needs rather than surrendering America's technological future. Shattered.io cautioned that the polling shows opposition to facilities in voters' own communities, not a blanket rejection of all data centers, and that salience does not show how many votes actually moved. It also noted that a local ban can stop a new facility without touching existing ones, and the articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Has Wales already lost the AI revolution?
stories.Summary:
Wales has been slow to capture the growth of artificial intelligence businesses, according to new UK Government research published last week. The Artificial Intelligence Sector Study 2025 identifies 10,488 AI businesses across the UK, generating £33.6 billion in revenues and employing more than 130,000 people. Wales accounts for just 1.6% of these firms, well behind Scotland at 3.7% and the North West of England at 5.9%. The gap is especially striking because generative AI, which took off after ChatGPT appeared in November 2022, gave regions a chance to build new economic strengths relatively quickly. The writer, Dylan Jones-Evans, argues that Wales had real assets to build on, including talented researchers, established universities and expertise in semiconductors, cybersecurity and financial technology.

He notes that AI firms do not need expensive factories, so small teams with modest funding can compete internationally. He suggests Wales could have launched a national programme in early 2023 to identify and invest in hundreds of new AI businesses. Instead, he says, the Welsh Government's AI Plan arrived in November 2025, almost three years after ChatGPT's launch. The Welsh Government has since announced £2.1 million to support AI adoption, including £600,000 for Business Wales, £1 million for skills development and £500,000 for tourism and events. The writer welcomes these measures but points out that they mainly help existing companies use AI rather than create businesses that develop and sell the technology.

In his view, that distinction matters, because a Welsh firm building AI products for global markets could generate jobs, intellectual property, exports and wealth on a far larger scale. He places responsibility on the Welsh Government, Business Wales and the Development Bank, which he says must act if Wales is to change course. The article frames the situation as a warning rather than a settled verdict, arguing that the window is still open. The writer's central point is that adoption support and business creation are both useful but serve different ends, and that Wales has so far leaned towards the former. The articles do not set out a detailed timetable for further action or any new targets beyond the existing funding and plans.

stories.Headline: Christopher Nolan Previews DGA’s Next Phase of AI Protections: ‘It’s Down to the Studios’
stories.Summary:
Christopher Nolan, who has been president of the Directors Guild of America since fall 2025, spoke on the Hollywood Insiders podcast on Saturday, November 7, 2026, about the guild's fight against artificial intelligence in film and television. He praised the DGA and the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers for negotiating what he called excellent language and guardrails on AI in production. He also said the next challenge, protecting copyrighted work from AI, rests mainly with the studios. His remarks were reported by TheWrap and Deadline in articles published on November 7 and 8, 2026.

Nolan said the guild is focused on holding studios accountable for protecting their copyrights, but that the DGA cannot do this itself because, with very few exceptions, its members do not hold the copyrights to the films they work on. He argued that "AI" is too broad a term, one that companies use to avoid responsibility by portraying the technology as an uncontrollable force. He said existing laws already protect creators and that companies hiding behind fair use arguments will not hold up in court in the long run, pointing to some significant judgments already issued against that defense. He also said he was pleased that the closing credits of his film The Odyssey, from Universal, include for the first time a notice stating the film cannot be ingested or used as AI training data.

Nolan compared this principle to the long-settled rules on sampling music, saying that taking another's work, feeding it into a machine, and selling the output even in disguised form should not count as fair use. He acknowledged the matter will have to be settled through courts and legislation, and that it will take a long time. Deadline reported that Nolan had earlier said the guild needs a voice in how AI tools are used and in shaping the legal framework, because members' residuals depend on how their work is monetized. He described the effort as an ongoing fight rather than one with a fixed endpoint.

stories.Headline: Here’s a look into student and faculty opinions on AI use
stories.Summary:
Some professors at San Diego State University and Penn are mixing firm bans with cautious openness about AI, according to recent campus reporting. The Daily Aztec reported that SDSU partnered with OpenAI to give students free ChatGPT memberships, and that Google Gemini held a two-day pop-up on campus. The same report noted that the California State University system's annual AI survey, run by researchers David Goldberg and Elisa Sobo, was most recently collected in 2025. It also said that 49 percent of American adults report using AI chatbots, and 66 percent of those users are between 18 and 29.

The survey found that students in SDSU's Colleges of Professional Studies and Fine Arts, Arts and Letters, and Education reported the lowest rates of AI use, while the Fowler College of Business reported the highest. Among Fowler business students, 80.5 percent agreed that AI will play a significant role in their future careers. At Penn, the Daily Pennsylvanian reported that its PennChat portal, launched in July after a pilot phase finished a month later, gives members access to select Claude and ChatGPT models within the university's network. Penn's technology leader, Tiffany Hanulec, said the portal has nearly 6,000 registered users and that web search and image generation have been added. Penn's guidance asks users to avoid entering identifiable health information unless it is necessary for the task.

At SDSU, professors take very different positions on AI in their courses. John Francis, a management professor, bars generative AI in his course unless the instructor approves it, but he argues that rules should focus on using AI well in professional settings. Eunice Uhm, an art history professor, bars AI-generated ideas or writing submitted as a student's own, and she argues that such tools are not ethically situated or intellectually committed. Benjamin Gonzalez O'Brien, a political science professor, says any generative AI use violates his academic honesty policy. Crosby Noricks, a public relations professor, takes a middle path, treating AI as a baseline research skill while keeping academic honesty expectations.

At Penn, professors and students are similarly divided over the portal's value and risks. Matthew O'Donnell, an Annenberg lecturer, sees PennChat as a potentially useful teaching tool because it could make AI use easier to track and document. Etienne Jacquot, an Annenberg systems administrator, stressed that enterprise licenses keep university data under the university's control, while commercial subscriptions may use the data for training. Engineering senior Thomas Fanjul said he prefers PennChat for document work but rarely uses it because it requires Penn's Wi-Fi or a VPN connection. Both campuses' reporting suggests the debate over AI policy is likely to keep evolving as the technology spreads through professional fields.

stories.Headline: SK hynix to expand U.S. workforce to deepen ties with key clients
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, a South Korean chipmaker, is preparing to expand its U.S. workforce, according to its parent company SK Group, which made the announcement on Monday, November 9, 2026. The move appears aimed at strengthening ties with major American clients, including Nvidia Corp. The company plans additional executive appointments and a reorganization of its U.S. operations around December 3. The timing follows a recent executive reshuffle at SK Group, a Korean conglomerate with interests in semiconductors, construction and other sectors. SK hynix had created a new executive-level post to oversee its U.S. operations and named Ahn Hyun, its president in charge of development, to fill it. Ahn has led development of artificial intelligence memory products, including high bandwidth memory, known as HBM.

The appointment represents a change in how the company manages its U.S. business, which has traditionally been run by executives with sales and marketing backgrounds. Industry sources said the shift reflects how HBM contracts are now won, since memory makers increasingly work with customers from the early stages of product development to tailor chips to their AI infrastructure. An industry insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said companies can no longer stay competitive without close collaboration with customers from the research and development stage. The articles attribute the plans to SK Group, which confirmed the expansion and the timing of the executive appointments and reorganization. The articles do not name a specific individual who made the decision beyond the appointment of Ahn Hyun.

The industry insider's comments were given without attribution, so the view is presented as coming from unnamed sources. The company itself is described as a major supplier in the AI memory market, where its customers include Nvidia. The reporting places the expansion within a broader context of rising demand for AI chips and closer cooperation between memory suppliers and their largest customers. The articles do not say what size the expanded U.S. workforce will reach or how many new positions will be created. They also do not describe the outcome of the December 3 reorganization, which remains a planned step.

stories.Headline: Camerimage Opens With a Robot, an AI Reckoning and a Minute of Silence for Kraków
stories.Summary:
The Camerimage Film Festival opened on Saturday in Toruń, Poland, with artificial intelligence as its central theme. In place of festival director Marek Żydowicz, a humanoid robot called Edward Warchocki gave the opening address and then took part in a long conversation with Żydowicz about AI's role in cinema. The festival also began with a minute of silence for the victims of a mass shooting in Kraków earlier that day. Local politicians acknowledged the attack before the program started.

The opening ceremony at the Jordanki Culture Centre lasted three hours and included video messages on AI in entertainment from Francis Ford Coppola, Gal Gadot, Christopher Nolan, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Steven Spielberg and Ben Affleck. Darren Aronofsky received the festival's honorary Award for Director, and he is a strong supporter of generative AI since launching his studio Primordial Soup last year. He said it was his third visit to the festival and praised it for honoring everyone who makes films possible. Karolina Gruszka and Janusz Kamiński also received awards during the evening.

The opening film, Luca Guadagnino's Artificial, continued the AI theme. Guadagnino and cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed discussed the film on stage, and Sayeed described AI as just a tool, like any other. Guadagnino, who shot the film on 35 mm, said its real subject is the economic and political power that tech leaders have gained over people's lives. Neon will release Artificial in the United States on December 25.

The festival was overshadowed by the Kraków shooting. According to reports, at least six people were killed and more than a dozen injured when a gunman suspected of far-right ties drove into the city's historic Main Market Square and opened fire. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three more bodies were later found at the suspect's home, making it Poland's deadliest shooting in decades. Camerimage runs through November 14.

IBM's stock slipped 0.1% on a Friday, a move that media coverage did not tie to any clear company-specific catalyst. Meanwhile, the day brought several developments: a new quantum error-correction platform, a quantum system commissioned in Chicago, and the general availability of identity controls for AI agents. Taken together, these items painted a much busier picture than the flat share price suggested. On the research side, IBM is building a joint platform for quantum error correction with AMD and the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The setup connects IBM quantum hardware, including its 120-qubit Nighthawk processor, to Oak Ridge's Umbra high-performance computing system, which runs on AMD chips.

The effort is placed under the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission. Separately, IBM unveiled its first quantum system in Illinois, the IBM Quantum System Two, which is already operating at Hyde Park Labs and is slated to move to the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park once that campus is finished. On the AI side, IBM made Agent Identity generally available in watsonx Orchestrate on a Tuesday, giving AI agents their own identities along with audit logs and a kill switch. The launch builds on controls IBM announced about two weeks earlier, spanning HashiCorp Vault and watsonx Orchestrate, which covered access controls and tools to detect, contain and assess agents. IBM-owned Confluent also announced its Streamhouse architecture, aimed at keeping business context current for AI agents, applications and analytics.

Roughly two weeks ago, IBM and the USTA extended their partnership by five years, keeping IBM as the official AI and cloud partner of the US Open through 2031. The articles do not say that any of these announcements moved the share price, and they describe the stock's slight dip as muted and unexplained. The U.S. Open partners reported that the tournament's digital offerings recorded more than 270 million interactions in 2026. The articles give no further guidance on what comes next for these projects, beyond the planned relocation of the Illinois system and the wider rollout of agent controls.

stories.Headline: Apple plans to turn Siri into an AI agent with new iPhone updates: Report
stories.Summary:
Apple is reportedly pressing its software team to turn Siri into a more capable AI agent, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, as the company works to catch up with rivals. CEO John Ternus is said to be pushing Craig Federighi, the company's AI chief, to accelerate Siri's roadmap so it can compete with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse. The report says Federighi's team has already shipped a working version of Siri AI on what insiders called an incredibly short timeline. Insiders also describe Apple executives as privately admitting that they are not keeping pace with rivals whose agents can perform multi-step tasks on their own. The report, published on November 8, 2026, marks an unusual acknowledgment of vulnerability from a company that typically sets the industry's tempo.

Two significant upgrades are reportedly headed to Siri in the coming months. The first would give the assistant granular control over Apple's native apps, such as rotating and cropping images in Photos, organizing Safari tabs by topic, or managing Mail workflows with less prompting from the user. The second wave would push further into automation, though the report gives no specifics on it. The article notes that Apple has not announced release dates for these features. Building such an agent is difficult for Apple because modern agents need broad access to user data and coordination across apps, which conflicts with the company's privacy-first approach.

The pressure is coming from the top of the company, with Ternus reportedly demanding a competitive agent rather than incremental gains. The article notes that OpenAI recently closed an $11 billion funding round valuing it at $1.25 trillion, and that its Dots agent can book travel and manage schedules with minimal input. Meta has been rolling out Muse across its apps, and Amazon has launched its own text-to-shop Alexa feature after blocking Muse from its platform. Apple has also begun integrating ChatGPT support into its HomeView smart hub, which the article presents as a sign that the company will partner with rivals when its own technology lags. Observers cited in the piece argue that Apple's usual wait-and-perfect approach does not suit fast-moving AI competition.

Whether Apple can compress its timeline enough to matter remains unclear, according to the article. Users now expect agents that anticipate needs and coordinate complex workflows, which the article says may require architectures different from what Siri was built on. The coming months should show whether internal pressure produces external progress. Developers are another concern, since the article warns that if third-party apps optimize first for OpenAI and Meta agents, Apple could lose ground in its own ecosystem.
