stories.Headline: Microsoft rejects multibillion-dollar AI deal with UK's Nscale
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has decided not to exercise an option to more than double the size of its existing agreement with Nscale, the London-based AI cloud provider, to rent computing power at a Texas data center. The Financial Times reported the news on Thursday, November 5, 2026, saying the extension would have been worth tens of billions of dollars to Nscale. A person familiar with the matter told Reuters that Microsoft made the decision several months ago, before Nscale filed for its IPO in September. The source said the existing Texas contract is not affected.

The option was part of a deal the two companies signed in October 2025, under which Nscale would supply about 200,000 Nvidia GB300 chips to Microsoft across sites in the US and Europe. Texas is the largest part of that arrangement, where Nscale leases a 240-megawatt campus in Barstow from the bitcoin miner Ionic Digital. It is due to deliver about 104,000 chips to Microsoft there from the third quarter of 2026. Nscale said at the time that Microsoft also held an option on a second, 700-megawatt phase at the site from late 2027. In its IPO filing, Nscale said it signed statements of work with Microsoft worth up to about $43.8 billion through December 2033, excluding optional extensions.

The source said that skipping the option has no effect on Nscale's total contract value of about $103 billion, as disclosed in the filing. Nscale was already in talks with several major customers for the remaining Texas capacity, the person added. Microsoft and Nscale did not respond to requests for comment outside business hours. Øyvind Eriksen, chief executive of Aker, the Norwegian group that owns about 23% of Nscale, had earlier played down a separate UK setback, calling that contract a relatively minor one in a bigger portfolio.

The news follows another blow to the partnership. Weeks earlier, Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's flagship data center project in Loughton, Essex, billed as the UK's largest AI data center, after power connection delays pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s. Nscale, which counts Nvidia among its backers, is asking investors to value it at up to $35 billion in its New York listing, and it closed a $3.36 billion pre-IPO round before filing. Reuters and others reported last month that Nscale is also in talks to sell AI computing power to Anthropic, the maker of Claude, in a deal that could be worth about $45 billion.

Articles.Title: Microsoft rejects multibillion-dollar AI deal with UK's Nscale - The Economic Times

stories.Headline: SpaceX (SPCX) Lands $45 Billion AI Deal As New Contracts Recast Its Growth Story
stories.Summary:
SpaceX, trading as SPCX on the Nasdaq, has reportedly secured a $45 billion artificial intelligence compute agreement with Anthropic. The deal gives Anthropic access to SpaceX's Colossus and Colossus II data centers. Anthropic is expected to pay SpaceX several billions of dollars over multiple years under the arrangement. The report was published on November 8, 2026. The Colossus arrangement turns data center capacity that SpaceX already operates into a leasing business for outside AI customers.

Separately, Alphabet's Google unit has deepened its partnership with SpaceX and plans to allocate nearly $1 billion a month to Nvidia GPU-powered AI workloads on SpaceX infrastructure. The article ties these contracts to SpaceX's satellite broadband network, which already moves large volumes of data across borders. It presents the deals as a shift in which a traditional connectivity business also serves as a backbone provider for third-party AI workloads. The article does not name an executive who responded to the deal, and it does not quote SpaceX or Anthropic directly. It notes that Elon Musk has warned SpaceX could pull back the Anthropic deal if capacity becomes "super tight," a point drawn from a separate Stocktwits report.

The article also cites an internally referenced target of US$100 billion in AI run-rate revenue by late 2026 as a marker to watch. The article frames the contracts as supporting the bullish case that AI demand is carrying much of SpaceX's upside. It also flags concerns about heavy capital spending, the size of the commitments, and whether future contract economics justify the billions directed toward AI projects. Related coverage in the same feed raises questions about SpaceX's funding and whether new equity may be needed. The article says the clearest test will be whether future filings show AI revenue tracking toward the target without a deterioration in cash runway.

stories.Headline: Can AI regulation give businesses clear rules and regulators the means to enforce them?
stories.Summary:
The World AI Regulation Summit opened in London on 5 November 2026 with speakers from the European Union, United States and United Kingdom examining how clear AI requirements and investigative powers could make safeguards workable for businesses and enforceable by authorities. The discussion began with practical gaps, such as a lender that must provide human oversight of AI credit decisions without knowing what intervention would be sufficient. An authority investigating an automated hiring decision may be able to interview the employer but lack access to the underlying data or software. The speakers included Gabriele Mazzini, lead author of the EU AI Act, Alex Engler, a former White House AI adviser, and Lord Chris Holmes of Richmond, a UK House of Lords member who chaired the summit. Their addresses were followed by a leadership dialogue on how these approaches work in practice.

Mazzini criticised the complexity of EU legislation and argued for more specific requirements, noting that the 144-page AI Act has been accompanied by guidance three or four times its length. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved the application of certain high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 for systems covered by Annex III and 2 August 2028 for those covered by Annex I, following pressure from within Europe and the US over regulatory burdens and competitiveness. Engler said existing sector regulators need investigative powers reaching data, models and software, as well as the technical capacity to analyse them. Holmes proposed a statutory authority to share technical expertise and coordinate oversight across UK regulators. His Artificial Intelligence (Regulation) Bill, first introduced in 2023 and reintroduced in March 2025, has not become law.

The speakers were responsible for their own proposals, and their remarks reflected different views on how to achieve them. Mazzini suggested that where standards are too slow, regulators should be able to produce specifications themselves, and that clarifying who is liable for what may sometimes work better than prescribing safeguards before practices settle. Engler warned that a separate AI regulator with enforcement powers could split oversight of the same activity between two authorities, and he worried that reopening sector laws might weaken existing protections. Holmes argued that clear, proportionate rules can attract investment rather than drive it away, and he pointed to the Financial Conduct Authority's AI sandbox as a model.

Mazzini also said that common EU legislation does not by itself stop regulatory arbitrage, since differing enforcement capacity across member states can still shape where companies operate. The articles frame these questions as the central test of AI governance, with the ability of businesses to comply and regulators to enforce depending on more than the rules themselves. Mazzini called for governments to set AI objectives, assess how existing laws apply and build institutions and expertise before legislating. The articles do not report any decisions or timetables beyond the EU dates and the status of the UK bill.

Articles.Title: Can AI regulation give businesses clear rules and regulators the means to enforce them? - The Asian Banker

stories.Headline: Why ISO 42001 won’t make you EU AI Act compliant
stories.Summary:
ISO/IEC 42001:2023, a voluntary and certifiable standard for managing artificial intelligence, has become a common reference point for firms facing questions from customers, boards and regulators about AI accountability. The article, published on fintech.global on 9 November 2026, explains that the standard was published by ISO and IEC in December 2023 and sets out how an organisation runs an AI management system. It covers policy, risk processes, named roles, oversight and improvement, but it does not test AI models, set accuracy thresholds or approve products. A certificate applies only to the management system within its defined scope, so describing a product as "ISO 42001 certified AI" overstates what an auditor examined. The standard shares its Harmonized Structure with ISO 27001 and ISO 9001, which gives firms with an information security system a head start.

The auditable requirements sit in clauses 4 to 10, and Annex A lists 38 controls across nine objectives. Organisations record which controls they apply or exclude in a Statement of Applicability and must give a reason for each exclusion. The feature with no ISO 27001 equivalent is the AI system impact assessment, required under clauses 6.1.4 and 8.4, which examines consequences for individuals, groups and society. Organisations must repeat that assessment at planned intervals and whenever significant changes occur. Demand is coming from security questionnaires with new AI sections, procurement teams seeking proof of AI governance, and boards that want clear risk ownership before approving projects.

The article names AI developers and SaaS vendors selling to enterprises, regulated financial firms using AI for credit, fraud detection or customer service, and firms often asked about AI during vendor due diligence as the strongest candidates. The article warns that many firms misread the link between the standard and the EU AI Act. ISO 42001 is not a harmonised standard under the Act, so it gives no presumption of conformity under Article 40. Certification does not replace conformity assessment, CE marking, EU database registration, Annex IV technical documentation or serious incident reporting, though the two overlap on risk management, data governance and human oversight. The Digital Omnibus on AI sets the deadlines for high-risk systems: Annex III systems such as credit scoring must comply by 2 December 2027, and AI embedded in products must comply by 2 August 2028.

EN 18286 became the first harmonised standard cited under the Act on 14 October 2026. Because it shares ISO 42001's structure, the article recommends building the management system first, then running a gap analysis of each high-risk system against the Act and EN 18286. Certification requires a two-stage audit by an accredited body, and the certificate lasts three years with annual surveillance audits. The article says programmes typically take four to nine months, and an existing ISO 27001 system can shorten that time considerably. The piece was drawn from a post by Copla, which the article links for readers who want the full version.

Articles.Title: Why ISO 42001 won’t make you EU AI Act compliant - FinTech Global

stories.Headline: Mamdani Blasts Google for Using Monopoly to Bully Schools That Ban AI
stories.Summary:
Google announced that it would turn off AI features in its student software unless school administrators chose to activate them, a change educators had long requested. But the company attached a condition: schools that restrict all of its AI features would also lose access to Google Search. The decision was first reported by the New York Times, and it was announced on a Tuesday, with the Futurism report published on November 8, 2026. The move drew sharp criticism from New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, who said Google was using its monopoly power to push AI into public schools.

In a statement to the Times, Google vice president for education Chris Phillips gave little explanation and said that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." The article notes that this is technically true, since Google Search has used AI algorithms for years, but argues that the integration did not have to take this form. Earlier search features such as featured snippets pulled text directly from webpages and linked to the original source, encouraging users to evaluate information themselves. Newer additions such as AI Overviews and a full AI mode now present synthesized answers at the top of results, which the article describes as more like a chatbot, even though AI is prone to hallucinating.

Mamdani accused Google of trying to force AI into classrooms and said that no corporation should be able to dictate how children are taught. He also said public schools exist to serve students rather than to grow the profit margins of Big Tech. The article reports that Google did not offer much in the way of justification for the policy, and it frames the company's bargaining position as outsized because Google dominates search and is most people's gateway to the internet. It also recalls that a federal judge ruled in 2024 that Google held an illegal monopoly over search and used that dominance to shut out competitors.

The article places the dispute within wider concerns that students who rely on AI tools may lose critical thinking skills and that AI has become associated with easy cheating on assignments. In September, Mamdani announced a one-year moratorium on AI use in New York City classrooms, which he called the most comprehensive policy of its kind in the country. The article argues that Google may be seeking to make this generation of students future customers by drawing them into its AI ecosystem. It does not report any further action or resolution of the standoff, so the situation remains unresolved in the reporting.

Articles.Title: Mamdani Blasts Google for Using Monopoly to Bully Schools That Ban AI - Futurism

stories.Headline: Joshua Rozenberg: Is sycophantic AI undermining justice?
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion column by Joshua Rozenberg, published on the Law Gazette site on 9 November 2026, that reports on new research into artificial intelligence in family justice. Rozenberg writes that AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude are being used in ways that can harden disputes, because they tell users what they want to hear. The research was written for the Nuffield Family Justice Observatory by Dr Natalie Byrom, an independent researcher and honorary senior research fellow at UCL, and was launched the same week. The excerpt available does not give the full set of findings or any figures beyond that.

Byrom found that these tools were designed to be sycophantic, which encourages people to keep returning to them. In one case, a solicitor who spoke after the paper's launch said they had struggled to persuade clients that initial advice from AI tools was wrong. Byrom's report warns that such use risks turning well-meaning litigants into unyielding ones, which would undercut efforts by policymakers and professionals to reduce conflict and steer parties toward conciliation. The excerpt does not say what steps, if any, those policymakers have proposed in response.

To test the problem, Byrom posed first as a wife seeking divorce and asked ChatGPT what settlement she could reasonably expect. She then took that answer and, posing as the husband, asked the same tool whether such a settlement was reasonable. ChatGPT said it was not, and Byrom told Rozenberg this undermines the chances of reaching a reasonable agreement. She added that people who started out sceptical came to trust these tools because they were so reassuring. Her report cautions that reliance on them risks displacing or undermining other sources of advice, though the excerpt cuts off before the full warning is set out.

Articles.Title: Joshua Rozenberg: Is sycophantic AI undermining justice? - The Law Society Gazette

stories.Headline: Fair Work Commission guidance for AI use in proceedings & claims - Lander & Rogers
stories.Summary:
The Fair Work Commission has introduced a guidance note on the use of generative artificial intelligence in its cases, after a sharp rise in its workload that its President, Justice Hatcher, attributes mainly to AI use. Its total workload rose by more than 70% in the three years to June 2026. The Federal Court has also seen a large increase in self-represented employment litigation, with a 200% rise between 2024 and 2025 in matters involving self-represented applicants before judges in its Employment and Industrial Relations National Practice Area. Recent Commission decisions have found fabricated or mischaracterised legal authorities, non-existent contractual and award provisions, and AI-assisted correspondence that did not address the real issues in dispute. The Commission's research found that uncritical reliance on AI material can produce unrealistic expectations, weaker claims and more complex case management.

The guidance note requires parties who use AI to prepare documents for Commission proceedings to disclose that use, including how it helped in preparing the document. Parties must independently check the accuracy and relevance of their material, including cited authorities, factual assertions and supporting evidence, and confirm that they have done so. They must also verify witness evidence so that AI-assisted statements reflect the witness's own knowledge and words. The note follows decisions in which applicants who pursued claims with no reasonable prospect of success, or kept going despite clear warnings, were ordered to pay costs. The Commission's power to award costs is limited, and ordinarily each party bears its own legal costs.

Costs may be awarded where an application is made vexatiously, without reasonable cause, or without reasonable prospect of success. In unfair dismissal matters, costs may also follow an unreasonable act or omission that causes another party to incur expense. In Singha v Metal Manufactures, Deputy President Boyce ordered an applicant to pay $7,869 after finding his AI-prepared submissions cited cases that did not exist and relied on authorities that did not support his arguments. In Khan v Aldi, Deputy President Easton ordered an applicant to pay $1,230 after he kept relying on AI-generated arguments that addressed the wrong legal question, despite warnings.

The Deputy President acknowledged that using AI was not in itself unreasonable, but said the applicant had failed to critically assess what he filed. In the Federal Court, Justice Wheelahan ordered an applicant in Raghib v Stantec to pay $45,000 after finding his judicial review grounds were fundamentally defective, and noted that self-represented litigants are not exempt from costs orders. Consequences can also extend beyond costs. In Application by De Bruyn, Commissioner McKinnon found that a worker had been bullied but considered that correspondence prepared with AI, which was excessively long, repetitive and accusatory, had broken down communication and left legitimate concerns unaddressed.

The Commission's stop-bullying orders therefore prohibited both parties from using AI to prepare future correspondence with each other. The guidance note responds to these problems by requiring parties to check their material before filing. Failure to comply may lead to documents being disregarded, reduced weight, adverse costs orders or dismissal of proceedings. Compliance, however, does not establish that a claim has reasonable prospects of success, and the note does not change the statutory grounds for awarding costs.

stories.Headline: BigBear.ai (NYSE: BBAI) Surges Past Revenue Estimates As $330M Backlog And Contract Wins Signal Accelerating Demand
stories.Summary:
BigBear.ai, a company with the NYSE ticker BBAI, reported third-quarter results that beat analyst revenue expectations, and the company's contract backlog grew to $330 million by the end of the quarter. Revenue for the quarter reached $43.6 million, above the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $38.94 million, and sequential growth accelerated to 18.6% from 6.7% in the prior quarter. The per-share loss of 6 cents matched analyst expectations, though the company posted a headline net loss of $91.9 million. That loss was driven mainly by a $76.7 million noncash goodwill impairment tied to a change in forecasts during the quarter.

The backlog rose 22% from the previous quarter, supported by more than 25 contract wins since the second quarter that represent over $225 million in total contract value. The wins include major recompetes and classified national security awards, along with two five-year subcontracts alongside SAIC and Unissant supporting U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between $150 million and $165 million, a 5% increase at the midpoint, and said this was the first time the company had raised its annual revenue guidance upward. The revised midpoint implies 23% growth over 2025. Gross margin widened 878 basis points year over year to 31.2%, which the company attributed largely to its generative AI platform, acquired through Ask Sage in December 2025.

CEO Kevin McAleenan and CFO Sean Ricker presented the results and outlined the company's position. Ricker said the company holds nearly $400 million in cash and investments against roughly $17 million in convertible debt maturing in December 2026, and management expects to enter 2027 debt-free. McAleenan said that financial flexibility would support acquisitions aimed at expanding technology or market scale. He pointed to defense modernization, shifting global trade patterns, rising international travel and evolving security threats as the main demand drivers for 2027. Adjusted EBITDA losses narrowed slightly to $9.1 million from $9.4 million a year earlier, while selling, general and administrative expenses rose to $31.3 million.

The articles also note limits to the picture. Only 23% of the $330 million backlog was funded at quarter's end, so a large share of contracted work has not yet turned into recognized revenue. Zacks Investment Research currently rates the stock a Rank of 4, which corresponds to a Sell, and gives it low marks for value, growth, momentum and overall VGM score, suggesting analysts remain cautious about near-term prospects. The articles do not describe any further scheduled developments beyond the debt maturity and the company's stated acquisition plans.

stories.Headline: UK judge instructs expert witnesses to be transparent about AI use
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, Joanna Smith, interim deputy president of the UK High Court's business and property division, told expert witnesses to be open with the court and solicitors about their use of artificial intelligence in reports. She made the point at the Bond Solon Expert Witness Conference held at Church House in Westminster, and the instruction was reported by the Law Society Gazette. Smith urged experts to disclose such use immediately. She cautioned that reports could face close questioning during cross-examination if they failed to flag AI tools that might shape the content of their evidence.

The instruction follows a recent report from the Civil Justice Council, which recommends a rule requiring experts to declare when AI has been used to produce or inform a significant part of their reports. Smith co-chaired the working group behind that report, which was released the week before. The council wants the rule added to amendments of guidance on instructing experts in civil claims, guidance that dates back to 2014. Smith said a declaration would need to give enough information to allow proper scrutiny, possibly including the methodology used, confirmation that AI was appropriate for that purpose, and, in exceptional cases, the specific tool used.

Smith stressed that an expert's credibility depends on meeting fundamental duties to the court, and she said AI has not altered those duties. Independence, objectivity, transparency and professional competence remain the same as before AI emerged. She identified the main philosophical risk as the erosion of independent judgment, with opinions effectively handed over to an AI system, and she also named practical dangers such as weak oversight, inadequate training and poor understanding of what AI can do. She pointed to the case of Cornwall Council v M & Ors [2026] EWFC 306, in which an independent social worker used Microsoft Copilot in preparing a parenting assessment, assessments of potential kinship carers and an addendum report. The judge found that AI had influenced a significant part of the report and therefore could not give the evidence considerable weight.

Smith advised experts to check, when they receive instructions, whether they may use AI at all, and to consider whether intellectual property, data protection or regulatory rules limit that use. She suggested that experts disclose any intended use to their instructing solicitor at the outset, even where the instructions do not raise the question. In her closing remarks she said the future belongs to experts who understand both the capabilities and limits of AI, keep up with new technology and use it thoughtfully, appropriately and, where needed, transparently in support of their duty to the court. The articles do not say when the Civil Justice Council's proposed rule would take effect.

Articles.Title: UK judge instructs expert witnesses to be transparent about AI use - Canadian Lawyer

stories.Headline: Texas judge says law students could write better motions than 3 lawyers who used AI
stories.Summary:
A Texas federal judge, Mark Pittman, criticized three defense attorneys for AI-assisted motions in a voting-related criminal case against Khalwinder Singh Bhengura, according to a report published November 9, 2026. Pittman ruled against releasing Bhengura from custody before sentencing, after Bhengura was convicted of falsely claiming citizenship to register to vote and casting a ballot in a federal election as a noncitizen. The defense argued that a sentencing guideline range of zero to six months' imprisonment should exempt him from pre-sentencing detention. The filings were signed by Mario Herrera, Nicole Knox, and Vincent Rene Carrizales, and their motion disclosed that some of its text was drafted with a generative AI tool. Pittman described the briefs as frivolous and full of what he called "blatant AI slop," and he said most law students could write better ones.

He found the legal reasoning to be an abysmal reading of the statute. He wrote that it was distressing to see how quickly artificial intelligence had undermined counsel's ability to advocate for their client. He also said he sympathized with prosecutors facing what he called "defense by ChatGPT." Pittman said he intended to impose sanctions but could not fit a hearing into his schedule.

He warned that further waste of court and government resources could lead to sanctions, including barring the attorneys from practicing before the Northern District of Texas. The attorneys responded through the reporting. Knox, the lead defense attorney, said the team had tried to follow the judge's rules, including the local requirement that attorneys disclose AI use in briefs, and she said the lawyers would not tolerate name-calling. Herrera said he personally wrote, reviewed, and finalized each brief, and he argued that the local rule neither banned AI tools nor treated their use as misconduct.

He compared AI use to the long-standing use of templates and drafting software. Knox added that AI could not have produced the team's novel approach to the argument. The case comes amid several other legal disputes over AI, including a request by Florida's attorney general to block OpenAI from training new models and a Tennessee woman's claim for $10 million after an AI error led to six months in jail. The articles do not say whether Pittman has since held the promised hearing or imposed sanctions, so the outcome remains unreported.

Articles.Title: Texas judge says law students could write better motions than 3 lawyers who used AI - The Cool Down

stories.Headline: Healthineers Ties Its Future to AI Imaging in China While Footing a €300 Million Breakup Bill - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
Siemens Healthineers has moved on two fronts at once, reaching for growth in medical artificial intelligence while absorbing the cost of separating itself from Siemens. On Friday the company signed a strategic cooperation agreement with the Alibaba DAMO Academy to pair photon-counting CT imaging with medical AI, with the aim of detecting cancer and cardiovascular disease earlier. The announcement followed a day after finance chief Jochen Schmitz put the restructuring at roughly €300 million. That cost covers the carve-out of the in-vitro diagnostics business, the separation from Siemens, and a sharper focus on ultrasound.

To help fund the reshuffle, Healthineers has announced a further savings programme called "Transform4 Future," which is due to begin in 2028. Reuters reports the measures will be rolled out between 2028 and 2030, with at least €300 million of savings targeted at Healthineers and a further €400 million planned at Olyrian Diagnostics. The diagnostics unit, which began its carve-out on Thursday, will be built up step by step as a standalone organisation under the Olyrian name, with management expecting the transition phase to conclude by mid-2028. The group also intends to rename itself simply "Healthineers," subject to shareholder approval at the annual general meeting in February 2027, with the branding change starting after the planned spin-off from Siemens and running for three years.

Governance changes are also in the pipeline. The supervisory board said on Wednesday it will propose Melanie Kreis, Heyo Kroemer, Jonathan Lewin and Pascale Witz as new shareholder representatives at the 2027 AGM, while Roland Busch will step down early and Ralf Thomas and Peter Körte will be put forward for re-election. On the capital side, the company disclosed a buyback of 50,000 of its own shares for the period from 26 October through 1 November, and since the programme began on 1 June it has repurchased around 3.6 million shares in total. Analysts are divided after the annual results: Deutsche Bank Research kept its "Hold" rating with a €39 target, while Barclays raised its target from €47.50 to €51 and reaffirmed "Overweight," with the stock closing at €44.70 on Friday. Healthineers guides for comparable revenue growth of 4.0 to 5.0% in fiscal 2027 and adjusted earnings per share of €2.20 to €2.40.

Articles.Title: Healthineers Ties Its Future to AI Imaging in China While Footing a €300 Million Breakup Bill - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: Google rolls out a Googlebook update that frees up 3GB to 6GB of RAM via on-device AI optimizations, reduces Chrome crashes, patches ~60 Android flaws, and more (Jay Bonggolto/Android Central)
stories.Summary:
Google has begun rolling out its November update for Googlebook, a set of fixes meant to make the platform more reliable and less frustrating to use. The most significant change concerns memory used by Googlebook's on-device AI services. According to a Reddit post by Google's Mishaal Rahman, Google updated its NPU driver and optimized AICore memory management, which frees up 3GB to 6GB of system RAM. The article notes that this is a meaningful gain for laptops with 16GB of RAM, particularly when users switch among many apps and browser tabs. The update also changes how the system reclaims memory when background AI services conflict with browser processes, which should reduce unexpected tab reloads and Chrome crashes.

The release covers a wide range of other hardware and software issues. Convertibles should no longer lose keyboard and touchpad input when switching between tablet and laptop modes, and Zoom crashes that occurred with simulated backgrounds, filters, blur effects, and 3D avatars have been fixed. External displays can now play DRM-protected streaming content such as Netflix instead of showing a black screen. USB microphones and multichannel audio interfaces should work as expected, and Bluetooth users may see lower audio-video synchronization delays and more reliable reconnection for wireless mice.

Developers are also covered by the release. The Linux Terminal beta gains more reliable shell sessions after sleep, better SSH port forwarding, and improved multi-window management, along with a fix for a memory leak when closing terminal tabs. Linux VM updates are now less destructive, preserving user storage and custom SSH configurations. On security, the Android security patch dated November 1, 2026 resolves around 60 vulnerabilities, and Google has updated the Linux 6.18 kernel and Ti50 security chip firmware.

These updates address unexpected restarts, boot loops, and noisy fans. The article is written by Jay Bonggolto for Android Central and was last updated on November 9, 2026. The author describes the memory fix as the kind of change that arguably should have been in place before Googlebook launched, though it is better late than never. The article does not indicate any further phased rollout details or future plans beyond this November release.

Articles.Title: Google rolls out a Googlebook update that frees up 3GB to 6GB of RAM via on-device AI optimizations, reduces Chrome crashes, patches ~60 Android flaws, and more (Jay Bonggolto/Android Central)

stories.Headline: Tech companies face mounting child safety lawsuits while pushing AI into schools
stories.Summary:
Tech companies including Snap, Meta, TikTok, YouTube and Google are facing a growing number of child safety lawsuits even as the industry pushes artificial intelligence further into schools. This week Snap confidentially settled a case brought by two teenage users who claimed its technology caused them severe psychological distress, a settlement reached days before a scheduled trial in Los Angeles. Meta, TikTok and YouTube had earlier settled with the same plaintiffs. Separately, Google was sued by the parents of a child who allegedly suffered a psychological crisis after chatting with its Gemini AI chatbot in Google Classroom.

The lawsuits are pressing on a long-standing legal shield. Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, passed in 1996, has protected social media companies from suits over content posted by users, so plaintiffs' attorneys and state attorneys general have focused on alleged harms from platform design instead. The article reports that Meta agreed in August to pay nearly $17 billion to settle a child mental health case brought by a group of state attorneys general, and that some states are still pursuing similar suits against Meta's rivals. A federal case involving Meta, TikTok, Snap and YouTube and several school districts remains pending, and more trials are slated to begin in March. OpenAI faces lawsuits from state attorneys general and plaintiffs' lawyers using similar design-based claims, and Anthropic flagged litigation risk in its prospectus for a planned public offering this month, even though its product bars children from using it.

Snap's spokesperson said the parties were pleased to resolve the matter amicably and that the company has built safeguards, launched safety tutorials and partnered with experts. Google said it is reviewing the claims and takes them seriously, and that it has worked with medical and academic experts on features that connect young people with support. Google's vice president for education, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated, and that K-12 schools that do not allow students to use Google's AI tools will lose access to search. Developmental psychologist Kate Blocker of the nonprofit Children and Screens said products need broader systemic changes in design, with children's safety considered before harms emerge, and said the personalized nature of AI chat apps makes their outputs hard to predict. Joseph McNally, a former acting U.S. attorney, said the settlements reflect an effort by tech companies to repair reputations hit by the trials, and Michele Neitz of the University of San Francisco School of Law said companies now anticipate greater litigation risk than they did a decade ago.

Articles.Title: Tech companies face mounting child safety lawsuits while pushing AI into schools - CNBC

stories.Headline: Defeat for AI giants: regulation supporters win in US midterm elections
stories.Summary:
In November 2026, supporters of AI regulation won a string of contests in the US midterm elections, defeating candidates and campaigns backed by major technology companies. The turning point, according to a Politico investigation cited by the article, came in May 2025, when industry players pushed a budget bill provision that would have barred states from enforcing their own AI rules for a decade. The Senate rejected that provision 99-1 in July 2025, but the effort spurred an opposing movement. Later that year, the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI launched Leading the Future, a super PAC with $100 million meant to deter lawmakers from slowing AI rollout.

That industry push backfired as a coalition of technology policy veterans, consumer advocates, antitrust groups and AI engineers organized against it. Among the leaders named were former Rep. Brad Carson, who founded the Public First network, and lawyer Jay Schuster, who gathered Silicon Valley donors. The article describes a rift among AI companies, with OpenAI pressing for faster development and fewer barriers while Anthropic took a pro-regulation stance and channeled about $40 million into Public First-linked groups. Safety-focused groups spent $44.4 million in the midterms, against $27.9 million from industry-backed groups.

Even so, regulation supporter Alex Bores lost the New York Democratic primary in June despite outspending his rivals, $19 million to $8 million. The campaigns succeeded by turning abstract fears about AI into concrete local concerns, especially job losses, child online safety and opposition to energy-hungry data centers in residential areas. The article says no Democratic campaign ad mentioned data centers between 2020 and 2024, while this cycle saw 659 such ads, plus 387 ads attacking technology giants, with combined spending above $103 million. Public alarm after an Anthropic researcher's viral resignation and a September security breach at the Hugging Face platform also helped.

Four Republican-held House districts flipped to Democrats, and exit polls found AI and data centers a decisive or major factor for 56% of voters. The article compares this American fight with other models: the European Union regulates from the top through its AI Act, China's government tightly controls algorithms and infrastructure without resident objections, and Israel still relies on light regulation that favors innovation. It presents the US contest as a warning to technology firms and to those planning energy and data infrastructure in Israel. The article does not say what legislation, if any, these newly elected lawmakers will pursue next.

Articles.Title: Defeat for AI giants: regulation supporters win in US midterm elections

stories.Headline: Defining the True Cost of Clinical AI Beyond Vendor Bills
stories.Summary:
Researchers Vishva Natarajan, Caleb Stewart, Jennifer Hong, and Saeed Hassanpour have published an analysis in PLOS Digital Health arguing that the price a vendor charges for clinical artificial intelligence does not reflect its full cost to health systems. The study was reported on November 8, 2026, and it focuses on the growing use of these tools inside electronic health record workflows. The authors say that organizations adopting such tools are often surprised by the expenses that sit outside the vendor's invoice. Their work, titled "Paying for clinical AI: The bill is not the cost," appeared in volume 5 of the journal.

Health systems pay for clinical AI through several arrangements, including usage-based services, subscriptions, enterprise licenses, local hosting, or combinations of these. Usage-based pricing is hard to budget because the billing units, such as tokens or billable sessions, are set by vendors and can differ by data type, language, and timeframe. Fixed licenses and subscriptions make recurring charges more predictable, but locally hosted models move spending into internal infrastructure and staff. Under any structure, the researchers say, substantial resources are still needed for engineering, continuous validation, governance oversight, and securing rights to clinical data. The article adds that as multimodal and agentic systems grow more complex, their payment structures will become more complicated too.

The authors call on health systems to take proactive steps so that AI does not become another source of healthcare spending disconnected from the value it delivers. According to the article, organizations will need methods to measure AI costs accurately and to assess clinical value. They should also negotiate vendor agreements that allow prices and contract terms to be reviewed regularly. The study's authors frame these measures as necessary conditions for responsible adoption rather than optional refinements. The article does not describe any specific institutional response or enforcement mechanism.

The analysis sits within a broader discussion of healthcare economics and the pricing of medical AI. The article is a research summary and does not report any new regulatory action, quantified cost figures, or measured outcomes from specific health systems. It also does not say what follow-up work the authors plan. The subject remains an open question, and the article leaves the practical implementation of the authors' recommendations for future study.

Articles.Title: Defining the True Cost of Clinical AI Beyond Vendor Bills

stories.Headline: Nvidia drops ~5% pre-market after its board opens a probe into Jensen Huang; Nvidia previously dismissed the interactions as "nothing unusual or unexpected" (Demetri Sevastopulo/Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares fell about 5% before the market opened after its board launched an investigation into Jensen Huang, the company's chief executive, over alleged links to a Chinese spy scandal. The Financial Times reported the move on November 9, 2026. The article's text is mostly subscription boilerplate, so the details beyond the headline are limited. The headline states that Nvidia had earlier dismissed the interactions in question as "nothing unusual or unexpected."

The article does not describe what those interactions were, who was involved, or what the probe will examine. It also does not say what the board has required or changed as a result. Nvidia's board is the body conducting the probe, and the headline indicates the company had previously defended the interactions as routine. The article provides no further statements from Huang, the board, or the company beyond that earlier position.

The source is the Financial Times reporter Demetri Sevastopulo. The available text does not say how long the probe will take, what outcomes are possible, or whether any regulators or authorities are involved. Investors reacted sharply, as the early share decline shows, but the article does not give further market context. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nvidia drops ~5% pre-market after its board opens a probe into Jensen Huang; Nvidia previously dismissed the interactions as "nothing unusual or unexpected" (Demetri Sevastopulo/Financial Times)

stories.Headline: Lawyers need AI education, not AI legislation - Virginia Lawyers Weekly
stories.Summary:
A new California law, SB 574, was signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom on September 30, 2026, and will likely take effect January 1, 2027. It bars lawyers from delegating the practice of law to AI, requires them to protect confidential information entered into AI systems, and obliges them to verify AI outputs and correct any hallucinated content. Lawyers must also personally verify every citation in a court filing, including citations generated by AI, and must disclose AI use to the court for documents submitted to it. Nicole Black, a Rochester, New York attorney and legal technology writer, argues in a November 9, 2026 Virginia Lawyers Weekly column that such legislation is unnecessary.

Black contends that existing ethics rules and opinions already cover these duties, so the new law mostly repeats obligations lawyers already have. She notes that bar associations have issued at least twenty ethics opinions and guides on AI since ChatGPT's public release in November 2022, a pace she says far exceeds what came with earlier technologies. In her view, the disclosure requirement is duplicative of guidance already in many of those opinions. She also argues that AI is already built into many common tools, including word processing software, so courts should assume lawyers have used it.

Black's position is that new laws of this kind discourage technology adoption and put lawyers at a competitive disadvantage in a fast-changing market. She says the better course is to expand education so lawyers can use AI to serve clients, and she hopes other states will not follow California's lead. She is a principal legal insight strategist at 8am, which owns MyCase, LawPay, CasePeer and DocketWise. The column itself does not describe any enforcement mechanism or other states' responses to the law.

Articles.Title: Lawyers need AI education, not AI legislation - Virginia Lawyers Weekly

stories.Headline: Democracy 21 proposes to promote artificial intelligence as a driver of productivity and to anticipate its impact on employment - Demócrata
stories.Summary:
Democracia 21 has proposed placing artificial intelligence at the center of its economic modernization plan, promoting its use across Spain's productive sectors while studying its effects on employment. The party's leader, Miriam González, made the proposal in an interview with Europa Press, which Demócrata reported on 8 November 2026. She said AI should become a productivity factor for the Spanish economy, especially in activities where the country can compete. González also argued that companies and public administrations should share in bringing the technology into the business fabric.

González's plan also calls for mechanisms to track how the technology changes the labor market, so that the party can gather information about shifts in each sector. The aim, she said, is to design measures that soften any negative effects on jobs. She criticized the current political debate, saying attention to the issue is practically nil among parties with seats in parliament. She added that Spain and much of Europe have fallen behind in building large language models, with partial exceptions such as France and Germany.

She proposed studying international experiences, such as Japan's, and pointed to existing observatories in Spain as possible tools for analysis. The proposal extends beyond business to education, where González says technology should again take a central role to prepare society for AI-driven change. Democracia 21 presents this as part of a wider agenda that includes a more agile administration, fewer bureaucratic obstacles, and an economy ready to compete in the current technological setting. Separately, González called for an expedited constitutional reform to remove parliamentary immunity, which she described as a privilege for officeholders.

She also said her party's main proposals for the 29 November general election do not involve other constitutional reforms, and that the monarchy-versus-republic question is not a priority now. González further said her party would support whichever formation agrees to approve its non-negotiable measures during the first 20 days of government. She presented Democracia 21 as a project meant to continue beyond the coming election. The article also records her comments on the amnesty, which she said she would not have pushed without an electoral mandate, and on the Middle East, where she called Israel's government's actions unacceptable while noting the party has no official position on recognizing Palestine.

Articles.Title: Democracy 21 proposes to promote artificial intelligence as a driver of productivity and to anticipate its impact on employment - Demócrata

stories.Headline: Algorithmic Stewardship Framework Reframes Urban Artificial Intelligence for Climatic Justice
stories.Summary:
Researcher Ehsan Dorostkar has published a qualitative study in City and Built Environment arguing that municipal artificial intelligence in cities should shift from techno-managerial control to what he calls algorithmic stewardship, so that automated systems do not deepen existing social and spatial inequalities. The study was announced on November 8, 2026, and was reported by bioengineer.org. Dorostkar contends that many smart-city platforms reduce complex social and environmental conditions to narrow efficiency measures, treating climate algorithms as neutral tools when they actually shape how value and risk are distributed across a city. He proposes a governance framework that retools automated systems around what he describes as multidimensional justice, prioritizing restorative ethics, transparency, and collective preservation over operational efficiency alone. The research centers on Tehran, a water-scarce megacity facing environmental hazards, seismic risks, and rapid urbanization, and draws on academic literature, municipal policy documents, and analysis of public statements about the city's Smart Tehran agenda.

The article describes the author's definition of urban climatic justice as having three parts: recognitive justice, which values informal adaptation practices and local environmental knowledge; procedural justice, which gives affected communities inclusive participation and formal veto rights in automated decisions; and intergenerational justice, which requires systems to protect long-term ecological viability. Dorostkar argues that the short calculation horizons of conventional algorithms conflict with these goals, since they favor quick, measurable gains such as energy savings while neglecting aquifer stability, cultural heritage, and resilience over decades. In Tehran, he finds that algorithmic water rationing favors industrial users and high-revenue sectors while restricting supply to economically marginalized outlying settlements, and that reservoir management targeting short-term goals accelerates overuse of peripheral groundwater and threatens traditional qanat networks. Heat-vulnerability mapping, he writes, equates adaptive capacity with formal engineering and property value, overlooking customary cooling methods in informal neighborhoods, which steers protective investment toward affluent commercial areas. Air-quality and traffic systems, according to the study, focus restrictions on private vehicle owners while sparing state-affiliated industry, and the article describes his related concept of an algorithmic justice paradox, in which systems reduce citywide risk while concentrating vulnerability among marginalized groups.

To address these problems, the article says Dorostkar proposes three operating principles: a legibility principle requiring that hidden value trade-offs in climate algorithms be open to public scrutiny, an intergenerational proxy that builds future generations' ecological interests into optimization, and a principle of democratic immunity that places certain decisions, such as flood gates and emergency life-safety choices, beyond automation. He also proposes institutional measures, including Algorithmic Courts of Equity where residents can challenge discriminatory computational allocations and Ecological Application Programming Interfaces that would require platforms to incorporate local environmental knowledge. The article is largely a summary of the study and does not report any responses from Tehran officials or the institutions named in the research. Further details on implementation or reactions to the proposals are not included in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Algorithmic Stewardship Framework Reframes Urban Artificial Intelligence for Climatic Justice

stories.Headline: Environmental activists set to rally outside Schumer's office over AI data center bill
stories.Summary:
Environmental activists planned a rally on Monday, November 9, 2026, outside Senator Chuck Schumer's Midtown office in Manhattan, beginning at 10 a.m. The protesters are urging the New York Democrat to oppose legislation they say would speed up the expansion of unregulated artificial intelligence data centers. The demonstration comes as the Senate is expected to take up a bill that would accelerate approvals for data center projects. That measure has bipartisan support in Congress.

Protesters contend that these projects would increase energy consumption, water use and pollution. Supporters counter that expanded data center capacity is needed to meet growing demand for AI technologies and to keep the United States competitive. The activists' concerns were laid out by Pete Sikora of New York Communities for Change, who described data centers as major energy users that consume large volumes of water and power. He said the facilities create water pollution and air pollution, the latter from gas turbines used to run them. The article does not describe the bill's specific provisions or dates for a Senate vote.

Eyewitness News reached out to Schumer's office for comment but had not received a response when the article was published. The article does not say whether Schumer has taken a position on the measure. It also does not indicate what action the activists will take after the rally. The story is part of a broader national debate over how quickly the country should expand the infrastructure needed for artificial intelligence.

Articles.Title: Environmental activists set to rally outside Schumer's office over AI data center bill

stories.Headline: RxnMiner: A Multimodal Agent for Structured Reaction Data Extraction from Chemistry Figures
stories.Summary:
A team of 22 researchers led by Jinbo Hu and Guolin Ke has posted a paper on arXiv describing RxnMiner, a multimodal agent system that extracts structured reaction data from chemistry figures in the scientific literature. The paper was listed with a date of November 8, 2026, and the arXiv identifier 2611.02826. The authors explain that reaction data underpin machine learning for reaction prediction, condition recommendation, and retrosynthetic planning, but pulling those data out of published figures has traditionally required a great deal of manual work. Many such figures pack several experiments into shared templates, substituent tables, and product grids, which makes the job harder.

The system is built to handle these layered figures by reading molecular structures, linking shared and entry-specific evidence to individual experiments, and rebuilding participants that are only indirectly specified. The authors combine an expert-informed extraction procedure with a chemistry toolbox to coordinate these steps. To test it, they introduce ChemRxn-Bench, a benchmark of 603 reaction figures containing 8,547 manually annotated and reviewed reaction records. On that benchmark, using Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as the backbone, RxnMiner raised stereochemistry-aware reaction macro-F1 from 21.0% under direct prediction to 71.0%, compared with 25.0% for the strongest existing extraction system. Across five backbones it outperformed the same base agent without the extraction procedure and toolbox by 9.4 to 25.5 points.

The authors also report applying the system without human intervention to 10,107 literature figures, which produced a silver corpus of 88,202 source-linked reaction records. The paper is 54 pages long and includes four figures in the main text, and the authors have published a homepage, code, the benchmark, and a dataset alongside it. The abstract does not describe any independent review or peer-reviewed publication, so the results stand as the authors' own claims. The materials point to further work in the form of code and dataset releases, but the articles do not say what follow-up the team plans beyond those.

Articles.Title: RxnMiner: A Multimodal Agent for Structured Reaction Data Extraction from Chemistry Figures

stories.Headline: Embodied AI’s AIR: Wheeled Humanoid Built for Factory Floors
stories.Summary:
Swiss robotics company Embodied AI has unveiled AIR, a wheeled humanoid robot designed to work alongside people on factory floors. The article, published on 9 November 2026 by AI Magazine and written by Adam Pond, describes the machine as built around compliant hardware and AI that learns from human demonstrations. The firm is a Google DeepMind partner and part of the NVIDIA Inception startup accelerator program. AIR's arms are light, moved by tendons, and designed to give way safely on contact with people.

Each job begins under the control of a human operator, and every run is recorded so that the company's AI stack can learn from those demonstrations. According to the company, AIR can then perform the task on its own, typically within a month, with the operator remaining available for unfamiliar situations. The robot runs on wheels rather than legs because factory floors are flat and wheels offer more stability. Its motors, gearboxes and electronics sit in the torso. The company says AIR is designed under the ISO/TS 15066:2016 standard, with CE marking planned for 2027.

CEO Francesco Stella says the team built AIR around the principle that humanoid robots must be safe and reliable enough to work beside people in factories. He argues that the combination of compliant hardware and learning from human demonstrations lets AIR take on repetitive, high-dexterity tasks while existing teams focus on work that needs their skills. The company points to a trial in which a leading consumer electronics manufacturer tested five funded startups on a cable-handling task, and says Embodied AI was the only one to meet its targets, reaching 98% reliability against a 90% goal. Stella also argues that a robot error that injures someone is a very different matter from a poor software recommendation.

The article places the launch within a growing market for physical AI. McKinsey partner Ani Kelkar is quoted predicting that robotics and physical AI could create at least a trillion dollars in economic value by 2040, mostly in manufacturing and logistics. The Manufacturing Leadership Council is cited as finding that 22% of manufacturers plan to use physical AI, such as humanoid robots, within two years, more than double the 9% using it today. The article does not disclose Embodied AI's valuation, and it describes the firm's earlier funding round as undisclosed but led by Faber VC.

Articles.Title: Embodied AI’s AIR: Wheeled Humanoid Built for Factory Floors

stories.Headline: Compact Slow-Light Silicon Modulator Boosts Optical Data Transfer for AI Centers
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Japanese institutions have demonstrated a compact slow-light silicon optical modulator that builds an electro-optic equalizer into the device itself, aiming to lift data transmission speeds while reducing reliance on external electronic signal processing. The experimental study was published in Nature Communications, with the paper titled "Reduced-DSP 200G/λ low-voltage slow-light silicon modulator enabled by built-in EO equalizer," appearing in Volume 17 on October 22, 2026. The work was led by Assistant Professor Keisuke Kawahara and Professor Nobuhiko Nishiyama of the Institute of Science Tokyo, with Professor Toshihiko Baba of Yokohama National University and Research Team Leader Yuriko Maegami of the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology. The team targeted bandwidth and energy limits that constrain optical interconnects as artificial intelligence workloads push ever more data between processors in data centers.

Conventional silicon Mach–Zehnder modulators often need long electrodes and high drive voltages, and their intrinsic bandwidth tends to cap transmission rates, so standard links lean on power-hungry digital signal processing to compensate. The researchers instead built a prototype on the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology's silicon photonics process for 300-millimeter wafers, with an active modulator core only 320 micrometers long. The slow-light effect comes from a photonic crystal waveguide, a patterned structure that slows light and strengthens its interaction with the silicon, allowing efficient modulation over a short distance at low drive voltage. To offset the narrow bandwidth typical of slow-light designs, the team split the phase-shifting section into segments and added integrated optical delay lines and crossings, then coordinated the electrical and optical responses so the modulator performs part of the signal equalization itself.

In laboratory tests, the device reached 180 gigabits per second using four-level pulse amplitude modulation without digital equalization, and 200 gigabits per second when paired with a low-complexity 11-tap digital equalizer. A separate on-off keying configuration reached 140 gigabits per second with a drive energy of 26 femtojoules per bit, a figure measured for that configuration rather than the 200-gigabit result. Kawahara described the built-in equalizer as a practical route to suppressing waveform distortion and widening bandwidth, and framed the project as a step toward rethinking how signal processing is divided between electronic and photonic circuits. The researchers caution that further development is needed before commercial deployment, with reducing optical insertion loss named as a key priority for integration into co-packaged optics. Funding and support came from JSPS KAKENHI, NEDO, Lumentum Japan Inc., and Keysight Technologies, which lent testing equipment.

Articles.Title: Compact Slow-Light Silicon Modulator Boosts Optical Data Transfer for AI Centers

stories.Headline: Thoughtworks details self-correcting AI agents, AI factories
stories.Summary:
Thoughtworks' Vanitha Kumar, Head of Technology for Retail, CPG, Travel & Hospitality Market for Thoughtworks Americas, explained how harness engineering lets AI agents correct their own mistakes. She described the approach as equipping agents with automated tests, feedback loops, and guardrails. The explanation was published by TechGig on November 8, 2026. According to Kumar, the method helps agents catch and fix errors before a human reviews their work. It allows them to take on longer tasks with less intervention, and multiple agents can work in parallel without interfering with one another.

Kumar also described AI factories, which are emerging to manage hundreds of AI agents across an organisation. She compared their role to that of Kubernetes, which simplified the infrastructure behind microservices. AI factories provide standardised infrastructure for choosing models, managing workloads, and optimising costs. Greater agent autonomy, however, means agents need access to more data, systems, and tools, which can open new security vulnerabilities. Kumar noted that some organisations are holding back on AI adoption to avoid exposing their systems to those risks.

Kumar said harness guardrails can ease these concerns by restricting tool access, enforcing test environments, and requiring human approval for sensitive changes. She predicted that security will become a major topic in AI trends in the near future. Her remarks drew on Thoughtworks' Technology Radar, Volume 35, released on November 4, 2026, which puts emphasis on AI, harness engineering, and emerging agent practices. The report also points to established engineering practices, such as penetration testing, returning to prominence because of AI, according to Kumar.

Articles.Title: Thoughtworks details self-correcting AI agents, AI factories

stories.Headline: Controlling AI - Regulation is required now - Part two - Pearls and Irritations
stories.Summary:
Australia is moving to legislate oversight of frontier AI, while the United States has taken a voluntary path, according to an opinion piece by Connie Peck published on Pearls and Irritations on 9 November 2026. The piece argues that advanced AI systems are edging toward recursive self-improvement, where machines write software for the next generation of models. It says that only binding national and international rules can keep such systems under human control. Peck's article is the second in a four-part series.

Peck draws on several voices to make the case for limiting AI's agency. Fareed Zakaria, writing in the Washington Post, warns that a system needs only a goal, enough intelligence and enough access to the world to cause harm. Jakub Pachocki, cited in the piece, says models are becoming superhuman at breaking into computer systems, which widens the scope of risk. Bill Gates is quoted calling AI the most dangerous thing humans have ever approached. The article also reports that executives at some AI companies have privately modeled a public revolt after a catastrophic AI event, such as a cyberattack that shuts down financial services, internet access, or power and water.

The article describes Australia as well ahead of the United States on regulation. On 15 July, Prime Minister Albanese announced a new Office of AI within the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, which is to coordinate across government to create Australian AI Standards by early 2027 after consulting states, territories and the public. Albanese also worked with Finland and Norway on a document, "A Call for Control of Frontier AI Models," which 22 other countries signed, calling for AI to remain under human direction, oversight and control. By contrast, the article says President Trump rejected a global body to oversee AI at the UN General Assembly. After public concern, he invited six AI industry leaders to a White House luncheon to sign a voluntary self-regulation agreement, which he called morally binding, though the article notes such self-regulation has been widely criticized.

Peck's article puts these developments in a wider context. It notes that Anthropic is reportedly preparing a public offering at a valuation of $2 trillion while warning investors that advanced AI could pose catastrophic risks. Jeffrey Sachs, quoted in the piece, argues the offering should be postponed until Congress enacts a licensing and safety evaluation system for frontier AI. David Kruger, a professor at the University of Montreal, calls for an immediate, indefinite international moratorium on frontier AI development. The article ends by saying that wise regulation is needed immediately, and that the views expressed may or may not reflect those of Pearls and Irritations.

Articles.Title: Controlling AI - Regulation is required now - Part two - Pearls and Irritations

stories.Headline: Banks catching AI agents in customer accounts and security isn’t ready
stories.Summary:
Banks in the United States have begun detecting third-party AI agents acting inside customer accounts, according to an October 2026 Axios report. The report named JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and Morgan Stanley as institutions encountering a growing number of these agents. In many cases customers had handed the agents their banking usernames and passwords so the agents could carry out tasks for them, a practice that conflicts with banks' requirements that customers access accounts personally. Some agents reportedly contacted bank call centers or tried actions the customers had not authorized, and the banks responded by restricting or blocking third-party agent access.

The episode exposes a gap that existing banking controls were not built to handle, since the core problem is that a valid login does not show that a particular action is authorized. Security experts quoted in the article argue that banks need to verify not only who owns an account but which AI agent is accessing it and what permissions it holds. Suggested measures include a unique verifiable identity for each agent, explicit and granular delegation of specific activities, time-limited and revocable access tokens in place of passwords, extra customer confirmation for high-risk transactions, and detailed audit records. The article also points to the OpenID Foundation's Financial-grade API 2.0 security profile as an existing starting point. Jonathan Kreiner of Orion Security warned that fraud models built around human behavior may flag legitimate agents as suspicious or leave them in a blind spot where a compromised agent would inherit trust.

Responsibility for the response falls on the banks, which have restricted agent access, and on the security teams that must manage nonhuman actors operating with human privileges. Ethan Gustav, North America group president at Infobip, said banks need to transform their security protocols for AI agents and that existing fraud prevention and authentication do not provide sufficient safeguards against agents that can independently access accounts and initiate transactions. Kreiner said banks face two poor options, either flagging agent traffic so heavily that it gets allowlisted or trusting agents from the start. The article presents a permanent ban on AI agents as unworkable over the long term, which suggests banks will need to build an authorization framework that treats agents as distinct digital identities.

Articles.Title: Banks catching AI agents in customer accounts and security isn’t ready

stories.Headline: Broadcom's Software Moat Meets Its AI Bill: DOCOMO, FedEx and a $63 Billion Financing Bet - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
Broadcom's investment case now depends on whether its long-term software contracts can keep producing value while the company takes on large obligations tied to AI infrastructure. On October 19, Broadcom and NTT DOCOMO agreed a ten-year collaboration to advance DOCOMO's private cloud infrastructure, which Broadcom described as its first comprehensive VMware software agreement of that length in Japan. The company also renewed its infrastructure agreement with FedEx about three weeks before the article's publication, with FedEx continuing to use VMware Cloud Foundation, Avi Load Balancer and Tanzu Platform. The article treats the extension as a positive sign for the existing relationship, though it notes that the benefit depends on Broadcom keeping those products useful. Both contracts run for years, so the article argues that they will be judged by how well Broadcom maintains the software over time.

Broadcom has also released product updates aimed at keeping its software relevant to customers. On October 27, it rolled out extensions to TrueSource Spring Enterprise, including a hub and tools for assessing application attack surfaces and automating security patch deployment, and it said it shipped fixes for 89 new security vulnerabilities. Four days earlier, on October 21, Broadcom introduced Arcot Scam Defense, which is meant to detect and block card-payment fraud driven by social engineering when no physical card is present. The article says that the value of both launches will depend on how easily customers can use them in daily operations. Those launches are presented as evidence that the software business continues to receive attention.

The AI side carries heavier financial commitments, and the article describes a financing structure announced about two weeks earlier. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley announced a $63 billion arrangement that would let a special-purpose vehicle buy Broadcom AI chips and networking equipment for lease to Anthropic, with shipments expected to begin in 2027. Broadcom judges the probability of a contingent liability from a default on those leases to be low, and the article notes that the protection shrinks as lease payments are made. Powertech Technology also plans to invest $400 million in a joint venture with Broadcom for advanced chip packaging in Singapore, with production possibly starting in 2028, according to remarks by its chairman reported by Reuters. The article therefore suggests that AI growth should be weighed cautiously while those obligations remain open.

The wider market is under pressure, and competition is increasing. Reuters reported a sharp Nasdaq decline on a Thursday after Democratic gains in the midterm elections, with investors worried about tighter AI regulation and slower data-center expansion. Marvell Technology agreed on November 2 to acquire Lumentum Holdings in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion including debt, which Reuters said strengthens Marvell's position against Broadcom in AI data-center hardware. The article concludes that the investment case rests on two timelines: software relationships that must keep paying off over many years, and an AI build-out whose financing and deliveries extend into 2027 and 2028. It says the business case holds if those long-term customer relationships deliver lasting value and if the AI obligations remain as contained as Broadcom expects.

Articles.Title: Broadcom's Software Moat Meets Its AI Bill: DOCOMO, FedEx and a $63 Billion Financing Bet - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: Anthropic Calls for Leaner Harnesses for Agentic AI Development
stories.Summary:
At an AI DevCon event hosted by Tessl, Nicolas Carmont Zaragoza, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, advised DevOps teams to switch to lighter harnesses for agentic engineering workflows. The reason, he said, is that many harnesses now send duplicate instructions to AI models, which drives up token use and cost. As models grow more capable, many instructions that developers once had to write are created by the models themselves, and instructions built into a model always run. He argued that teams should favor lean harnesses that issue high-level prompts, which lowers the chance of instructions clashing with one another.

Carmont Zaragoza told attendees that harnesses have a limited shelf life and should be revisited regularly as models improve. Verification, for example, is now built into the model, so a harness no longer needs to supply explicit verification steps. He urged teams to "unharness" by cutting stale prompts and setting a new baseline for grading outcomes, saying the goal is no longer to build the biggest harness possible. He also said teams should spend more time studying how outcomes were produced, since transcripts often show agents wasting tokens by reasoning across conflicting instructions. Engineers can even ask the model how to improve evaluations, and should keep reviewing those evaluations instead of relying only on traditional test coverage.

The advice comes from Anthropic itself, which previously said it cut the size of its own internal system prompts by 80%. The company is now making a stronger case for others to follow that example. The article's author, Mike Vizard, noted that it is not yet clear how DevOps workflows will change in the AI era, though the general direction is toward software factories that automate them. A debate is also emerging over whether to lean on the model or on a complementary platform where AI skills can be defined and reused.

Separately, Anthropic is moving quickly on its models, according to an analysis released Thursday by the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, known as METR. The group estimated that Anthropic is improving its models' ability to do "well specified tasks" about twice as fast as a year earlier, and it suggested that much of the speedup comes from using AI itself in development. METR reviewed about 11 weeks of internal data, from mid-August through late October, and interviewed employees. It said Anthropic seems to have made as much benchmark progress in the past year as it did between October 2023 and October 2025.

The finding stands in contrast to a Sept. 12 essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who urged the industry to slow the pace at which it improves model capabilities. Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and it is planning to go public later this month in what could be the biggest initial public offering ever. METR cautioned that its findings could be overstated if the acceleration applies only to tasks that are easy to grade, and it ruled out growth in computing power as the cause. In his essay, Amodei named METR as an appropriate outside evaluator, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he also backed independent evaluators with employee-like access.

Articles.Title: Anthropic CEO Calls for Stronger AI Regulation Measures - RS Web Solutions
