stories.Headline: AI infrastructure grows in Texas with new facilities in Dallas, College Station - NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth
stories.Summary:
In Bryan, a 73-megawatt data center is being developed on 25 acres of Texas A&M's RELLIS Campus by Austin-based ThisWay Global, which calls its project the Research and AI Compute Center, or RACC. The facility is focused on sovereign artificial intelligence, a model that lets organizations keep tighter control over their data and the output of AI systems. The center plans an eight-week course for eligible students and community members, extending training beyond Texas A&M's own students. The company expects to begin computing at the Bryan site by June 2027. Students and researchers say that a nearby facility would make it easier to keep their work on campus instead of seeking outside partners for large computing systems.

In Dallas, technology integrator GDT has opened what it calls an "AI factory," a supercomputer lab where businesses can build and test AI applications before investing in their own systems. The lab runs on NVIDIA GPUs, NetApp storage and Cisco networking, and companies can use it to judge whether a given AI use case makes sense for their operations. GDT executives say large enterprises now need to deploy AI at scale, which is far more complex than casual use of a public chatbot. GDT's vice president of advisory and transformation, Chris Kapusta, said the lab is meant to speed companies from exploring AI to confirming real value. He added that the facility gives North Texas businesses local access to the technology and draws national attention to the region.

GDT's CEO, Shawn O'Grady, compared AI to a hammer, arguing that the tool itself is not the problem and that its effect depends on how people use it. Kapusta said bad actors are already using AI to search for security weaknesses, while companies can use the same technology to find and fix vulnerabilities first. ThisWay Global's CEO, Stefan Fable, said AI will become part of everyday systems, including payment systems and points of sale. He also stressed that users keep control over both inputs and outputs in a sovereign setup, which he called important for research, regulated industries and defense. Together, the two projects reflect a push to put computing power within reach of more people as AI spreads through business, research and daily life.

stories.Headline: Airbnb is building an AI travel agent
stories.Summary:
Airbnb said on Thursday, November 5, 2026, that it will launch its own AI travel agent in the first half of 2027. The company confirmed the timetable in its third-quarter shareholder letter and gave more detail on its earnings call. CEO Brian Chesky said the agent is meant to help users research, plan and book trips on the platform, and it will go beyond a text chatbot. It will build an interface around each question, drawing on hundreds of travel-specific elements such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries, and assembling them in real time.

The agent is meant to cover more than the initial booking. Airbnb says it will help with changing a reservation, resolving a payment issue, refunds, rebooking and 24-hour safety support, though it did not explain what that safety help will involve. Chesky said it will act in a way that feels a little like generative AI, offering something like a small custom display for a car rental, or help inviting co-travellers, while keeping a chat element. Over time, Airbnb wants the agent to plan a whole trip in one place, across homes, hotels, services and experiences, and Chesky said it will be able to go outside Airbnb's own listings while staying within travel.

The company also reported strong results alongside the announcement. Third-quarter revenue grew 19 percent to about $4.9 billion, topping Wall Street estimates, and net income was $1.9 billion. Airbnb raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky said it was the company's fastest revenue growth in more than three years, and that Airbnb is back in growth mode. In its shareholder letter, the company said it shipped more than 50 products and features in the quarter, nearly 70 percent more than a year earlier.

Chesky explained why Airbnb is building its own agent rather than relying on others. He said agents such as Meta's Muse and the invite-only Instinct are good at routine tasks like booking a restaurant or scheduling an appointment, but that planning a trip is different because travel is aspirational and discovering where to go is part of the experience. He cited a figure that 80 percent of travellers enjoy researching trips, and said people want to look at photos, compare homes and decide together with their companions. In his view, general-purpose agents are not the best tool for that.

The travel agent is separate from Airbnb's AI customer support assistant, which is already running. That assistant resolved around 40 percent of customer support issues without human agents in the third quarter, up from about 30 percent the previous quarter. The company has said before that it planned an AI agent within the next year, and it is now committing to the first half of 2027 for the consumer rollout. The agent is still under development, and the articles give no further detail on how it will be released.

stories.Headline: AI may be helping Anthropic make two years of progress in one, METR estimates
stories.Summary:
METR, an AI evaluation group, has estimated that Anthropic may now be making roughly two years of progress in one on clearly defined AI tasks. According to the assessment, the company's use of AI is helping its researchers build more capable models faster. The estimate draws on 11 weeks of access to Anthropic's internal research data and staff, with the review covering August 12 to October 29. METR judges that by October 2026, progress ran at about twice the company's pace between March 2024 and October 2025. Anthropic's version of the Epoch Capabilities Index showed benchmark performance improving at an estimated 1.9 times its earlier rate.

The report suggests researchers now spend less time writing code and more time testing ideas, with several interviewees saying AI lets them turn ideas into experiments more quickly. METR says most of the gains come from AI helping human researchers rather than working autonomously, though early signs of more independent contributions were noted. About 80 percent of the acceleration is attributed to Anthropic's internal use of its models for research and development, though METR did not find decisive evidence and staff disagreed on the figure. METR also said faster growth in training compute did not explain the acceleration, and it found no clear constraints on algorithms, computing resources or data that would block rapid progress over the next 12 months. Its estimate is uncertain, and it said the true pace could fall anywhere from 1.3 to three times the historical rate.

METR's full report ran to about 100 pages, and Anthropic redacted most of the evidence the assessors found most informative, citing the need to protect confidential information that could help other AI developers. The omitted material includes detailed estimates of algorithmic progress and analysis of specific constraints on future development. METR said it gave Anthropic the longer report before preparing the public version and agreed the withheld material fit that description, though it did not judge whether the redactions were justified overall. The assessors could not freely search Anthropic's internal systems, and METR said the public must rely on its judgment more than it considers ideal. METR received no payment from Anthropic, which supplied devices and free AI tokens, and it disclosed that one assessor held equity in a competitor and had discussed a possible Anthropic role before declining an offer.

The findings bear on concerns about recursive AI self-improvement, in which AI systems help develop later systems. This assessment followed Anthropic's October 15 announcement that six METR employees would gain access to certain internal systems, equipment and office space through its safety review arrangement. Anthropic also canceled a planned examination of how it allocated computing resources between capabilities and safety before METR reached substantive conclusions, saying it wanted to focus on risk assessment and would revisit that work later. The articles do not say whether any further assessment is scheduled.

stories.Headline: AI: The Blue Wave & AI Data Centers, a Glass Half Full. AI-RTZ #1265 - AI: Reset to Zero
stories.Summary:
Election night brought a Democratic blue wave that won control of both chambers of Congress and several governor's races, with AI data centers a central issue on the ballot. Democrats won governor's races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia after promising to pause or slow data center construction, states that together hold more than 40 percent of planned US data center capacity by one estimate. Dozens of local governments in Ohio, Kansas, Florida and California also voted to halt or restrict new facilities. Survey data cited in the coverage found that about 56 percent of voters called data centers a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote.

The market reaction that followed was severe, with the Nasdaq 100 falling 6.4 percent on Thursday, its steepest drop since the March 2020 pandemic selloff. Chip stocks fell harder, and the companies that build the physical infrastructure of the buildout, including Vertiv, Quanta and Comfort Systems, lost between 12 and 17 percent each. The Nasdaq Composite was reported to have lost roughly $2.5 trillion in value in a single day. Some analysts later noted that the large hyperscale cloud companies fell less, and that a slower buildout could even help their margins.

Newly elected officials have signaled that their approach will be more measured than their campaign rhetoric suggested. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who takes office January 19, has said she does not oppose data centers outright but objects to how they have been treated in the state, and she has pledged to work with the industry on Texas's terms. Outgoing Governor Abbott had already paused grid connections and air permits for data centers pending audits through December. Local coalitions in Hinojosa's region have drafted terms for what data centers should provide in return, such as broadband and telehealth access.

The article's broader view is that the buildout will slow and change shape rather than stop. Demand for AI compute remains strong, and some states competing for investment and jobs are unlikely to want to lose that to a neighbor. Projects already approved will continue through 2027, while the new rules will shape what comes after. Companies are responding by moving to other locations and by paying for their own power. The outlook also depends on large financing needs, including more than $300 billion in stock sales by technology and chip companies so far this year, and on the still-uncertain policy path.

stories.Headline: Asia stocks roar back as Taiwan jumps 6%, Nvidia probe rattles AI trade
stories.Summary:
Asian stock markets rebounded sharply on Monday after a turbulent week, with the MSCI Asia Pacific index rising 2.3%, Japan's Nikkei 225 gaining 3.5% and South Korea's KOSPI climbing 1.6%. Taiwan's Taiex led the recovery, jumping as much as 6.4%, its biggest advance since July. The rally followed a week in which Japanese and Taiwanese equities entered bear-market territory and Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each lost more than 16%. The rebound also came as Nvidia futures initially slipped as much as 1% after the company's board announced an independent investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence operation.

Taiwan's market regulator and finance ministry moved to steady investors after the Taiex endured a seven-session losing streak, its longest since 2022. The Financial Supervisory Commission cut the permitted volume of intraday short-selling orders using borrowed securities to 3% of a stock's average daily trading volume over the previous 30 sessions, down from 30%. It also raised the minimum margin requirement for short-selling to 130% from 90%. Authorities said the NT$500 billion ($15.2 billion) national stock stabilization fund remained available. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and MediaTek each rose at least 6% in the rebound.

The Nvidia board said it had no reason to believe its secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised, and Huang had acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife. Earlier in the week, U.S. chip stocks had rallied as investors bought beaten-down shares, easing worries that a Democratic-controlled Congress would tighten restrictions on the AI industry after the party's midterm gains. Still, the S&P 500 posted its steepest weekly decline since April 2025, and the Nasdaq 100 lost $2.3 trillion in market value on Thursday alone. Investors were also weighing inflation data due Tuesday, with markets pricing in nearly an 80% chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase by year-end.

Elsewhere in the region, mainland China's CSI 300 rose 0.3% and the Shanghai Composite gained 0.5%, while India's Nifty 50 fell 0.2%. Chinese October inflation showed higher factory-gate prices from energy and commodity costs, but weak domestic demand left many manufacturers unable to pass those costs on. Australia's ANZ Group shares fell 4.5% despite a full-year cash profit of A$7.59 billion that narrowly beat expectations, as the bank raised provisions. Analysts and investors remain cautious about AI valuations, regulatory risks and infrastructure spending, with attention now turning to the U.S. inflation report.

stories.Headline: Inside Inner Mongolia, China's fastest-growing AI data center region, where construction is accelerating with low building cost and no public backlash (SemiAnalysis)
stories.Summary:
Envision Group, a renewable systems integrator, has opened a wind-powered AI data center campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, which SemiAnalysis visited in September 2026. The campus, called Galaxy, is planned for up to 800MW of IT capacity, roughly the size of the core Stargate Abilene campus in Texas. Its first 120MW phase was delivered within a year, at about a fifth of US costs, and the full campus is expected by the end of 2027. The article describes the region as China's fastest-growing AI data center area, with construction accelerating and little public backlash.

Envision designed and integrated much of the campus itself, which the article describes as one of the most vertically integrated setups the authors have seen. The company builds its own wind farms and a dedicated power line to supply the site, and its blade factory sits across the road. Inside the campus, Envision designed the low-voltage power modules and an 800V system, made the battery storage that smooths the load, and co-designed the prefabricated substation. In one 5MW hall, solid-state transformers convert 10kV AC from the grid directly to 800V DC for the racks, removing several conversion stages. The cooling design shares one water loop between liquid- and air-cooled servers and uses no central chiller plant.

The power model, which China calls source-grid-load-storage, pairs a project's own wind or solar farm and batteries with its datacenter through a dedicated line rather than the public grid. Galaxy's two wind farms have a combined 420MW of capacity, about 1.75 times the 240MW datacenter load, and Envision aims to supply over 60% of the first two phases' power from them. The authors say siting, oversizing and a 4-hour battery make this possible, and they note that the wind farms sit about two hours' drive from the campus. The article also explains that Inner Mongolia holds about 57% of China's usable wind resources, a region with more wind than its existing industry and population can use. Envision's datacenter plans in the region total 3GW, and Galaxy is the first.

The authors frame Galaxy as part of a wider pattern in which Chinese industrial groups with strengths in energy, construction or electrical equipment are moving into AI infrastructure, often because returns on the projects themselves are thin. They say Galaxy's scale and its use of wind rather than gas turbines set it apart from Abilene, which Crusoe built and leased to Oracle for OpenAI. The article says a further expansion could take Galaxy to about 1GW if a nearby wind turbine factory is converted. The authors plan a later report on the constraints on Inner Mongolia's datacenter growth, including power, land and water.

stories.Headline: Lee pledges more firefighters, AI disaster response
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung used a ceremony in Sejong on Monday, November 9, marking the 64th Firefighters' Day, to promise more firefighters and greater investment in their capabilities. He spoke to government officials, firefighters, families of those who died on duty, and others gathered for the event. The president said the climate crisis is making disasters more varied and larger in scale, which in turn makes them harder for firefighters to handle. He argued that preparing for changes ahead of time is the way to protect lives and keep people safe.

Lee laid out specific measures for the coming period. He said the government would hire more firefighters, strengthen their command system, and expand spending so crews can respond faster and more systematically. The plan also calls for using artificial intelligence and drones to identify risk factors and carry out dangerous rescues. To protect firefighters themselves, the government intends to deploy advanced defense technology, including unmanned surface vehicles and high-tech firefighting suits. The articles give no figures for how many new firefighters will be hired or how much money will be committed.

The president tied these promises to the wellbeing of the people who do the work. He said the government would more thoroughly look after the treatment and working conditions of firefighters who respond to accidents. In a message to those in the field, he told them that their duties are only complete when they return safely to their families and colleagues. The articles present these remarks as the president's own pledges, with the government as the body that would carry them out.

The speech came as the president's approval rating was a live political issue. A separate report said his rating had climbed back above 40 percent for the first time in two months, while another poll had put it at 35.9 percent amid disputes over a special counsel bill and market volatility. stories.Headline: "By 2027 we could witness a Chernobyl of artificial intelligence": the warning of Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton
stories.Summary:
Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel Prize winner and one of the founders of artificial intelligence, has warned that AI could cause a large-scale accident within the next year or so. In an interview with the Guardian, published in early November 2026, the British computer scientist said such an event might hit financial systems or electricity grids. He compared it to the Chernobyl disaster, though he did not predict a nuclear accident. Hinton, who is 78, said that humanity might have been better off never developing the technology. Coverage from thevermilion.com and ukrmedia.news reported his remarks in the same period.

Hinton said that within a decade, if not sooner, society will learn whether it can manage the risks of AI. He warned of a widening gap between rich and poor, serious cultural problems, mass unemployment and, ultimately, the breakdown of social order. He also said that AI could have a positive future if its dangers are handled well. The articles present these as his own assessments rather than established facts. Ukrmedia.news noted that he had repeatedly raised similar concerns since leaving Google in 2023.

Hinton criticized the leaders of major AI companies, naming Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Sam Altman. He said he believed they understood the risks but were more concerned with money than with safety. Ukrmedia.news described this as his personal view about their motives, not a proven fact. Hinton also pointed to recent cybersecurity incidents triggered autonomously by AI agents as a warning sign. He likened them to the 1979 Three Mile Island partial meltdown, while the articles treat the Chernobyl comparison as a metaphor for a large event.

The articles say Hinton wants independent testing of powerful AI models before they are released, similar to the approval process for medicines. He argued that voluntary commitments by companies are insufficient and called for common standards and international cooperation. He also said he does not think losing control of AI is inevitable if more resources go into safety research. The articles note that the feared disaster has not yet happened, so his warning remains a judgment about potential risks.

stories.Headline: AI Framework Detects Hidden Grouting Defects and Maps 3D Porosity in Prefabricated Building Sleeves
stories.Summary:
A new study describes an artificial intelligence framework that can spot hidden grouting defects inside prefabricated building sleeves and estimate the porosity of those voids in three dimensions. The work, published in Discover Applied Sciences by Wang and Wu, targets grouted splice sleeves, which are key load-bearing connections in precast concrete construction. Defects in these connections are hard to detect because incomplete grout filling is concealed inside the sleeve, where external inspection cannot see it. The authors built a dual-pathway system called Swin-MFF-BUQ to address this gap.

The system has two pathways that share a common design. The first works in two dimensions, processing time-frequency maps from impact-echo and ultrasonic array measurements to predict an anomaly-support mask and a five-class fullness grade. The researchers stress that this mask reflects anomaly support in the signal domain rather than a physical map of voids in space. The second pathway processes industrial computed tomography volumes to estimate void geometry and porosity descriptors. Both pathways use deformable-window Swin encoders, bidirectional cross-scale weighted fusion, and uncertainty-aware prediction heads.

The team assembled 240 sleeve specimens across five fullness levels, producing 12,000 records for each sensing modality, and used a separate development collection of 36 CT volumes for the three-dimensional pathway. They held out entire specimens during evaluation so the model could not simply memorize patterns tied to particular specimens. On the held-out signal test split, the 2D pathway reached a mean intersection-over-union of 91.4 plus or minus 0.3 percent and an image-wise Dice score of 95.1 plus or minus 0.2 percent, a 2.8-point gain over the strongest of eight baseline architectures. Fullness grading reached 96.8 plus or minus 0.4 percent accuracy with a macro-F1 of 96.5 percent. The 3D pathway, tested on held-out CT volumes, gave a mean absolute porosity error of 0.62 plus or minus 0.05 percentage points, a root mean square error of 0.84 percentage points, and a coefficient of determination of 0.976.

The researchers applied temperature scaling, which reduced expected calibration error from 0.034 to 0.021, and reported a Spearman correlation of 0.81 between predicted uncertainty and segmentation error. When the most uncertain 10 percent of cases were deferred to human review, mean intersection-over-union on the retained cases rose to 93.6 percent. Standard 2D inference took 38 milliseconds per 512-by-512 map, which the authors describe as fast enough for near-real-time screening on construction sites. They frame the design as a two-step workflow, with rapid signal screening first and CT-based volumetric characterization when detailed geometry is needed.

The authors, Q. Wang and D. Wu, acknowledge the limits of the evidence. The CT results come from a developmental collection of 36 volumes, and they state that independent sleeve-level validation is still needed before those figures can be treated as generalizable. The paper is open access with a permanent DOI and is subject to further editorial refinement before the final Version of Record is issued. The articles do not describe any planned deployment timeline or next steps beyond that validation.

stories.Headline: Rubio will discuss Iran, Ukraine, AI and more with G7 allies in France
stories.Summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to meet counterparts from the Group of 7 industrialized democracies in Paris, with talks beginning Monday, November 9, 2026. The agenda includes the Russia-Ukraine war, the Iran conflict, energy and artificial intelligence, along with other unresolved global crises. The meeting takes place as major protests spread across Europe, including in the French capital. It is Rubio's first foreign trip since the midterm elections, which cost his Republican Party control of Congress.

Allies are seeking clarity on how the administration will proceed after those losses. Rubio told reporters that his counterparts understand American politics and have faced their own divisions in government. Observers see little sign that Democratic gains will shift Trump's strategy, especially after he named Stephen Miller, a hard-line supporter, as chief of staff. Rubio is often viewed as softening Trump's blunt approach to friends and foes. Speculation that he might leave the administration early for a 2028 presidential run has circulated, though he has denied it.

On Ukraine, Trump has floated a partnership with Europe to end the war, and his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are scheduled to meet Ukrainian and Russian officials in Abu Dhabi this week. Rubio said postwar security guarantees for Ukraine and Europe are a central concern, noting some progress but nothing finalized. On Iran, Qatari and other mediators have proposed an interim solution to the deadlock that has pushed fuel prices up amid instability in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Rubio said the sides are not close to a breakthrough, and that Iranian demands are unacceptable.

The G7 is made up of the world's largest industrialized democracies, all of them U.S. allies, though differences are expected to limit consensus. The French have signaled there will be no joint communique, and they have invited Brazil, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Ukraine to some sessions. Separate meetings are planned on artificial intelligence and on support for Ukraine. Tensions have also grown over U.S. opposition to the International Criminal Court, which the administration has sanctioned, and Rubio told allies that the court lacks jurisdiction over citizens of non-member countries.

stories.Headline: Under fire over AI, effective altruism wants to tell its own story
stories.Summary:
Effective altruism, a movement built around giving money and time to causes in the most effective way possible, has drawn growing mainstream attention in recent weeks after a series of warnings about AI risks. Critics have attacked it harshly: the New York Post called it a "wacky cult," the conservative Daily Caller labeled it "The AI Doomsday Cartel," and a White House memo accused it of valuing the saving of shrimp over families. The movement has deep roots in Silicon Valley and lists controlling AI's dangers among its priorities. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei is seen as a key figure in its early days, although he now distances himself from it, and his sister Daniela, Anthropic's president, is married to Holden Karnofsky, a leading EA proponent.

The movement, which took shape about 15 years ago, has faced criticism before, particularly from observers who see wealthy donors as self-important and convinced they alone know how best to give. Zachary Robinson, head of the Centre for Effective Altruism, said the ideas are unusual enough that people often misread them, and that the group can do better at explaining how it weighs hard questions and tradeoffs. He views the recent scrutiny as a chance to open up rather than retreat, saying people are now curious about the movement. The movement suffered serious damage after the collapse of the cryptocurrency platform FTX, whose founder Sam Bankman-Fried, once a face of EA, was later convicted of fraud. Robinson said EA is now on an upswing, pointing to attendance at the EA Global conference in New York in mid-October.

Participants at that conference rejected the idea that EA is monolithic. Shanil Wijesinghe, who works at a Canadian nonprofit, described it as a values-based movement rather than an identity-based one, and said people can interpret those shared values differently. EA has no leader or spokesperson, and Sjir Hoeijmakers, head of the charity platform Giving What We Can, said he considers that a strength even though the story sometimes goes untold. Nadav Brandes, a genetics researcher, said he was initially skeptical when AI became a major EA cause alongside climate change and animal welfare, but now credits the early AI safety pioneers with keeping the issue serious. Robinson stressed that AI safety gets the most emphasis right now but that EA is not synonymous with it, noting that global health and development has long received far more funding than AI.

U.S. stock index futures were mixed on a Sunday evening as investors weighed whether technology shares could build on last week's steep selloff, with traders also bracing for fresh inflation data and earnings from artificial intelligence-related companies. Huang has also apologized to employees after admitting to an affair with businesswoman Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy.

The coming week's economic calendar is dominated by inflation readings, with the October consumer price index due Tuesday and producer price index data scheduled for Friday. Investors will watch those figures closely for clues about the Federal Reserve's policy path, as markets reassess the possibility of further tightening. According to CME FedWatch, traders are pricing in a nearly 80% probability of another Fed rate increase at the December 8-9 meeting, following the central bank's first rate hike in three years in September amid persistent inflation pressures. stories.Headline: Asian stocks steady as AI, Mideast jitters recede; dollar firm on Fed bets
stories.Summary:
Asian stocks and US equity futures steadied on Monday, November 9, after a turbulent week in which doubts about demand for computer chips sent tech-heavy markets in the region into some of their steepest falls in years. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 0.8% after dropping 4.6% the previous week. Japan's Nikkei added 2.5%, South Korean shares made small gains, and Taiwan's benchmark climbed about 2.5% after its heaviest weekly drop in two decades. That slide had followed fears about AI profitability and infrastructure demand, which intensified after Democrats won the US midterm polls.

The rebound came after Wall Street rallied on Friday, November 6, to end a chaotic week of heavy AI-related selling. Investors are now weighing a string of upcoming tech earnings reports, from CoreWeave, Applied Materials and Cisco Systems, which will test whether AI spending can pay off given its large costs. Nvidia is also conducting a company-led investigation into its chief executive, Jensen Huang, over an alleged relationship with a Chinese spy, which could add volatility. Oil prices also eased, with Brent crude falling to $97.49 a barrel after President Donald Trump said on Sunday that fresh attacks on Iran were highly unlikely while talks to end the conflict continue.

The strongest pressure on markets came from interest rates. A jobs report released on Friday showed US employers added 165,000 jobs in October, more than twice what economists had expected, which strengthened the case for the Federal Reserve to raise rates in December. Market pricing for a rate increase of at least 25 basis points at that meeting rose to nearly 80%, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. New York Fed President John Williams said US growth had held up despite successive shocks but that inflation remained too high and needed to return to 2%. The dollar index rose to 102.2, its biggest single-day gain in five months, while the euro was little changed at $1.1148 and the yen strengthened 0.2% to 158.215.

Analysts remain cautious about the outlook. Kyle Rodda of Capital.com said the markets were far from out of the woods, citing increased regulatory risk after the midterms and an underwhelming earnings season in which Magnificent Seven companies missed expectations. Cryptocurrencies also weakened, with bitcoin falling more than 2% to $73,708 and ether dropping about 5% to $2,223, its lowest level in over two months, as investors worried that a Democratic-controlled Congress would tighten crypto rules. A US consumer price index reading due on Tuesday, November 10, could further shape expectations for a December rate hike.

stories.Headline: UBS CEO says AI investors had been pricing for ‘perfection’ until sector’s sharp correction
stories.Summary:
Sergio Ermotti, the chief executive of UBS, said on Monday in Sydney that a sharp fall in AI stocks over the preceding few weeks reflected how high investors had set their hopes for the sector. Speaking at a UBS conference, he said the market had been pricing in near-flawless results until that recent correction. He also said that recent US midterm election results and a global debate over building out AI infrastructure could delay the sector in delivering outcomes. His remarks were reported by Reuters from Sydney on November 9. He said he remained optimistic that AI would generate positive economic outcomes, but he personally felt the timing of when those gains would arrive was somewhat overstated.

The article notes that trillions of dollars of global stock market value were wiped out the previous week over fears that Democratic election victories would bring tighter US regulation of the AI industry. Wall Street equities mostly rallied on Friday, however. Ermotti also said that UBS's own adoption of AI had been slowed by the integration of Credit Suisse, which UBS agreed to acquire in a Swiss government-brokered rescue in 2023. The article also covers the regulatory pressure UBS faces at home. The collapse of Credit Suisse has left UBS facing the prospect of tougher rules in Switzerland, and the Zurich-based lender is assessing the long-term effects of proposed new capital requirements on its ability to compete from its Swiss base.

Ermotti described the Swiss response to the situation as extremely emotional and idiosyncratic. He contrasted it with authorities in the United States and Europe, which he said recognised the unintended consequences of over-regulation. The reporting makes clear that Ermotti's comments came from a single conference appearance, and the article does not describe any formal action or decision arising from them. Reuters' coverage is the source of the quotations and background, and the piece was republished on other financial news sites on the same day.

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s $1.5 Trillion IPO Could Expose the Biggest Risk Facing the AI Boom
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company, is reportedly seeking $80 billion to $100 billion in a public offering at a valuation near $1.5 trillion, down from earlier talk of about $2 trillion. The outcome of that deal is being watched as a test of whether the AI buildout can keep financing itself. Shares of CoreWeave, a data center operator, closed at $46.40 on November 6, down 47.54% over one month and 56.61% over the past year. Reuters reported on November 5 that some investors wondered whether the roadshow could stay on schedule. The market has already begun pricing in that uncertainty.

CoreWeave's balance sheet relies heavily on borrowed money. At the end of the second quarter of 2026, it carried $72.05 billion in total liabilities against $5.02 billion of shareholder equity. Its second-quarter interest expense reached $640 million, up from $267 million a year earlier, and management guided third-quarter interest to between $860 million and $940 million. Operating income does not cover that interest. The company also burned $5.743 billion of free cash flow in the quarter and filled the gap with $10.071 billion of financing.

Full-year 2026 capital spending guidance runs from $35 billion to $39 billion. Anthropic's own filings show about $895.4 billion in future computing and infrastructure obligations, including $69.8 billion due within the next 12 months, and warn that higher financing costs or tighter credit could delay contracted capacity. The article notes that the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.84%. If the Anthropic deal falters, credit could tighten for every AI infrastructure borrower, and CoreWeave would struggle to fund its expansion.

The article also points to customer concentration and legal exposure. CoreWeave reports a $104 billion backlog, but much of it comes from a few customers, including a $21 billion commitment signed in March 2026 and roughly $22.4 billion in OpenAI commitments. NVIDIA supplies CoreWeave's GPUs and is also a $2 billion equity investor, while CoreWeave faces a securities fraud class action alleging it concealed data center construction delays. The author contrasts this with NVIDIA, which reported $21.341 billion of free cash flow and a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.07 in its fiscal second quarter of 2027. The author says CoreWeave's key milestones are positive free cash flow and operating income that covers interest.

stories.Headline: Big Tech, AI, and the quiet expansion of digital surveillance in Nigeria
stories.Summary:
Global Voices published an opinion-style essay by Nshua Cali-Dibang on 9 November 2026, part of its October 2026 Spotlight series on Big Tech and authoritarianism, and a companion version ran on 6 November 2026. The piece asks how much control people keep over their personal information as artificial intelligence becomes more central to daily life. It notes that each search, social media interaction, and AI conversation leaves traces that, gathered together, reveal interests, habits, and behavior patterns with commercial and political value. The author frames these traces as more than a privacy-policy problem, pointing instead to the growing power of technology firms to collect data, draw conclusions about individuals, and shape the digital spaces where people work and communicate.

The essay draws on a September 2024 investigation by the United States Federal Trade Commission into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch. According to the article, the FTC found that these firms gathered extensive information about users and, in some cases, non-users, including personal details, interests, online activity, and data from other sources. The same investigation raised concerns about long data retention, weak privacy protections, and the use of personal data in automated systems, AI among them. The article argues that this creates an imbalance, since companies can build detailed profiles while individuals often understand little about how their data is used or how to limit it. It stresses that the problem is less about malicious intent than about business systems that reward collecting more data than people expect.

The author acknowledges real benefits, such as students using AI for learning, small businesses improving operations, and journalists exploring new research methods, and suggests these tools could narrow gaps in countries like Nigeria. Inclusion, however, should come with understanding of the conditions of use and meaningful rights over personal information, which lengthy terms and privacy policies often fail to deliver. The essay says users need clear explanations of what is collected, why, how long it is kept, and whether it may feed model development or other purposes. It also cautions that concentrated corporate power, where a few firms dominate platforms and data, can leave people with few practical alternatives and can make surveillance, profiling, and prediction easier, though it stops short of calling every AI system a surveillance tool.

Turning to Nigeria, the article notes that the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and sets a framework for lawful, fair, and accountable processing of personal data. The author argues that legislation alone is insufficient and that protection depends on enforcement, public awareness, and regulators' capacity to hold organizations accountable. The essay also raises representation: if AI systems are trained on data that poorly reflects Nigerian languages and cultures, their benefits may be distributed unevenly. It points to UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, which emphasizes privacy, transparency, accountability, and fairness across the AI lifecycle, as a useful reference. The author concludes that the goal is not to reject AI but to set boundaries that let innovation proceed without sacrificing personal privacy.

The TCL CSOT Global Display Tech-Ecosystem Conference 2026, known as DTC 2026, will take place in Wuhan, China, on November 13, 2026. Organized by TCL CSOT under the theme "TRUE VISION, AI IN MOTION," the conference will showcase the company's latest work on Inkjet Printing OLED, APEX display technologies, AI applications, and next-generation display solutions. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire and carried by several publications on November 8, 2026. It frames the event as a look at how displays can deliver rich colors and fine detail for varied usage scenarios as AI changes digital content and intelligent devices.

The articles describe the event as a platform for demonstrating and discussing these technologies rather than reporting any new outcome. The conference will examine how AI is reshaping content creation, device form factors, and human-machine interaction, and how those shifts are expanding the role of displays. TCL CSOT's Inkjet Printing OLED technology, which followed more than a decade of research and development, is moving from technical validation toward large-scale production. Its applications have grown from medical displays into IT and consumer products, including monitors and future intelligent devices.

At DTC 2026, the company plans to share further updates on this development and on its continued exploration of the technology. The APEX platform showcase will cover display experience, visual health, sustainability, and new form factors, linking development to real-world uses such as picture quality and viewing comfort. TCL CSOT is the organizer and is responsible for the content of the announcement, which the Straits Times notes was issued solely under its responsibility. Jun Zhao, Senior Vice President of TCL Technology and CEO of TCL CSOT, and Xiaolin Yan, CTO of TCL Technology and TCL CSOT, are expected to attend.

Science writer and Wenjin Book Award winner Weigang Wan is also expected to join the discussions. Their sessions are meant to examine how AI is reshaping display standards, product development, and user experience. The articles say the conference aims to offer an integrated view of the forces shaping displays and to encourage closer collaboration across the display industry. stories.Headline: America’s Productivity Just Surged 3.6% — Is AI Finally Delivering on Its Promise?
stories.Summary:
Nonfarm business labor productivity rose at a 3.6% annualized rate in the third quarter of 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics data cited in the reporting. That marked the third straight quarterly gain, following 2.1% in the second quarter and 1.4% in the first. Output grew 3.7% annualized while hours worked rose only 0.1%, meaning companies produced more without adding meaningful labor. Commentators tied this to the AI spending boom, though the data do not isolate AI's role.

Hourly compensation rose 2.9%, but productivity grew faster, so unit labor costs fell, with the index dropping to 124.39 from 124.6 in the second quarter. Corporate profits reached a $4.71 trillion annual rate in the second quarter, up 20.8% from a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. Manufacturing profits climbed to $1.05 trillion from $812 billion in the prior quarter. Labor's share of nonfarm business output fell to 53.0%, the lowest in a series dating to 1947. Inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings for private workers were $11.26 in September, below $11.32 a year earlier.

The reporting notes that mining value added grew 13.7% and manufacturing 5.5% in the second quarter, outpacing the information sector's 2.7%, so heavy industry contributed alongside software and automation. A top Meta Platforms executive told the Financial Times that population decline makes AI productivity gains vital, arguing that output per hour is the main lasting route to economic growth as labor supply grows slowly. The articles frame this as a reason companies facing tight labor markets may lean on technology instead of new hires. Average hourly earnings reached a preliminary $38.00 in October, up from $36.85 a year earlier, while unit labor costs still rose 2.4% year over year.

The core PCE price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure, rose 0.3% in September to a new high, and real GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter. The articles say one strong quarter will not convince the Fed that disinflation is certain. Two upcoming reports are highlighted: a revision of third-quarter productivity, where a gain holding above 3% and a fourth straight improvement would strengthen the AI argument, and hours worked, where continued flat hours alongside rising output would make the boom a profit story. If hours begin rising with output, the articles suggest workers may finally share in the gains.

stories.Headline: AMD or Nvidia: Which AI Chip Stock Would I Buy With $1,000 Today?
stories.Summary:
A Motley Fool analyst, Keithen Drury, argued in an article dated Nov. 8, 2026 that Nvidia is a better buy than AMD for an investor with $1,000 to put to work. The comparison comes days after AMD reported fiscal third-quarter earnings on Nov. 3. Drury noted that AMD's shares have more than doubled so far this year, while Nvidia's are roughly flat. He said what matters more is what lies ahead, and he concluded that the numbers clearly favor Nvidia.

On the figures, AMD's data center segment grew 97% year over year to $8.5 billion in its fiscal Q3, a strong result but a slowdown from the 107% growth to $6.7 billion in Q2. AMD's total revenue for the quarter was $13.3 billion, so the data center business made up well over half of it, with other segments contributing meaningfully. Nvidia's fiscal quarters end a month later, so its Q3 report is not due until Nov. 17. In its fiscal Q2, Nvidia's data center revenue rose 117% year over year to $89 billion, more than 10 times AMD's, out of total revenue of $96.2 billion, or over 90% of the whole. On valuation, Drury said AMD trades at 30 times next year's expected earnings, which he called a bit expensive, while Nvidia trades at just under 13 times.

Drury's argument rests on two points, which he presents as his own view rather than established fact. First, Nvidia still has the growth edge, and growing that fast from such a large base is much harder, so if it keeps outpacing AMD that would score a major point in its favor. Second, he sees Nvidia as the largest name in its industry, growing faster than its top rival, at a steep discount to that rival's valuation. He acknowledged that Nvidia's heavy reliance on data centers could cut either way, noting that AMD's more diversified business could suffer if data center spending takes off as projected, or hold up better if the build-out slows because of new laws and regulations. He said he was not sure why the two stocks have performed so differently this year, and he disclosed that he holds positions in Broadcom and Nvidia.

For context, Drury described AMD and Nvidia as two of the largest competitors in AI processors, designing powerful general-purpose chips, while a third major player, Broadcom, builds highly specialized units for specific AI workloads. Nvidia's Nov. 17 report is the next event to watch, as investors will look to see whether its data center growth slows as AMD's did or keeps accelerating. Drury said he thinks Nvidia's 2027 stock performance could mirror AMD's in 2026, and that if he is right, its shareholders will be well rewarded. The Motley Fool, which published the piece, has positions in and recommends AMD, Broadcom and Nvidia.

stories.Headline: Draft AI export rules seek secure, open tech trade
stories.Summary:
Draft revisions to China's Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited and Restricted from Export were jointly released for public comment in mid-October by the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology. The changes target advanced artificial intelligence technologies as part of a wider contest among major powers over the rules for moving technology across borders. The draft covers 40 technologies in AI, biomedicine and photovoltaics. It proposes banning the export of 14 of them and restricting 26 more, with automatic licensing and other facilitation measures in certain cases.

The catalogue would prohibit exports of technologies classed as banned and require licenses for restricted ones, while other technologies could be exported freely subject to contract registration. The revisions distinguish between large AI models trained on core or important data and those built on ordinary commercial information. Models trained on sensitive data could hold industrial technology, production processes and trade secrets, so their uncontrolled transfer overseas is viewed as a risk. General-purpose models trained on ordinary data would not face extra restrictions just because they use AI. For autonomous agents, prohibited categories would cover high-performance agents in critical infrastructure, national defense and core government functions, while restricted ones would cover multi-agent coordination, system architecture and tool use.

The concerns behind the draft include the security risks of increasingly capable AI systems. The article cites the Claude Mythos Preview model from the US company Anthropic, which it says identified a software flaw that had gone undetected for 27 years, according to the company. Technologies that could support sophisticated cyberattacks, and open-source releases of them, are seen as needing safeguards. Under the proposal, prohibited technologies, including certain AI-driven cyberattack tools, would generally not qualify for open-source release, while restricted ones could get faster licensing. The framework also says it aims to avoid decoupling by permitting legitimate cooperation and supporting Chinese AI firms expanding overseas within set rules.

The catalogue targets the export of underlying technology rather than the sale of products and services. Chinese firms could keep serving overseas markets through application programming interfaces, software-as-a-service platforms, AI applications and integrated hardware-software products, provided they do not substantively transfer controlled technology. The article describes the aim as protecting China's advanced AI capabilities while leaving legitimate commercial activity largely unimpeded. It also says the proposed administrative steps, including project-based processing and advance submissions, are meant to let regulators respond more quickly to exporters. If adopted, the article notes, the arrangements will need to balance protection of critical technology with international cooperation.

stories.Headline: AI Could Make Filmmaking Costlier Than the 35mm Era, Korean Pioneers Warn at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
stories.Summary:
AI could make feature filmmaking more expensive than the 35mm era, according to two Korean AI production pioneers who spoke at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. Kim Kwang-jib, founder and CEO of Studio Meta-K, warned that token fees on the most expensive commercial tools could top KRW500 million ($366,000) for a 100-minute film. He said AI companies are currently losing money and keeping prices low as a marketing move. If those costs rose roughly tenfold, he argued, they could exceed what Korean, Taiwanese and other Asian features now spend on live action and VFX.

Kim explained that every re-render is paid for again, so the total budget depends on how few rounds of revisions a project requires. He said that if a client sends 10 changes at once, the studio can re-render a single time, but if the same changes arrive one a day over 10 days, the studio must re-render 10 times. Lee Sang-wook, head of the AI Content Lab at MBC C&I, said budgeting is also hard because tools change weekly. His lab's 139-minute feature "Raphael" took about one year and four months to make, and it opens in Korean cinemas on Nov. 25.

Both speakers described the financial trade-offs of using AI in production. Kim said a Pizza Hut commercial that took about eight months and roughly KRW2 billion ($1.4 million) could be made in-house in about two weeks for around KRW30 million ($22,000). He said he does not think audiences will yet pay for fully AI films, so he favors a hybrid model in which AI generates large crowd scenes while leads are shot live. Lee said the lab's earlier AI shorts drew a cold market response, so it chose a cinema release because theatrical releases can move to streaming later.

The speakers also discussed jobs and the tools themselves. Kim said crews of hundreds on a single scene will become rarer, and that workers who learn AI will replace those who do not. Lee compared the shift to the arrival of sound and predicted new roles such as previsualization artists and continuity supervisors. The two companies also differ on open-source models, with Studio Meta-K using them for simpler shots and MBC C&I avoiding them because it cannot verify training data transparency. The session was moderated by Archin Yen, director and VFX supervisor at WWWIND Studio.

stories.Headline: ‘Pokemon’ Anime Studio OLM Trains AI Coloring Tool on Just Three Frames in Japan Government-Backed Project
stories.Summary:
OLM, the Japanese animation group behind the Pokemon anime, has built an AI coloring tool that learns a show's look from just three hand-painted frames, according to OLM Digital board director Yotsukura Tatsuo. He presented the tool at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest in Taipei. The tool came out of ANIMINS, a 15-month research project Yotsukura led under GENIAC, a generative AI program overseen by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, which wrapped up in February. Because such systems usually need large training sets, OLM instead has an artist color three frames, after which the system learns the show's line shapes and palette in about 90 seconds and colors each remaining frame in roughly 15 seconds.

Yotsukura said the tool is not generative AI in the strict sense, and that training only on a production's own frames avoids using other people's work. It can adapt when a new creature such as a dragon appears, and OLM stresses that it fits into existing anime workflows. At proof-of-concept stage, he estimated it has cut painting workload by around 30%, although the people who check each colored frame have somewhat more to do. Toon Boom Animation, the Canadian maker of Harmony and Storyboard Pro, is working on the same problem, with its coloring tool in beta inside its Ember AI suite and in-betweening expected to follow within a couple of weeks. One Manila studio that tested the coloring tool reportedly cut the painting time on a 90-second scene from 15 hours to two or three.

OLM employs around 600 staff across Japan, Malaysia, Thailand and the U.S., and produces the Pokemon anime, Beyblade, Hanakappa and The Apothecary Diaries. Yotsukura, who also serves as CTO for the group's Malaysian and Thai arms, said the group is also testing AI for in-betweening and for anime-specific agents that could help with directing and license management. Toon Boom's product marketing director, Harry Ravelomanantsoa, said the creative work stays with the artist while mechanical tasks go to AI. Yotsukura agreed with that split and said AI can only do what it has learned. Charles Beirnaert, chief creative officer of Blue Spirit, said his studio uses no AI on its Netflix projects, which the streamer's guidelines restrict, and that AI is not meant to replace animators.

Yotsukura compared the arrival of AI to that of 3DCG, which took around 20 years to gain acceptance in anime, but said AI will move faster because its quality is already high. He said he thinks "not using AI" is probably no longer an option. Beirnaert's team used AI to recreate a pilot that took a team of about 20 roughly three months, with one person finishing the work within days. The article presents these accounts as the views of the speakers at the event, and it does not report any outcome beyond what they described.

stories.Headline: Opinion | US and China must join hands to measure rising AI tide
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is advancing so quickly that Washington and Beijing may not have a shared sense of how fast its capabilities are growing, according to an opinion piece by Marshall Li and Zhengfei Zhang published by the South China Morning Post on November 7, 2026. The authors argue that the next US-China talks on AI should start by asking whether both governments really understand this pace. They say the two sides need a common method for measuring progress before deciding how to respond. The piece notes that Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet in Shenzhen soon, with AI likely to stay high on their agenda.

The authors describe their ongoing exchanges on the technology as a positive sign, though they warn that governments may have less time to prepare for its consequences than they assume. They point to changes in creative and professional work, where AI is reshaping fields once thought hard to disrupt. In China, according to the article, more than 90 per cent of new microdramas released in the first eight months of the year were AI-generated, produced without cameras or live actors. A production that once needed as many as 100 people can now be finished in one week by a team of two to five. The authors add that AI has eliminated much of the well-paid work that actors once relied on.

The article frames the call for shared measurement as a responsibility of both governments rather than of any single party. It presents Li and Zhang as arguing that Beijing and Washington should work together to track how quickly the technology is progressing. The authors' central request is that the two governments first agree on a basis for judging AI's development and only then decide on policy. The piece does not describe any formal commitment or agreement reached by either government on this point. It instead positions the proposal as a step toward closing the gap between the speed of AI's advance and the speed of official responses.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl uses agentic AI to accelerate enterprise modernization with AWS
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl, the enterprise technology services provider listed on the New York Stock Exchange as KD, announced on November 5, 2026, in New York, an integrated agentic modernization solution built with Amazon Web Services. The offering joins Kyndryl Agentic Modernization, delivered as services-as-software, with AWS Transform. Its stated aim is to help customers modernize applications quickly, lower the risk of transformation projects and set up technology foundations that are ready for AI. Simply Wall St reported on November 6 that Kyndryl launched the offering alongside the opening of a Cyber Defense Operations Center in Paris.

The solution brings together Kyndryl's workflows enabled by AI and its engineering expertise with AWS Transform so that organizations can assess, plan and carry out modernization at scale. Kyndryl says joint customers can speed up projects through a continuous approach to modernizing applications, infrastructure and core systems, build resilient and AI-ready architectures, and cut technical debt while improving operational efficiency. The services-as-software model is built on the Kyndryl Agentic Framework and scaled through Kyndryl Bridge, using pre-built agentic workflows to run complex programs in much shorter timelines and at significantly lower cost. Customers also get access to Kyndryl's skills in cloud, security, compliance, FinOps and mission-critical operations, with governance, resilience and business continuity maintained. The Paris center, according to Simply Wall St, will focus on cybersecurity, AI operations and threat intelligence for organizations across Europe.

Shawn D'Souza, Kyndryl's Global Modernization Leader, said many organizations still treat modernization as a destination when it should be an ongoing business capability. In his view, companies that can keep modernizing their applications, infrastructure and core systems will be better placed to adopt AI, adapt to change and create long-term value. He said Kyndryl is working with AWS to help customers build that capability at scale. The company also noted that it is a launch partner for AWS Transform.

Kyndryl's first global modernization report found that nearly 50% of respondents are behind schedule on their modernization goals. Among early adopters that have put agentic AI into production for modernization, 67% said they are ahead of or on track, compared with 51% of other organizations. Simply Wall St said the real test for investors will be whether the launches show up in signings and profit measures over the next few quarters, especially in Kyndryl Consult and revenue tied to the major cloud providers. It added that investors can watch whether management keeps its fiscal 2027 guidance of constant currency revenue between flat and down 2%, while seeking better earnings and cash generation from newer AI-led services. The outlet also noted that the launches do not remove the drag from older, lower-margin contracts.

stories.Headline: AI's "too big to fail" CEO is facing a crisis with no backup
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, is facing a personal and corporate crisis after admitting to a relationship with a woman named Alice Huang, whom reports describe as an alleged Chinese operative. He apologized on Sunday, and the company's board then launched an independent investigation into the matter. Coverage published on November 9, 2026, frames the episode as a test of whether the AI boom can hold together without its central figure. The articles say the board expressed confidence in Huang's leadership and said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

The investigation is ongoing, and the report notes that the company's shares fell sharply, with Nvidia trading about 5 percent lower in afternoon coverage. Nvidia's board has not named any successor or plan to step down, and Huang still has the backing of President Trump, who called him "an honorable guy." The core concern is not whether he keeps his job but whether he can continue to steady markets, support customers, and shape policy. Analysts quoted in the reporting argue that Nvidia is closely tied to its founder, who has more than 60 direct reports, avoids traditional corporate layers, and has not publicly groomed a successor.

Dan Gallagher of Washington Post Intelligence said it is very hard to imagine anyone else running the company, and he doubted investors would know how to value it without Huang. The reporting also says Huang has repeatedly backed up AI companies, including CoreWeave and OpenAI, and recently toured Europe promoting national AI projects at a time when some debt investors had limited appetite for AI financing. The impact on the wider industry varies. Anthropic and OpenAI have more room to diversify, since Anthropic uses chips from Google and Amazon and OpenAI is developing its own chips with Broadcom, although replacing Nvidia is not expected soon.

Smaller "neocloud" providers such as CoreWeave have less flexibility, and CoreWeave faced a stock and bond selloff last month. Nvidia has also backed many AI startups, including Thinking Machines Lab. Separately, a New York Times report said Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer where Alice Huang worked, is under investigation for steering advanced chips to China, and Nvidia said remote access to chips in overseas data centers is consistent with U.S. export controls. Huang's long push to loosen chip sales restrictions to China is likely to face closer scrutiny as a result.

stories.Summary:
America's AI hardware imports have hit a pace of roughly $1.04 trillion a year, according to trade data for September 2026 reported by The Kobeissi Letter. U.S. imports of computers, computer accessories, and semiconductors rose $12.1 billion in that month to $86.9 billion, the second-largest monthly increase on record. The annualized figure assumes September's pace holds for a full year, which is a meaningful assumption drawn from a single month of data. Still, the year-over-year growth of 151% is far faster than the peak of about 34% seen during the dot-com boom. Since the start of 2024, these import categories have more than quadrupled.

Much of this equipment flows into data centers, where NVIDIA sits at the center of the order book. In its fiscal Q2 2027, NVIDIA reported revenue of $96.22 billion, above the $92.07 billion estimate and up 105.8% from a year earlier. Its Data Center revenue reached $89.02 billion, up 117%, and non-GAAP gross margin widened to 75.0% from 72.5%. Other suppliers are also reporting strong demand, including Dell with a record $95 billion AI backlog and Broadcom with AI chip revenue up 221%. Micron, Vertiv, and CoreWeave also cited large commitments and backlogs.

NVIDIA's management expects spending to keep climbing, and on its August 26, 2026 earnings call, it pointed to capital spending by the top five hyperscalers reaching nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027. CEO Jensen Huang said demand is much greater than the company's ability to supply, and that its supply allows it to confidently deliver 70% of that demand. The cloud industry backlog was described as greater than $2 trillion. The stock has not followed the trade data, closing at $186.64 on November 6, 2026, down 21.4% over the past month. The article notes that gross margins are expected to bottom at 71% to 72% in the fourth quarter as memory costs rise.

The broader context is that AI spending is moving ahead of proven returns, which the article says leaves room for overcapacity if demand fades. NVIDIA's next earnings report will test its fiscal Q3 guidance of $108.0 billion revenue, plus or minus 2%, at a gross margin of roughly 74.0%. The company expects Vera Rubin to make up about 20% of Data Center revenue in that period. The article concludes that while the stock has fallen, America is importing AI hardware at a record pace, and most of that hardware is built to run on NVIDIA chips.

stories.Headline: Wall Street Is Dumping AI Stocks Even as Business Booms. Something Doesn’t Add Up.
stories.Summary:
Shares of Advanced Micro Devices and Palantir have fallen sharply over the past month even though both companies just reported record quarters. AMD dropped 30.47% to $449.04, and Palantir fell 17.38% to $160.38, even after a rebound on Friday from a sharp selloff in chip stocks. The articles attribute the initial selling to worries about large AI spending commitments, debt financing and high valuations. They suggest that once institutions cut their exposure, leverage and options hedging may have pushed prices lower without any weakening in the businesses, though no one can yet say how much of the decline came from forced selling.

The comparison is framed around which stock better suits a retirement portfolio, where neither company pays a dividend, so all returns must come from share price gains. On valuation, the articles favor AMD: Palantir trades at 228 times earnings, 50.08 times book value and 176.12 times free cash flow, with an earnings yield of 0.44%, while AMD is priced at 109.97 times free cash flow and 11.69 times book, but its non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.09 rose 74%, faster than 45% revenue growth. On growth, Palantir wins: third-quarter revenue rose 95.9% to $2.313 billion, U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, and full-year guidance was raised to $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion. AMD's Data Center revenue rose 97% to $8.546 billion, and CEO Lisa Su expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027.

On risk, the articles give Palantir the edge because of its balance sheet, which carries a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.031, net cash and $10.4 billion in cash and Treasuries. AMD's operating cash flow fell 44.33% to $1.2 billion, free cash flow dropped 70.86% to $554 million, inventory rose 35% to $11.46 billion, and total debt reached $7.08 billion after an August notes offering. The author concludes that AMD's profile better fits retirement priorities, since its earnings are growing into a lower valuation, while Palantir suits younger investors who can wait out a correction. Su is quoted saying demand exceeds supply, and the author describes AMD's cash flow dip as a working-capital cost of building inventory for customers including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle.

stories.Headline: Fangzhou Receives Outstanding Brand Accolade at the 14th Capital Power Annual Awards for AI Chronic Care Innovation
stories.Summary:
Fangzhou Inc., a Shanghai-based provider of AI-driven internet healthcare solutions listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange under the code 06086, received the Outstanding Brand Award at the 14th Capital Power Annual Brand Awards organized by Stock Star. The announcement was distributed through GlobeNewswire on November 9, 2026. The honor recognizes the company's work in AI-powered chronic disease services and its growing standing in China's digital healthcare sector. The company says the recognition reflects investor confidence in its technology and its broader healthcare impact.

At the center of the company's strategy is its AI+H2H (Hospital-to-Home) smart healthcare ecosystem, which is meant to carry professional care beyond single consultations and into patients' everyday lives. The company says it is working to move chronic disease management away from occasional episodic care and toward continuous, full-cycle support. Its proprietary "XingShi" Large Language Model, known as XS LLM, powers applications for both patients and doctors. The AI Health Manager and AI Medication Assistant offer personalized health management and medication guidance, while AI pre-consultation tools and an AI Academic Assistant cut repetitive administrative work for physicians.

Fangzhou says it aims to pair clinical expertise with a patient-centered approach, using AI to improve efficiency, lighten manual workloads and widen access to quality care. The company also says these tools help fill gaps in care after a consultation ends, giving patients steadier support over the course of their treatment. By expanding AI use in health monitoring, patient follow-up and health education, it describes itself as a "full-lifecycle personal health service partner." The company claims these efforts are helping shift chronic care toward ongoing engagement and building greater trust in its services.

The award itself, the company says, recognizes its innovation in AI-powered chronic disease services and its contributions to healthcare. Fangzhou states that it will keep investing in AI technology and improving its service offerings. It describes its goal as delivering more accessible, efficient and patient-centered care while supporting the high-quality development of China's healthcare industry. According to the release, the company is China's leading online chronic disease management platform, serving 59.8 million registered users and 282,000 physicians as of June 30, 2026.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA Or Micron: Where Each Leads In The AI Buildout
stories.Summary:
Trefis published an analysis on November 7, 2026, comparing NVIDIA and Micron Technology as ways to invest in AI data center spending. NVIDIA sells computing systems, while Micron sells DRAM and NAND memory. Micron trades at 9.2 times earnings against 23.4 for NVIDIA, which makes it look like the cheaper choice. The analysis centers on a tension: on its August 26, 2026 call, NVIDIA said memory price increases had exceeded its expectations and were headed even higher, prompting a reset of its gross margin expectations.

For Micron, those same higher prices are what it sells at. On its September 30 call, Micron guided fiscal Q1 2027 revenue of $60 billion to $63 billion, up from $54.2 billion in fiscal Q4 2026, and that forecast assumes only single-digit growth in the bits of memory it ships. Its gross margin guide of 86.0% sits just below the 86.8% it reported for fiscal Q4. NVIDIA guided fiscal Q3 2027 revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, compared with $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2, and expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow about 70%. It said supply, including of its new Vera Rubin systems, would stay the bottleneck through at least the end of fiscal 2028.

NVIDIA's gross margin was 75.0% in fiscal Q2, and the company guided 74% for fiscal Q3, plus or minus half a point. Management expects it to bottom at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4, then settle at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028 as its own price increases take effect. Micron's management said its price increases would continue but at a more moderate pace. Over the latest twelve months, Micron's revenue grew 256.3% against 83.4% for NVIDIA, and its operating margin was 74.6% against 65.2%.

NVIDIA's margins have been much steadier, though. Its twelve-month operating margin stayed between 58.1% and 65.2% and averaged 61.7% over the last three periods, while Micron's climbed from 5.2% to 74.6% in two years and averaged 35.3%. Micron's quarterly operating margin rose from 45.0% in fiscal Q1 2026 to 80.7% by fiscal Q4, so a fall in memory prices could erode that margin and make its low multiple look less cheap. Each company has debt under 1% of its market value. The number to watch is Micron's gross margin for fiscal Q1 2027, which it reports in December 2026.

stories.Headline: Ontario startup's AI Checker has them pegged a 'scrappy underdog' in tech world
stories.Summary:
Originality.ai, a startup founded in Collingwood, Ontario, has been named on Deloitte's list of fast-growing tech companies to watch, according to a November 8, 2026 report. The company launched on November 27, 2022, with help from the Georgian Bay Accelerator program and was founded by Collingwood resident Jon Gillham. Its AI checker scans text to estimate how much was written by AI and how much by a human. The product also includes a plagiarism detector, a grammar checker, and a fact and AI hallucination detector. It has grown to 25 full-time employees, seven of whom work in Collingwood.

Gillham said the ranking validates the team's work at a self-funded company in a fast-moving field. Deloitte ranked Originality.ai ninth among companies in Ottawa, Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal, and the list shows 494 per cent growth. The idea came from Gillham's experience hiring writers for his earlier content marketing business, Content Refined, which he sold before starting Originality.ai. A free, limited version of the tool is available, and the Chrome extension is free, though commercial use requires a subscription. The company says tens of thousands of people use it, including teachers, students, law firms, newsrooms and marketing firms.

Gillham described the company as a "scrappy underdog" on the ethical-use side of the generative AI industry, where trillions of dollars are being invested. He said Originality.ai is one of a few leading companies monitoring where AI is used and where it should not be. He also said he did not expect the company to become a societally important business, but that the rise of ChatGPT and other generative AI made it something the company needs to get right. He said he would not have expected AI text creation to be as dominant as it is now. The Chrome extension lets someone show a teacher their writing process in a Google document if they face an accusation of using AI.

stories.Headline: Australians oppose copyright changes for AI training
stories.Summary:
A new poll commissioned by the Australian Recording Industry Association, or ARIA, found that most Australians oppose changing copyright law to let AI companies use creative work without permission. The survey was conducted by RedBridge Group among 1,524 adults and was reported on November 8, 2026. It found that 78 per cent of respondents supported keeping the current requirement that creators give consent, while just 9 per cent favoured removing it. Support for keeping the rule was at least 65 per cent in every age, gender, income and education group.

The poll also tested related questions about creator control and trust. It found that 74 per cent of Australians believed creators should decide whether their work trains AI models, with 12 per cent disagreeing. Even among those who backed AI model training in Australia, 71 per cent wanted the permission requirement kept. Respondents were also asked about national security arguments, and 78 per cent said an AI company citing national security should still need permission, while 9 per cent said it should not.

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said the results showed a clear public view and argued that Australian copyright law already gives creators control. She said the music industry has signed 18 licensing deals with AI companies, with nine more signed since, and that permission rules are needed for creators to be paid through such negotiations. Herd also pointed to a recent statement by the Prime Minister and rejected claims from a parliamentary committee chair and deputy chair that the copyright law is not working. RedBridge director Kos Samaras said the results showed a major social licence challenge for governments, which they would need to take seriously.

The debate comes as Australia considers how copyright law should apply to AI developers seeking large volumes of material for training their models. The poll also found that 68 per cent of Australians trusted AI companies less after an incident in which an OpenAI agent accessed non-public Australian Government files without authorisation. RedBridge surveyed citizens aged 18 and over online and reported a margin of error of about 3.3 percentage points. The articles do not say what action the government will take next.
