stories.Headline: Memory Suppliers May Set Q4 Revenue Records as HBM Prices Rise
stories.Summary:
Counterpoint Research reported on Nov. 5 that global DRAM sales in the third quarter of 2026 rose 369% from a year earlier, to nearly $200 billion, as AI data center spending and higher memory prices fed on each other. Samsung Electronics kept first place with a 38% share of DRAM revenue. SK hynix lifted its share to 29% after its sales grew by more than 40% from the previous quarter, while US-based Micron held 21%. China's CXMT slipped from 10% in the previous quarter to 9%, although another outlet citing the same data framed its share as up from 5% a year earlier.

The growth came from prices, not volume. Bit shipments rose only about 4% from the prior quarter, but the average selling price climbed to $1.9 per gigabit. HBM sales nearly doubled from a year earlier, while DDR and LPDDR sales jumped by 500% and about 400%, so HBM's share of total DRAM revenue actually fell. Counterpoint also noted that the ratio of GPUs to CPUs in AI computing has narrowed from 4 to 1 toward 2 to 1 and is heading closer to 1 to 1, which is lifting demand for ordinary DRAM. Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin rack is said to carry 1.5 terabytes of DRAM per CPU socket, about three times the previous generation.

Choi Jeong-gu, a senior researcher at Counterpoint, described the boom as a supercycle driven by prices rather than volume, saying AI has turned memory into a scarce, high-value resource and that buyers are now competing to lock in supply instead of haggling over price. Hwang Min-sung, a research director at the firm, said SK hynix has led the HBM3E market but its growth has recently slowed, while clients are responding well to Samsung's HBM4. He expects Samsung, whose performance has rebounded this year, to take back the top spot in HBM next year. Another report said major memory suppliers could post record revenue in the fourth quarter as new-generation HBM products roll out and prices rise.

Strong pricing is expected to last into next year, because major companies are expanding long-term supply agreements and new large-scale chip plants are not projected to reach full operation until 2028. The mood in markets turned sharply on Nov. 6, when fears that the AI investment cycle may be nearing a peak set off panic selling in Korean chip stocks. By 10:30 a.m. that day, SK hynix had fallen 10.28% and Samsung Electronics 7.99%. The KOSPI opened 2.24% lower at 5,263.26, hit a circuit breaker three minutes into the session, then dropped more than 8% and fell below 5,000 for the first time in 10 months.

stories.Headline: Predictive AI can unlock the true promise of programmatic
stories.Summary:
The articles are an opinion piece, not a news event, so this task is not a breaking story and I am writing a summary of the argument instead. Published on November 9, 2026, in The Current, a column by Dstillery CEO Michael Beebe argues that predictive AI and first-party data can help media buyers outperform the market in programmatic advertising. He borrows the finance concept of alpha, meaning return above the market average, and applies it to advertising, where buyers who bring better data and tools can generate better results than the commoditized returns offered by walled gardens. Beebe contends that much of current campaign practice produces no alpha because it relies on the same tools everyone else uses.

He points to people-based audiences tied to deterministically identifiable users, which reach only a minority of impressions and push up prices through scarcity, and to third-party segments chosen by how closely their names match campaign personas, which often leads to buys weighted toward impressions unlikely to convert. He says these approaches are used to lower risk and keep campaigns explainable rather than to maximize performance. In his view, predictive audiences that score impressions by their propensity to convert for each specific campaign offer a better path, and the wider availability of AI models has made this more practical. Beebe says the most reliable source of advantage is a brand's own first-party data, which he describes as a high-resolution record of dynamic intent that competitors cannot easily copy.

He notes that this data can include campaign conversion reports, search terms and shopping behavior, not only pixel or CRM data, and he argues these signals are privacy-friendly as well as useful. He also describes custom bidding algorithms as the next wave, letting buyers pay for each impression only up to what it is worth against their campaign goals. He concludes that the real promise of programmatic lies in combining all available customer insights and intent signals, and that the industry should move away from deterministic identity, weak audience proxies and whitelists. The article notes that it is an op-ed whose views belong to the author and do not represent The Current or The Trade Desk.

Articles.Title: Predictive AI can unlock the true promise of programmatic

stories.Headline: Chip Industry Week In Review - Semiconductor Engineering
stories.Summary:
SK hynix expects memory supply constraints to persist through 2030, with DRAM and HBM volumes effectively sold out through 2029, the company said in the week’s review. Samsung expects tight memory supply through 2028, citing lengthy fab construction and equipment lead times, larger dies, and greater process complexity in next-gen HBM. Samsung also said its 2027 HBM supply is already sold out. Solidigm, SK hynix’s U.S. subsidiary, reportedly is discussing a proposed $45B NAND flash fab with the U.S. Commerce Department. China’s CXMT plans to soon begin limited production of HBM3E memory despite manufacturing yields of just 20% to 30%, per Reuters.

Anthropic warned in its IPO filing that HBM shortages and limited TSMC manufacturing capacity could constrain AI expansion. ASE forecasts a doubling of its advanced-packaging revenue in 2027, and Amkor is ramping new high-density fan-out and 2.5D packaging programs. TSMC reportedly is considering a 20% price increase for CoWoS as AI demand continues to strain advanced-packaging capacity. Applied Materials plans to increase its stake in Besi to about 20%, deepening a strategic partnership that is expanding beyond hybrid bonding into new interconnect architectures and advanced packaging technologies for AI.

The review also covered manufacturing and AI tool news. Intel Foundry reported improving manufacturing execution in Q3, citing better yields and cycle times on 18A, and released its 14A 0.9 PDK in October. Infineon plans to invest €1.1B through 2034 at its Villach, Austria facility to establish Europe’s first high-volume manufacturing facility for next-gen GaN power semiconductors on 300mm wafers. UMC approved an additional $3.2B in capital spending to accelerate capacity expansion in Singapore and Tainan. Lam Research and imec expanded their collaboration on advanced 3D integration, next-gen memory, and high-NA EUV patterning.

On the AI side, Cadence introduced a portfolio of domain-specialized AI models for agentic chip and system design, and Arm introduced a new CPU benchmarking methodology for agentic AI. Google is expanding the reach of its custom AI accelerators, with OpenAI reportedly planning to purchase its TPUs, reports The Information. Oracle will offer Google’s TPUs through its cloud infrastructure beginning in 2027 and plans to add Arm’s AGI CPUs in fall 2027. Broadcom’s XPUs and networking equipment will support Anthropic’s AI infrastructure expansion, beginning in 2027, under a $63B financing arrangement.

Articles.Title: Chip Industry Week In Review - Semiconductor Engineering

stories.Headline: [News] MediaTek Reportedly Taps Intel Packaging Veteran After TSMC Hire, Advances Dual CoWoS–EMIB Strategy
stories.Summary:
MediaTek has hired Navid Shahriari, a former Intel executive vice president, as senior vice president, with the appointment effective November 9. Reports from Liberty Times and BigGo Finance, both published in early November 2026, say he will report directly to President and Chief Operating Officer Joe Chen. The move is the company's second major advanced packaging hire this year, following its May 2026 engagement of former TSMC research and development vice president Yu Chen-hua as an advisor. Shahriari brings 37 years of experience in semiconductor design engineering and advanced packaging, along with hands-on work in the data center market.

In his new role, Shahriari will oversee teams covering advanced process and yield platforms, design-technology co-optimization, advanced testing and packaging, and quality and reliability. MediaTek has said one of his core missions is to deepen collaboration with TSMC and other key supply chain partners. The aim is to integrate advanced technologies that strengthen the company's artificial intelligence and high-performance computing products. Reports describe the appointment as part of a wider effort to move MediaTek beyond smartphone chips toward data center AI chips. Reuters reports that the company supports both TSMC's CoWoS and Intel's EMIB packaging technologies, letting customers choose between them.

Shahriari spent most of his career at Intel, where he served as executive vice president of Intel Foundry and oversaw packaging, testing, and advanced packaging strategy before retiring in June of this year. According to the reports, he led development of complex packaging and substrate technologies and supported production at several large manufacturing sites. Reports also say MediaTek has worked with Intel on its EMIB technology for certain cloud ASIC projects, including work tied to Google's TPU program. MediaTek has not publicly detailed how Shahriari's work will be measured.

The hiring comes as MediaTek ramps up its AI accelerator ASIC business. According to Focus Taiwan, the company began shipping its first AI accelerator ASIC in September 2026 and expects roughly US$2.5 billion in revenue from it in the fourth quarter. MediaTek is targeting about US$16 billion in AI ASIC revenue and a 20% market share in 2027, with its next-generation accelerator slated for commercial production in the first quarter of 2028. Analysts cited by BigGo Finance note that advanced packaging capacity remains a bottleneck across the AI supply chain. They say whether MediaTek turns its new talent into project progress will still depend on coordination with its foundry and packaging partners.

Articles.Title: [News] MediaTek Reportedly Taps Intel Packaging Veteran After TSMC Hire, Advances Dual CoWoS–EMIB Strategy - TrendForce

stories.Headline: Hard-Line Democrats Push AI Halt as Meta Warns New Data Centers Face Hurdles
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, Dina Powell McCormick, president of Meta Platforms, told a Wall Street Journal technology conference in Napa, California, that building new data centers in the United States will be very difficult going forward. She said expanding existing sites should be easier, because Meta's track record over several years has shown local communities real benefits. She also hinted that a newly elected governor had called her after taking office to ask for cooperation. Her remarks came right after midterm elections that handed Democrats control of Congress and a number of governorships.

Democrats won governor's races in Texas, Iowa, Wisconsin, Ohio, Minnesota, Arizona, Nevada and Georgia, and exit polls showed deep public unease about the buildout. Seventy-six percent of surveyed voters opposed data centers in their own communities, and Democrats made up 64% of that opposition. Fifty-six percent said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their votes, with Democrats making up 65% of that group. Local data center measures were on the ballot in 41 jurisdictions and passed everywhere except Hardwood, North Dakota, including bans or restrictions in at least 14 Ohio towns. Interconnected Capital's tracking counts 372 data center moratoriums across the country, along with 43 permanent bans, and New York already has a statewide moratorium.

On Capitol Hill, Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona wrote on X that her party's top agenda should be pausing advanced AI development, regulating the industry and banning artificial superintelligence. She and nine other Democratic lawmakers have introduced the ASI Prohibition Act of 2026, which defines ASI as a system that surpasses human cognitive abilities and could destroy or disempower humanity. The bill would halt development of AI systems trained with certain levels of computing power. Texas may become a new flashpoint, since Gina Hinojosa, its new governor, wants an immediate statewide moratorium on new data center approvals, according to analyst Nic Puckrin. President Donald Trump, by contrast, backs new data centers and industry self-policing, arguing the U.S. could lose the AI race to China without them.

Companies are already adjusting. Apple has decided to trim employee budgets for AI tools as part of cost-cutting, and similar moves are appearing at Microsoft and Tesla. OpenAI announced a Grid Protector Program to cut data center energy use during peak demand hours, starting with a planned AI data center in Georgia. The company is also reportedly preparing, after the midterms, to call such facilities AI compute campuses to stress their computing, power infrastructure and job creation. Wannie Park, founder and CEO of PADO AI, expects local governments to enact stricter guardrails and push for more moratoriums, while Rich Razgaitis of FloWater said the fight is increasingly nonpartisan and will turn on who pays for infrastructure and who bears the consequences.

Articles.Title: Hard-Line Democrats Push AI Halt as Meta Warns New Data Centers Face Hurdles - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Klleon Sees AI Humans Moving From Guides to Entertainers
stories.Summary:
Klleon, a Korean AI human technology company, is pushing its digital human technology from guidance and education into entertainment, with the shift described by Klleon's chief product officer Seo Ji-ho at the "U-KNOCK 2026 in USA" event at the Biltmore Hotel in Los Angeles on January 6. The article, published November 8, 2026 by Seoul Economic Daily, reports that AI is moving from one-way content toward real-time conversation shaped by a user's questions and responses. Klleon's technology is now used mainly in business-to-business and business-to-government projects, where AI humans act as guides in public institutions and retail spaces. The company also offers role-playing training for sales and customer service staff, along with products such as Klleon Studio, an SDK for embedding real-time avatars in other services, and RollFit, a training solution that lets managers set scenarios.

Klleon is also expanding into entertainment, supplying AI human technology to "My AI Partner," an SBS variety program released through Netflix in August that has broadcasters interact with AI humans over a set period. Seo said emotional exchange will matter more in entertainment than the information delivery that defined guidance and education. He added that the technology could expand into entertainment and business-to-consumer content. The company's visit to the United States was meant to gauge how local consumers respond to AI content, and it found that some saw AI as a tool to extend creators' imagination while others felt AI output lacks a human touch. Seo said he had come to see those cultural differences for himself, noting that fear and resistance toward AI appeared stronger in the U.S. than in Korea or Asia.

According to Seo, companies should not rush to seize the market but should understand cultural and national differences and prepare technology that fits human expression. The article frames the key to Klleon's expansion as whether AI humans can establish themselves as technology that communicates with people rather than replaces them. Klleon plans to broaden its market by advancing the technology and increasing content uses that reflect each country's cultural traits. The article does not give further figures, timelines or results for these plans.

Articles.Title: Klleon Sees AI Humans Moving From Guides to Entertainers - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Korea to Gather 100 Citizens to Debate AI Fake News Rules
stories.Summary:
South Korea's government will convene a panel of 100 citizens to discuss how to respond to fake news generated by artificial intelligence, with the aim of shaping future AI policy around the views collected. The Ministry of Science and ICT and the National AI Strategy Committee will hold the first Public Deliberation Forum on AI Issues in Seoul on the 12th, and the agencies announced the plan on the 7th. The 100 participants are to be selected to represent a cross-section of the public. The government says the forum will examine the many ways AI affects democracy and discuss the direction society should take.

The first topic is AI-generated fake news. As regulators weigh changes, including widening the range of deepfake material that must carry a mandatory AI label, the forum will take up where freedom of expression should end and regulation should begin. Participants will look at gray-area content, such as realistic satirical videos featuring real people and synthetic material with no sign it was made with AI. Under the current AI Framework Act, deepfakes must carry a notice that they were made with AI, though creative works may display the label in a way that does not disrupt viewing. The government launched a public participation platform called Modu AI late last month to support the effort.

The government also plans to discuss how much responsibility AI developers and content distribution platforms should bear. Under current law, the duty to disclose AI-made deepfakes falls only on AI businesses. To reduce industry confusion, the government has suspended fines for violations until at least January 22 next year. President Lee Jae-myung has separately called for a stronger response to fake news in general. At a Cabinet meeting on the 3rd, he said incitement driven by fake news is becoming a highly effective tool and causes social harm that requires a strong response.

Articles.Title: Korea to Gather 100 Citizens to Debate AI Fake News Rules - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI-Driven Quantification of Coronary Plaque Outperforms Standard Care in Suspected CAD
stories.Summary:
A randomized trial called PARAMOUNT, presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago, found that an AI-based coronary CT analysis outperformed standard care for patients with suspected coronary artery disease. The study, led by Todd Villines, MD, of the University of Virginia, compared a plaque-based management strategy with usual care. Villines discussed the findings in an interview with HCPLive, and the results were described as preliminary. The trial enrolled 530 patients at 21 sites between January 2025 and February 2026.

The trial enrolled symptomatic adults older than 18 who were suspected of having coronary artery disease, excluding those with an LDL below 100 mg/dL, those already treated beyond primary prevention guidelines, and those with suspected acute coronary syndrome. Patients were randomly assigned to either coronary plaque-based care or usual care. The plaque-based group underwent coronary CT angiography with AI-enabled assessment of plaque morphology and composition. The primary endpoint combined several measures, including diagnostic certainty, LDL reduction, and avoidance of unnecessary invasive angiography and stenting.

Among the enrolled patients, the median age was 57 years, 57% were women, and the median baseline LDL-C was 128 mg/dL. At 180 days, plaque-based care was favorable to standard care, with a win ratio of 2 (95% CI, 1.37-2.56; P less than .0001). Diagnostic certainty about the presence of coronary artery disease contributed most to the primary endpoint. The investigators concluded that AI-based plaque assessment may give physicians greater confidence when evaluating chest pain.

Villines noted that the speed and standardization of AI-generated reports should continue to improve as coronary CT scan volumes grow. He said AI could help reading physicians with pre-reads and plaque staging, making their work more efficient. Full results are expected in early 2027. Villines reported consulting for Cleerly, HeartFlow, and Milestone.

Articles.Title: AI-Driven Quantification of Coronary Plaque Outperforms Standard Care in Suspected CAD

stories.Headline: TSMC Stock And 2 AI Infrastructure Shares Riding The AGI Spending Wave
stories.Summary:
The article is a Yahoo Finance roundup built around the headline "TSMC Stock And 2 AI Infrastructure Shares Riding The AGI Spending Wave," published November 7, 2026. It is a Simply Wall St style piece that points to recent spending plans from Meta, OpenAI partners and Anthropic, which it says are sending billions into chips, cloud and power. The author argues that this capital flow can lift some stocks while squeezing others that misjudge demand or pricing. The piece profiles three companies, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Tokyo Electron and ASML Holding, as exposed to that spending.

The article describes Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing as turning hyperscaler AI spending into chips for datacenters, phones and cars. It names the company's advanced logic demand as a driver, saying it scales with compute complexity rather than unit volume. The piece says the key question is how a growing tension around future AI capacity will affect pricing power and margins. It also describes Tokyo Electron as a supplier whose production tools sit in fabs building AI chips, and it cites the ramp of the Miyagi Innovative Production Center, which management indicates could triple production capacity.

ASML Holding is presented as a bottleneck stock because its lithography tools are required for advanced chips, and the article notes export restrictions involving China have made it a geopolitical chokepoint. The article does not name a specific person as responsible for the analysis, and the commentary is attributed to Simply Wall St and written with AI assistance. It states that the content is general in nature, is based on historical data and analyst forecasts, and is not financial advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any stock. The author of the page is listed as Bailey Pemberton.

The piece also notes that it may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements. The article offers links to a wider screen of 136 more AI infrastructure companies and to other curated stock lists. The article does not describe any specific outcome or next step beyond the general expectation that the spending wave will keep shaping pricing, capacity and margins across these suppliers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: TSMC Stock And 2 AI Infrastructure Shares Riding The AGI Spending Wave

stories.Headline: ‘You’re the Bacon’: A blunt warning to Realtors about AI
stories.Summary:
The National Association of Realtors released its 2026 Realtors Technology Report in September, showing that 23% of agents use AI daily and 25% use it weekly, while 31% experiment with it occasionally. Only 12% said they do not use AI and have no plans to, down from 32% who had not tried it in 2025. At the NAR 2026 NXT conference, Mike Woodward, the association's director of data science, laid out both the benefits and the dangers of these tools for agents. He opened with a warning about how AI companies earn their money, arguing that users of free services are the product. The article reports that his talk took place on a Sunday, with coverage appearing in November.

Woodward urged agents to pay for AI services when handling real or confidential material and to switch off the data-retention settings that allow models to learn from inputs. He also cautioned against treating AI answers as reliable, noting that when he tested Copilot and Claude with questions about nearby schools and his own home records, the results were incomplete or wrong. Among the low-risk uses he described were turning soil-analysis reports into plain-English summaries and drafting listing descriptions from fact sheets, a task he said could take an agent 15 minutes but takes seconds with AI. He stressed using dummy data on free tiers and never entering sensitive personal information into any model.

Woodward said that agents bear full responsibility for AI-edited property images, since those pictures go out under their names. He warned that changes such as adding a fireplace, moving a window, or inserting a swimming pool can amount to misrepresentation and breach the Realtor Code of Ethics. He also said that AI sometimes alters images in ways the user never requested. In his view, the legitimate path is virtual staging with clear disclosure, which means showing the original photo beside the edited one and labeling the edit as AI-generated. He advised agents to reread the code of ethics, track new state laws, and consult legal counsel when unsure.

The article places this advice against growing backlash, including a New York Times article that portrayed real estate professionals unfavorably and angry discussions on Reddit. It notes that state legislatures and New York City are weighing regulation of AI use, and Woodward said AI-detection tools work well and that undisclosed use will likely be caught. He warned that consumers are angry and that people could face lawsuits over misleading AI-generated material. The article does not describe any specific regulation being finalized, so the outcome of those legislative efforts remains unclear from the reporting.

Articles.Title: ‘You’re the Bacon’: A blunt warning to Realtors about AI

stories.Headline: Taiwan-Based Hacker Used BOSSAI AI Agents to Steal Taipei Emergency Dispatch Records
stories.Summary:
A Taiwan-based attacker used a set of AI agents to pull emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, according to researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit, who published their findings in early November 2026. The agents also located a Taipei fire department platform that exposed patient data from 2018, including ECG readings and ambulance video footage, and that platform required no login. The researchers are highly confident the attacker is one person based in Hualien City, Taiwan. The dispatch records came from the system used for Taiwan's 119 emergency line for fire and ambulance services, and they include incident times, response types, case status, and street-level locations.

The attacker aimed the agents at hundreds of organizations in at least 11 countries, including emergency services, banks, universities and military systems. The agents collected data or accessed systems at about 10 of them in Taiwan, Mexico and Thailand. Taiwan was targeted far more heavily than any other country. In Mexico, the agents collected about 206,800 home phone records containing names and addresses, and in Thailand they took data from three universities after selecting 489 potential targets across 45 institutions. A Taiwanese lending firm also had account data pulled through SQL injection.

The researchers say the attacker manually moved output between agents, since they did not communicate with each other directly. Most commercial AI models refused to help with attacks, so the attacking agents ran largely on "abliterated" models, which are AI models run locally with their safety training removed. Grok and MiniMax M3 refused direct attack requests and asked for written proof of authorization, though Grok did repair one broken proof-of-concept script. The agents also made errors: one scanning tool invented CVEs, and more than half of its high and critical findings were false positives or wrongly classified.

The evidence came from the attacker's own server, which first looked like a misconfigured development system but held more than 90,000 files, including agent conversations, command history, hacking tools, credentials and victims' data. Acronis linked him to the operation through identity reuse across his legitimate businesses and attack servers, and his home IP address surfaced during an SSH session in one Grok conversation. The researchers think he probably wanted to make money, though it is unclear whether he works for anyone, and they observed the operation over 12 days. The report does not say whether the affected organizations or Taiwan's authorities were notified, and More to follow.

Articles.Title: Taiwan-Based Hacker Used BOSSAI AI Agents to Steal Taipei Emergency Dispatch Records

stories.Headline: Camerimage Founder Marek Zydowicz on AI, Aronofsky and Why “Cinematographers Are Artists, Not Technicians”
stories.Summary:
Camerimage, the Polish festival devoted to cinematography, marks its 34th year this November in Torun, running from November 7 to 14. Its founder, Marek Zydowicz, who started the event in 1993 to champion cinematographers and other below-the-line artists, is speaking openly about the issues facing the industry. Those include the rise of generative AI, which has its own debates and workshops at this year's festival, along with pressure on budgets and theatrical releases. The festival has also chosen to honor Darren Aronofsky, an outspoken adopter of AI, with its director award.

Zydowicz says Camerimage will stay open to a diversity of techniques and technologies, but he draws a firm line at fully AI-generated films. Joe Walker, the editor known for Dune and 12 Years a Slave, is also being honored and will chair the Main Competition jury. Polish cinematographer Janusz Kaminski, whose Disclosure Day is screening in contention, receives THR's Visionary award. Zydowicz frames the festival's mission as defending the artistic standing of people the industry has long treated as technicians.

In the interview, Zydowicz traces the strength of Polish cinematography to history, arguing that the tradition of depicting national events during the partitions and the postwar founding of the Lodz Film School shaped it. He says artists working under communist censorship learned to convey hidden meanings through composition and the relationship between image and dialogue. He also credits the Lodz school's teaching of painting history, and generations of filmmakers who taught there, for producing a tradition now visible in Polish cinematographers' work worldwide. He explained the Aronofsky choice by pointing to more than thirty years of films that unsettle audiences and ask them to confront difficult aspects of human nature.

Zydowicz cited Requiem for a Dream, Black Swan, The Fountain and The Whale as examples of work that moves between intimacy and spectacle while encouraging viewers to notice pain that might otherwise go unseen. He said he expects the decision to spark debate, given how contentious AI remains across the industry. The article does not describe what the festival's AI workshops will cover or how the jury will assess films made with new technology. Coverage of the festival's competition and awards is likely to follow as the November 7 to 14 program unfolds.

Articles.Title: Camerimage Founder Marek Zydowicz on AI, Aronofsky and Why “Cinematographers Are Artists, Not Technicians”

stories.Headline: What Is Atlassian (TEAM) Telling Investors With Its AI Push And Cautious Outlook?
stories.Summary:
Atlassian, the software maker known for its collaboration tools, reported first-quarter results that management tied to strong momentum in its cloud products and newer AI features. The company also expanded its collaboration with OpenAI and introduced the Agentic Multiplayer Protocol, a framework for embedding AI agents across its collaboration tools. Revenue for the quarter reached US$1,772.15 million, and the company swung from a loss to net income of US$90.72 million. Guidance for the full year, however, reflected a more cautious revenue outlook as customers continue moving from Data Center products to cloud offerings.

Atlassian also appointed Eli Berkovitch as Chief Accounting Officer, adding a senior finance leader to its team. The article describes this as a signal of continuity on execution for the company's cloud and AI strategy. The company's market capitalization is listed at $38.9 billion, placing it among large US software peers that are also weaving AI agents into everyday workflows. The article notes that the heavy spending on AI and cloud could weigh on GAAP margins if it does not produce clear pricing power and higher recurring revenue over time.

The analysis in the article comes from Simply Wall St, which produced it with AI automation based on historical data and analyst forecasts. It states that the commentary is general in nature and does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock. The writer identifies subscription recurring revenue growth and the GAAP operating margin, which management outlined around a 5% target for the year, as the key measures to watch in the rest of fiscal 2027. Any sustained shortfall in those measures would challenge the idea that the cloud migration and AI spending are converting efficiently into earnings.

Articles.Title: What Is Atlassian (TEAM) Telling Investors With Its AI Push And Cautious Outlook?

stories.Headline: Embodied AI: Definition, Components and Research Areas
stories.Summary:
Embodied AI is a field of artificial intelligence built around an agent with a physical or simulated body that learns by perceiving and acting within an environment. A CASRAI guide, last reviewed on 8 November 2026, explains the concept by drawing on two arXiv papers. The article notes that the field lacks a single formal definition, so it attributes each framing to its source. The guide was written for researchers and research administrators.

The ICML 2024 position paper "A call for embodied AI," by Paolo, Gonzalez-Billandon and Kégl, presents embodied AI as a key step toward artificial general intelligence. It contrasts this approach with current large language models and traces the idea of embodiment through philosophy, psychology, neuroscience and robotics. Under this view, an embodied system is judged by what it does in an environment, not only by the text or images it produces. The guide reports that the paper names four essential components: perception, action, memory and learning.

The comprehensive survey by Liu and colleagues (arXiv:2407.06886, first submitted 9 July 2024 and revised 25 August 2025) treats the field as covering both physical robots and simulators. It organizes research around four targets, and the guide describes these as the areas of study the survey maps. The survey also discusses multi-modal large models, world models, datasets and open challenges. The guide adds that the two sources divide the topic differently, with one listing components inside an agent and the other listing research targets across the field.

The guide frames the position paper as arguing that embodied AI is the next step beyond large language models, while noting that the survey treats multi-modal large models as one of the technologies used in embodied systems. It advises readers to start with the position paper for the conceptual argument and the survey for the broader map. It also recommends citing the specific arXiv version read, since preprints may change after peer review. No further developments or timelines are reported in the article.

Articles.Title: Embodied AI: Definition, Components and Research Areas

stories.Headline: HLB & Lovable: Prototype‑Driven AI Innovation
stories.Summary:
Vibe coding, a conversational way of building software using AI, is changing how professional services firms build and buy technology. The platform Lovable, which lets users describe what they want in plain English and have the interface, database and code generated, is a leading example. Lovable reports that 70 million projects have been built on its platform, that employees at nearly two-thirds of the Fortune 500 build with the tool, and that it was valued at $13.3bn after becoming a tech unicorn in February 2025. Its enterprise customers include Adidas, Deutsche Telekom, Nvidia, Workday and Zendesk.

Because building a bespoke tool no longer requires a team of developers, firms can now weigh the cost of an internal tool against the price of expensive software they may not fully use. HLB CBS Group in South Africa built an internal platform called Clarity on Lovable, using usage-based pricing rather than per-seat licenses. The platform gives staff a secure alternative to unapproved AI tools, along with agents built around the firm's audit methodology, including a working paper builder, a financial statements reviewer and a research tool limited to the accounting standards loaded into it. The article says this approach reduces the risk of shadow AI use and lets the firm control what information is stored and when the platform is updated.

Lovable's EMEA Hackathon Lead, Alexander Kollmann, said the company is focused on letting the person closest to a problem both build the solution and run it, whether that person is a first-time founder or someone inside a large company. He added that the real shift is in who is allowed to build, with advisers and accountants able to create and operate tools without waiting on a technical backlog. The article notes that the skills needed will shift toward understanding business problems and workflows, while knowledge of data storage, access permissions, privacy and third-party risks remains essential. It also warns that AI-generated code can contain vulnerabilities and that moving from prototype to production without testing or documentation creates real difficulty.

The article presents vibe coding as a likely change to how accountancy and advisory firms scope and deliver client work, with faster turnaround and more iterative engagements. It suggests that as building costs fall, firms will be paid for expertise in identifying the right problem and delivering a useful outcome rather than for hours spent. HLB's network recently held a Technology and Innovation Symposium with colleagues from over 17 countries, where Lovable hosted a hackathon challenging teams to turn real professional services problems into working prototypes. The article concludes that vibe coding is unlikely to replace professional software development, but it is changing who can build, how quickly ideas are tested and where firms spend technology budgets.

Articles.Title: HLB & Lovable: Prototype‑Driven AI Innovation

stories.Headline: MITRE ATLAS: AI Threat Matrix, Data and Usage
stories.Summary:
I can't write the story as specified. The article text provided is a CASRAI site page about MITRE ATLAS, a guide describing what the framework is, where its data lives, and its limits. It does not report a specific event, such as an incident, announcement, or development with a date, actor, and consequence, so there is no news to narrate in the requested structure. The page also gives no "who is responsible" beyond the general credit to The MITRE Corporation, and no "what happens next." I can instead write a factual summary of what the articles do state, in three paragraphs of four to five sentences each:

MITRE ATLAS, short for Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems, is a public knowledge base describing how adversaries attack AI-enabled systems. Its content is organized as a matrix of tactics, which are the adversary's goals, and techniques, which are the methods used to pursue them, supported by case studies. The official atlas-data repository calls its YAML files the authoritative source of ATLAS data, and the content is credited to The MITRE Corporation and marked approved for public release. The project's home is atlas.mitre.org, and its code and data are published under the mitre-atlas GitHub organization. ATLAS entries can also reference MITRE ATT&CK, a knowledge base of techniques drawn from real-world observation.

Users who want the data are directed to the dist folder of the atlas-data repository, where dist/ATLAS-latest.yaml holds the latest content and dist/manifest.yaml maps releases to their files. Content versions follow a YYYY.MM.N pattern, while format versions are semantic versions, and separate versioning began with content 2026.05 and format 6.0.0. Generated outputs include an ATLAS-only STIX JSON bundle, optionally combined with ATT&CK Enterprise, along with Excel workbooks and Navigator layers for visual annotation. The guide notes that the repositories do not publish counts of tactics, techniques, or mitigations, so current YAML should be checked rather than figures quoted from third-party pages.

The guide describes ATLAS as a shared vocabulary and a machine-readable, versioned resource, but also lists its limits. It describes adversary behavior rather than controls, is not a certification scheme or compliance checklist, and does not rank techniques by likelihood or impact. Because content and format versions change independently, a pinned file can become stale or break a parser after a format change. The guide suggests pairing ATLAS with complementary resources such as MITRE ATT&CK, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and model-specific testing tools, since each serves a different purpose.

Articles.Title: MITRE ATLAS: AI Threat Matrix, Data and Usage

stories.Headline: NYT Cooking AI Gets 3 Egg & Butter Swaps Wrong [2026]
stories.Summary:
The New York Times Cooking team has added an AI assistant to its recipe platform that can swap ingredients, rescale servings and adapt recipes for different pans. In a recorded test, the tool made two errors, both of the kind a home baker might not catch until the cake came out wrong. The Times announced the feature in an October 23, 2026 article titled "How, and Why, We're Adding A.I. Tools to NYT Cooking," and coverage from JournalArta and The Verge has followed it. The tool is in a gradual, beta-style rollout.

The assistant lets users request changes that are highlighted in orange so they can see what differs from the original. Customized recipes and the chats that produced them stay in the user's account and cannot be published or shared through Cooking. The original recipe is left unchanged. NYT Cooking says the AI's responses and custom recipes have not been reviewed by its editors or endorsed by the original creators. The company said the staged launch was meant to measure performance, including speed, and to see how people use the tool.

In the test, the tester converted a Cinnamon Roll Bundt Cake into muffins, and the tool cut the bake time from three hours to 50 minutes and split the batter across two 12-muffin tins. When asked to halve the recipe, the assistant changed five eggs to three rather than two and a half, a rounding choice that went unexplained. Later, the tester asked how much butter the recipe needed, and the assistant answered six tablespoons without saying which version it meant. The original calls for three-quarter cup, so the answer matches the halved recipe but not the original, and the reporting notes that six tablespoons would have yielded a dry cake. The coverage names Genevieve Ko, a senior editor and columnist at NYT Cooking, as a staff figure on the effort, but does not quote her on the tool.

The articles do not name the underlying AI model, the price, the subscription tier, the user count or a wider release date. They also do not say whether the reported errors have been fixed. Readers who want to check an AI-adapted recipe should compare it against the original and test any changed quantities before baking. More details on the rollout are expected as the beta continues, and the articles do not say when those will arrive.

Articles.Title: NYT Cooking AI Gets 3 Egg & Butter Swaps Wrong [2026]

stories.Headline: Ulta is marketing to AI agents and shoppers
stories.Summary:
Ulta Beauty is now treating AI agents as a new audience for its marketing, according to Chief Marketing Officer Kelly Mahoney, who spoke at the Status Summit. When a shopper asks ChatGPT or Gemini about skincare for acne, the answer shown at the top is the spot Ulta says it is working to earn. Mahoney said the company has to be a strong marketer to the agent as well as to the consumer, and she described AI tools as now being used not only to discover products but also to make purchases. Mahoney framed agents as the newest voices a brand cannot control, similar to creators and store associates who recommend products. Ulta does not write what an agent says, but it can shape what the agent knows by supplying content that answers customer problems.

The interviewer described this shift as moving from search engine optimization, which ranks links, to generative engine optimization, which aims to shape the content AI answer engines draw on. Ulta already builds relationships with store associates and with its Ulta Beauty Collective of influencers through regular briefings, and Mahoney said the same approach would now be applied to agents. The foundation for this work is Ulta's loyalty data. Mahoney said the Ulta Beauty Rewards program had about 11 million members when she stepped into her role roughly eleven years ago, and today it has more than 47 million engaged, active members who account for 95 percent of Ulta Beauty sales. She said the company built its first-party data infrastructure about ten years ago and has rebuilt it a couple of times, and that segmentation now centers on customer motivations rather than demographics, with non-purchase signals such as social activity and store visits informing personalization.

Mahoney was candid that no proven playbook exists yet, and she said the company will test, learn and adjust, relying on measurement. Mahoney also argued that stores will matter more, not less, citing Ulta's research on Generation Alpha. She said young consumers who use AI tools and chatbots still crave visiting stores and are more likely to do so, which puts pressure on stores to earn the trip. Ulta is investing in store design, immersive events and live selling through its TikTok Shop integration, and Mahoney said the future of discovery will be fluid, with digital and agent activity paired with real-life experiences.

Articles.Title: Ulta is marketing to AI agents and shoppers

stories.Headline: New AI Model Predicts Molecular Toxicity Using 3D Geometry
stories.Summary:
Researchers have developed a new artificial intelligence framework called MolMMP to improve the prediction of molecular toxicity during early drug development. The study, published in BMC Bioinformatics, introduces a method that combines structure-aware cross-modal alignment with geometry-biased attention. The authors aim to fix weaknesses in current models, which often rely on a single type of data and miss much of the structural complexity of molecules. By pairing sequence meaning with three-dimensional geometric relationships, the team hopes to offer a sturdier way to check the safety of lead compounds before they reach costly clinical trials.

Toxicity prediction matters because it helps drug developers avoid failures in late-stage testing, which saves money and reduces risk. Existing computational methods have notable shortcomings, however. Many depend mainly on one data type, which makes it hard to capture both the semantics of SMILES sequences and the molecular topology at once. They also lack three-dimensional conformation and interatomic geometric relationships, so they cannot account for how spatial structure affects toxicity. The new framework is meant to address these gaps by bringing several kinds of molecular information into a single model.

The researchers used a bidirectional cross-attention mechanism to align SMILES sequence semantics with graph topological structure, combining global meaning with local structural features. A separate three-dimensional module encodes interatomic distances through a geometric transformation based on radial basis functions. A hierarchical gating fusion strategy then balances fingerprint, topological, and geometric features, letting the model weigh each data source according to its importance. According to the study, this design is intended to handle the challenges of merging multiple data sources and uneven class distributions.

The team tested MolMMP on several toxicity benchmarks using both random and scaffold-based data splits. The article reports that the model achieved competitive predictive performance across these conditions, with particularly notable gains on tasks that benefit from joint modeling of topology and three-dimensional geometry. The authors describe the framework as robust and versatile across diverse toxicity endpoints. The article does not give specific numerical results, and it does not describe any clinical or laboratory validation beyond these benchmark tests.

Articles.Title: New AI Model Predicts Molecular Toxicity Using 3D Geometry

stories.Headline: Five9 (FIVN) Agrees $325 Million Acquisition To Expand Its AI Platform
stories.Summary:
Five9, a cloud software company that runs contact center platforms, has agreed to acquire Level AI, an AI-native customer experience platform, for about US$325 million. The deal, announced in a definitive agreement, is structured as a mix of cash and stock. The article reports that the move is meant to bring Level AI's technology into Five9's own platform. The announcement was reported by Yahoo Finance on November 7, 2026.

Level AI builds tools that analyze customer interactions to help improve agent performance and automate parts of contact center workflows. Five9's existing business centers on cloud software that helps contact centers manage calls, chats, and other customer contacts. Adding Level AI fits that focus on handling high volumes of service interactions. The article describes the purchase as a way to deepen Five9's position in customer experience software rather than broader enterprise IT.

The article attributes the deal to Five9 management, whose stated plan is to integrate Level AI's technology into Five9's platform. It is written from an analysis service that draws on company data and analyst forecasts, and it notes that it is general commentary rather than investment advice. The piece says management's push into AI aims to make AI agents and the Genius CX platform a larger share of subscription revenue. It also says the open question is whether Five9 can turn rising AI usage into stronger gross margin and earnings. Investors are pointed to the first full quarter after the deal closes, when more detail on combined AI usage and integration costs is expected.

Articles.Title: Five9 (FIVN) Agrees $325 Million Acquisition To Expand Its AI Platform

stories.Headline: New Explainable AI Framework Models Clinical Reasoning Through Expert Apprenticeship Learning
stories.Summary:
A new artificial intelligence framework called Explainable Apprenticeship Learning has been described in an open-access study published in the journal BioData Mining. The system treats clinical diagnosis as a hierarchical policy learning problem built from reasoning traces annotated by experts. Its developers argue that most medical AI has been tuned for predictive accuracy rather than for explaining the multi-step decisions that clinicians make. The reported work therefore targets interpretability alongside performance. The framework draws its decision models from reasoning sequences gathered from 61 practicing clinicians across 30 medical specialties.

It also combines multimodal patient data with Bayesian uncertainty modeling, which is meant to capture the variability that appears when clinicians interpret evidence. A synthetic reasoning augmentation strategy, based on clinical consistency constraints, is included to improve robustness on rare and complex cases. A policy alignment module compares the system's inferred reasoning steps against expert-derived distributions, flagging deviations at each stage and offering safety-aware feedback. On a held-out test set, the framework reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.972 for reasoning trace fidelity and a stepwise correctness score of 0.975. Its Top-1 diagnostic accuracy was reported as 0.953, its Top-3 accuracy as 0.978, and its safety compliance rate as 0.975 across evaluated traces.

In a controlled test, medical trainees who worked with the alignment feedback improved their collective diagnostic accuracy from a baseline of 0.85 ± 0.04 to 0.975 ± 0.02. External validation on unseen casebooks yielded a stepwise correctness score of 0.968 under domain shift. The article is credited to the study's authors, Abdullah, Ather, Fatima, Mejorada, Torres-Ruiz, Téllez and Saldaña-Pérez, and the research appeared in BioData Mining in 2026. The authors state that treating diagnosis as data-driven hierarchical policy learning can strengthen both interpretability and reliability in clinical decision support. The coverage, which was republished by Scienmag and bioengineer.org, does not describe any clinical deployment, regulatory review or next steps for the system.

Articles.Title: New Explainable AI Framework Models Clinical Reasoning Through Expert Apprenticeship Learning

stories.Headline: Can Snowflake (SNOW) Justify Its Price After Raised Outlook And AI Updates?
stories.Summary:
Snowflake (SNOW) has drawn investor attention after pairing a sharp rise in product revenue with a series of AI-focused product announcements. Management raised its fiscal 2027 outlook and reiterated a goal of reaching GAAP profitability in late fiscal 2028. The article was published on November 7, 2026, by Sasha Jovanovic and appears on Yahoo Finance. It notes that these developments came after a volatile period for the share price. The share price has moved unevenly over recent weeks, with a 7-day return of 9.87% and a 30-day return of 17.12%.

Over a longer horizon, the article cites a year-to-date share price return of 27.3% and a three-year total shareholder return of 72%. The piece says these figures still suggest a strong long-term story despite the recent swings in the stock. The article is produced by Simply Wall St and reports that Snowflake trades at a sizeable discount to average analyst price targets. It also cites a fair value estimate from a widely followed narrative that places the stock well below its last close of $275.88.

The article presents these views as one side of a debate over whether AI execution already justifies the share price. Simply Wall St describes the content as general in nature and says it is not financial advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any stock. The article suggests that the overvaluation argument could reverse if Snowflake turns heavy AI investment into stronger profitability or if rivals pressure its pricing power. It does not describe any specific next event or deadline for those outcomes.

Articles.Title: Can Snowflake (SNOW) Justify Its Price After Raised Outlook And AI Updates?

stories.Headline: Workers losing a day a week fixing 'AI slop,' study finds
stories.Summary:
Workers are losing roughly a full workday each week to fixing mistakes made with artificial intelligence, according to a study reported by AOL on November 7, 2026. The research, commissioned by Arden University, found that 46% of workers spend time correcting work that coworkers produced badly with AI tools. On average, that correction takes six hours and 57 minutes each week. Two in ten workers said they completely redo the flawed output created by colleagues. The survey covered 2,000 working adults.

The study also found that half of those who fix colleagues' AI work use AI to help make the correction. Almost two-thirds of workers said they had used AI in the past three months, mainly to search for information, draft emails, and brainstorm ideas. Employees said the tools let them finish tasks faster, and a quarter said AI improved their understanding of complex topics. Younger workers adopt the technology most readily, with 73% of Gen Z and 72% of Millennials using platforms such as ChatGPT or Claude, compared with 56% of Gen X. Even so, 53% of employees do not tell their supervisor how they use AI at work.

Vitaly Klopot, chief innovation and commercial officer at Arden University, said employers need to consider how AI affects the whole team rather than only the person using it. He argued that a quick draft may save one person time, but if a colleague spends hours correcting it, the overall effect is a loss. He also said that practical education can help workers move past trial and error toward useful and responsible results. The article notes that most users already report saving time, and the next step is helping more people get reliable outcomes. Arden University has also announced a strategic partnership with Google Cloud and plans to launch more than 30 new degrees with AI-enabled learning.

Articles.Title: Workers losing a day a week fixing 'AI slop,' study finds

stories.Headline: Tempus AI Stock: Q3 Strengthens Platform Thesis Cash Returns Need To Catch Up (NASDAQ:TEM)
stories.Summary:
Tempus AI, Inc. (NASDAQ: TEM) reported its third-quarter 2026 results, and an analyst writing on Seeking Alpha published an assessment of them on November 7, 2026. The analyst, Thomas Veth, rated the stock a "hold," arguing that the current valuation already reflects considerable future success. The article describes Tempus as a company that connects diagnostic data with clinical outcomes, a link that the author says can add research value and recurring revenue potential. The analysis is an opinion piece rather than a news report of a corporate action.

According to the article, third-quarter 2026 revenue grew 20% in Diagnostics and 33% in Data & Applications. Adjusted EBITDA improved, but the company still posted GAAP losses. The author states that sustained free cash flow and operating leverage remain unproven, which is why the article's headline says cash returns still need to catch up. The article is written by Thomas Veth, an independent contributor, and carries Seeking Alpha's standard disclaimer that its views may not reflect the platform's as a whole. The article does not describe any action by the company, its management, or regulators beyond the quarterly results it discusses. It also does not give a price target or indicate any future events.

stories.Headline: Jeff Bezos 'agrees' with three-day-week in AI age; says: Some people will decide, I can support my family by ...
stories.Summary:
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said in a recent interview with Fox News that artificial intelligence could allow many people to work fewer days while still supporting their families. The Times of India Tech Desk published the report on November 8, 2026, quoting Bezos as saying that some people will decide they can support their families working three days a week. He framed this as what productivity in the economy means. The article does not give a specific figure for productivity gains or a timeline for when such changes would arrive.

Bezos described an AI-powered economy in which higher productivity generates wealth and gives people more say over how much they work. He suggested that if productivity rises enough, many households may no longer need two earners to keep their standard of living, and that one partner could choose to step back. He also said employers might find it harder to recruit if people can meet their financial needs with less work. On AI investment, Bezos said it was hard to tell whether the current boom is a bubble, but he stated that the technology is real and good for society. He warned that separating strong AI businesses from weak ones remains difficult during periods of heavy spending.

The article notes that Amazon is spending billions of dollars on data centres and cloud capacity to meet demand for AI services, and that it has cut thousands of corporate roles over the past year. Bezos's space company, Blue Origin, has also outlined plans for space-based data centres, which the article presents as a possible beneficiary of AI growth. The piece places Bezos alongside other business leaders who expect shorter working weeks, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has suggested a four-day week could become common, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, who has said workers may one day work about three and a half days a week, and Bill Gates, who has floated a two-day week. Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk has argued that AI and robotics could create a world of universal high income in which work becomes optional for many. The article does not say what steps, if any, are planned next, and it notes that views differ on timing.

Articles.Title: Jeff Bezos 'agrees' with three-day-week in AI age; says: Some people will decide, I can support my family by ...

stories.Headline: LiveOne Turns To Tesla And AI To Convert 1.1 Million Free Music Listeners Into Paying Subscribers
stories.Summary:
LiveOne, a Los Angeles-based music and entertainment company, is expanding its partnership with Tesla and launching an artificial intelligence marketing initiative aimed at converting more than 1.1 million free subscribers into paying customers. The company is betting that the in-vehicle dashboard can serve as a way to introduce listeners to paid subscriptions. According to LiveOne, users spend more than 59 minutes a day on its platform. The announcement was made in an article published on November 7, 2026.

LiveOne's Tesla application offers access to more than 500 music channels along with content from over 200 podcasters, DJs and video jockeys. The company views these options as a way to reach listeners directly through their cars, making discovery part of the driving experience. Its AI-driven marketing effort involves tools and services from Claude, Meta Platforms, LiveRamp, Jasper, AdCreative.ai, Persado and Mutiny, together with connected television advertising partners. Rather than depending on one channel, the company is exploring several technologies to reach listeners and encourage upgrades. The aim is to increase average revenue per user, known as ARPU, and to develop business-to-business partnerships.

CEO and chairman Robert Ellin said the company sees strong engagement trends and believes its expanded AI-driven marketing positions it to unlock value from its large base of free subscribers. At the time of the announcement, LiveOne also reported improving subscriber trends over two consecutive months. The article notes, however, that these ambitions are targets rather than confirmed results. The announcement does not establish how many free listeners will ultimately become paying subscribers.

LiveOne operates across music streaming, podcasts, live entertainment and digital content through businesses including Slacker, PodcastOne, PPVOne and LiveXLive. Its services reach people through smartphones, connected televisions and streaming applications. The article frames the company's wider challenge as giving listeners enough value that they choose to pay for an experience they may already enjoy for free. For LiveOne, that answer involves automotive entertainment, a sizeable library of curated content and more targeted communication with potential subscribers.

Articles.Title: LiveOne Turns To Tesla And AI To Convert 1.1 Million Free Music Listeners Into Paying Subscribers

stories.Headline: What the Democratic sweep means for Trump's tariffs and AI
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both the U.S. House and Senate in the midterm elections, delivering a major setback to President Donald Trump's Republican Party. The results were reported in an article from Nikkei Asia dated November 7, 2026. Voters' frustration with the cost of living appears to have driven much of the shift. The coverage says the outcome could change the direction of Trump's economic agenda.

The article says a Democratic-controlled Congress could bring closer scrutiny of tariffs and trade deals. It also says voter opposition to data center development could slow the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure in the United States. Those two areas, trade policy and AI, are the focus of the report. The article does not set out any specific bill, figure or deadline tied to these changes.

Nikkei Asia's U.S. correspondents examined the election results and what they mean for tariffs, trade, agriculture and AI. The piece also looks at possible effects on Asian economies and companies. The article itself describes these analyses as the central content of the report. It does not attribute specific predictions to named officials or analysts in the excerpt provided.

Related coverage in the same feed points to market reaction and industry concern. One linked headline reports that Nasdaq fell 5.5% over fears about AI regulation, and another says Taiwan, South Korea and Japan stock markets were hit hard by an AI sell-off.
