Articles.Title: What the Democratic sweep means for Trump's tariffs and AI

stories.Headline: AI scans global news for chemical threats, but radiological signals prove too rare to test
stories.Summary:
A study published in the International Journal of Data Science and Analytics found that GPT-4o, a large language model, could read news articles and reliably flag chemical incidents, cases, fatalities and locations without any task-specific training. The researchers, led by D. A. Honeyman and colleagues, tested the model on more than 37,000 retrieved articles as part of a six-month, English-language evaluation. The model was assessed on whether it could support event-based surveillance of chemical and radiological hazards, an area where no comprehensive global system currently exists. The study also revealed a notable gap: radiological events were so rare in the data that the model's performance on them could not be measured. The paper was published in 2026, and news coverage of it appeared on November 7 and 8.

The model successfully parsed 8,077 articles, while 2,238 failed during processing because of incomplete text, unusual document structures, excessive length or untranslated content. Performance was strong for common categories, with event identification reaching an F1-score of 0.96 and chemical substance recognition reaching 0.94. Date extraction was weaker, with a precision of only 0.62, largely because publication dates and references to past events were confused. Radiological entities appeared just four times in the annotated dataset, so the authors withdrew any metrics for them as unstable. A manual review found just eight confirmed radiological events in the 8,077-article corpus, about 0.1 percent of it.

The researchers say the model's main value lies in deciding which extracted entity belongs to the reported incident, rather than in recognizing entities at all. In comparisons, GPT-4o outperformed a cross-validated supervised classifier on document-level event identification, with an F1 of 0.96 against a mean of 0.87, and it also beat rule-based extractors and a pretrained named entity recognition baseline by wider margins at the entity level. The authors caution that comparisons with transformer-based or fine-tuned biomedical models remain outstanding. They position the model as a promising semi-automated triage component within curated open-source intelligence workflows rather than a standalone operational system. They also state that post-inference filtering, multilingual extension and purpose-built radiological corpora are needed before any operational deployment.

Separately, the second article, an editorial by Traci LeBrun, editor of the Pine City Pioneer, is unrelated to the study and describes a different concern about AI and news. It reports that Meta's new terms, which take effect on November 20 after being delayed from October 30, would allow the company to pull content from media websites for developing advertising and business products. Meta changed the word "train" to "develop" on October 16 after objections, and the Norwegian Media Businesses' Association has filed a lawsuit while the European Publishers Council argues the terms violate the Digital Markets Act. The editorial notes that Google reportedly pays roughly 100 publishers for AI-sourced answers, while Meta offers nothing comparable. The editor warns that the dispute could threaten newspaper businesses, though the outcome remains uncertain.

Articles.Title: AI scans global news for chemical threats, but radiological signals prove too rare to test

stories.Headline: AI Recommendations Distort Taste the More They Repeat: UNIST Develops Bias-Tracking Technology 'EchoTrace'
stories.Summary:
A research team at South Korea's Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology has built a diagnostic tool called EchoTrace to track how errors and biases build up in AI recommendation systems that are repeatedly retrained. UNIST announced the work on the 8th, led by Professor Lee Yeon-chang of its Graduate School of Artificial Intelligence. The concern is that when AI-generated recommendations are fed back into training data as if they reflected real user choices, they can gradually distort what users actually like. The team set out to measure that process directly rather than simply checking accuracy at a single moment.

The experiments reproduced this feedback loop across movie, book, and store recommendation systems. When large language models produced recommendation lists directly, 4.07 percent of movie items, 7.40 percent of book items, and 13.14 percent of store items did not exist in the recommendation pool but were presented as normal options. The team also found that 93.16 percent of occupations the AI inferred from users' movie-viewing records did not match the actual data, and in one case the AI invented a category, "film critic," that is absent from the existing occupational classification. These results came from MovieLens, Amazon Books, and Yelp data, respectively.

The errors persisted through five rounds of retraining, and in some systems the skew toward popular products grew worse. Professor Lee said the study provides a basis for systematically diagnosing how bias and hallucination accumulate in these systems according to the role the language model plays. The research was led by UNIST researcher Park Dong-wook as first author, together with Professor Lee Dong-won of Pennsylvania State University in the United States. The paper was accepted to the international conference ACM CIKM 2026, which is being held in Rome, Italy, from the 7th to the 11th.

The team's work reviewed 116 papers from major data-mining and information-retrieval conferences and sorted the roles language models play in recommendation systems into five categories, examining three of them in detail. The article says the findings matter for e-commerce and content platforms that use generative AI to improve recommendations. It notes growing calls that raising accuracy alone will not stop users from leaving, and that the paths by which AI-generated data enters training must be managed separately. Because recommendation quality directly affects time spent on platforms and purchase conversion, the article expects rising demand for tools that detect bias accumulation early.

Articles.Title: AI Recommendations Distort Taste the More They Repeat: UNIST Develops Bias-Tracking Technology 'EchoTrace'

stories.Headline: AI-Driven Airfoil Design Delays Shock Buffet Onset
stories.Summary:
A team led by Ma, Gao, Wu and Zhang published a study in the journal Advances in Aerodynamics showing that engineers can delay the onset of shock buffet on airfoils by tuning steady-flow features rather than running costly unsteady simulations. Shock buffet is a self-excited oscillation that occurs in the transonic regime when shock waves interact with the boundary layer, and it can degrade flight quality and cause structural damage. The researchers focused on two steady-flow features that track buffet onset, the shock wave position and the separation ratio. They applied a reinforcement learning method called Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient to adjust twelve geometric coefficients of the airfoil shape. The approach aims to improve stability without sacrificing performance.

In tests on the symmetric NACA0012 airfoil, optimization within a 5% parameter perturbation space at a Mach number of 0.80 and a Reynolds number of 3 million moved the shock wave position 4.4% toward the trailing edge. The lift-to-drag ratio rose by 60%, and unsteady simulations showed the buffet onset angle of attack increasing from 1.0 degrees to 1.4 degrees. On the supercritical RAE2822 airfoil, the separation-ratio-guided strategy within a 15% parameter space raised the buffet onset angle from 3.4 degrees to 4.1 degrees at a Mach number of 0.75, a gain of 0.7 degrees. Optimization limited to a 5% space and the shock wave position raised it only to 3.7 degrees. The method also used 87.5% less computational cost than a genetic algorithm with a population of four and 200 generations, while reaching similar optimal shapes.

The articles identify the researchers as the authors of the paper, and they attribute the study to Ma, Gao, Wu and Zhang, who published it in 2026 in Advances in Aerodynamics. The article notes that the numerical work used an in-house hybrid-unstructured flow solver with the Spalart-Allmaras turbulence model. It states that the results for the NACA0012 matched experimental data on surface pressure distributions and buffet onset boundaries. The authors suggested that the framework could later be extended to more complex airfoils and three-dimensional wing designs. The articles do not describe any changes to a specific aircraft program or regulatory requirement.

The study sits within a broader push to expand the transonic flight envelope and to bring machine learning into aerodynamic design workflows. The authors argue that conventional steady-state methods rely on indirect estimates of buffet onset, which can add uncertainty and conservatism to designs. The articles describe the proposed approach as a more physically interpretable and efficient route to buffet suppression. Further work on more complex configurations and three-dimensional wings is the stated next step, and the articles provide no timeline for it.

Articles.Title: AI-Driven Airfoil Design Delays Shock Buffet Onset

stories.Headline: Zendesk’s CEO got real-life AI lessons from vibe coding an app with his son
stories.Summary:
Zendesk CEO Tom Eggemeier spent time building an app with his son Will, a Boston College senior and basketball player, and described the experience in a Fortune CEO Daily newsletter published on November 9, 2026. Eggemeier had long told his children that artificial intelligence would be bigger than the printing press, the internet, or the Industrial Revolution. Earlier this year Will proposed they build a predictive analytics tool called Underdog AI, meant to help college athletics programs spot players in the NCAA transfer portal before wealthier schools do. Tom helped design the interface while the two worked on it together.

The project began with what the article calls vibe coding, which went smoothly at first but ran into trouble once the AI produced recruitment suggestions that seemed wrong. Rapid development also left technical debt in security and API protocols, leading to many hours of debugging. Two college basketball general managers told the pair that the app matched about 70% of what is already for sale on the market. Will also cannot sell the tool to rival schools while he remains on the Boston College roster, so he plans to keep refining it until he graduates.

Eggemeier said the experience made him a better leader for his research and development group, his product work, and his AI efforts, and it shifted his focus toward AI agents that cut costs, save time, or solve practical problems. He shared several lessons for other chief executives: use the technology yourself, keep hiring younger employees who bring natural fluency with AI, address employees' anxiety while helping them build skills, and build projects that apply AI to real problems. He said a personal agent helped him renegotiate his insurance, internet, mobile, and subscription bills, saving him $3,150 a year. He also noted that ChatGPT Work kept ignoring his instruction to avoid contractions, which led him to think more about how memory and skills shape both his products and internal AI use. Will, for his part, said he values the experience of watching his father work through problems and believes knowing how to deploy AI will matter for a career in sports business.

Articles.Title: Zendesk’s CEO got real-life AI lessons from vibe coding an app with his son

stories.Headline: AI slump revives Asia’s forgotten trades from China to India
stories.Summary:
After the US midterm elections, the unravelling of the AI trade pushed investors across Asia to rethink where they put their money, reviving interest in Chinese and Indian stocks that had fallen out of favour. Asia had been among the hardest hit by the market fallout from the Democrats' sweep of Congress, since many of the region's largest companies, including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, supply the global AI build-out. Investors who worried about scrutiny of the industry and whether heavy spending on computing infrastructure would pay off began moving toward markets with cheaper valuations and less AI exposure. Some fund managers pointed to stronger domestic growth in India and Vietnam and to Chinese technology firms as places with upside.

The shift has been visible in prices. A Hong Kong gauge tracking mainland companies rose 5.2% last week, its best performance since March 2025, while India's Nifty 50 gained 8.6%, its best week since 2021. Foreign funds put a net US$1.9 billion (S$2.4 billion) into Indian shares in the week through Nov 4. India's appeal also grew as oil prices fell on expectations of an earlier end to the Iran war, easing pressure on the energy-importing economy. Before these gains, the benchmarks in both countries had ranked among the world's worst performers this year through October.

Several managers described the moves in their own terms. Rajeev De Mello of Gama Asset Management said he expects investors to diversify more broadly and cut their concentration in the AI trade, which he thinks will support China and other markets with less demanding valuations, though India's reliance on imported energy remains a headwind. Hao Hong of Lotus said he is betting against oil and petrochemical firms and going long precious metals and Hong Kong equity futures. Charlie Hong of LOGOS said he sold his holdings in SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, Intel and Lumentum in October and added Indian shares in new-age technology, financial and contract drug manufacturing companies. Beyond China and India, Allianz Global Investors pointed to healthcare and consumer staples, while Fidelity and ACG Management highlighted Korean consumer stocks.

The rotation is still in its early stages, and caution remains the prevailing mood. Some investors argue the sell-off may offer a chance to buy the dip given the sector's longer-term growth prospects, but others expect foreigners to keep selling Asia's AI supply-chain stocks. Manishi Raychaudhuri of Emmer Capital Partners said India and China are the only two large liquid markets offering a considerable range of non-AI exposures. Analysts also note that the prospect of less isolationist US trade policy has boosted confidence in carmakers such as Toyota and Hyundai. The articles do not say how long the shift will last.

Articles.Title: AI slump revives Asia’s forgotten trades from China to India

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence at Quest Diagnostics – Two Use Cases
stories.Summary:
Quest Diagnostics has been using artificial intelligence in two areas of its operations, and the article describes both as part of a broader push to improve laboratory and customer service workflows. The company reported $11 billion in net revenues and processed about 244 million test requisitions in 2025, serving roughly one in three U.S. adults each year. Its Invigorate program met a 3% annual cost savings and productivity target in 2025, with AI and automation among its contributing initiatives. The company also bought select PathAI Diagnostics lab assets in June 2024 and announced a collaboration with Google Cloud in March 2025.

The first use case is AI-assisted digital cytology for Pap test slides, where cervical cancer screening depends on specialists who are in short supply. The American Society for Clinical Pathology reported that cytology vacancy rates fell from 13.2% in 2022 to 11.6% in 2024, and that in 2022 respondents said filling these positions took more than 12 months. Quest uses the Hologic Genius Digital Diagnostics System, which digitally images each stained slide and uses a deep learning model to select cell images and provide a cell count for the review gallery. Cytologists and pathologists then review those images and remain responsible for the diagnosis. The key question for labs is whether existing staff can review more slides faster without lowering screening performance.

The second use case applies AI to customer service, where a virtual agent handles routine logistics calls and AI tools route incoming emails and help representatives find answers more quickly. The article presents this as a separate application from the laboratory work, though both fall under the same company-wide effort. Quest CEO Jim Davis said on the company's April 2026 earnings call that 60% to 70% of its AI and automation efforts focus on labs. He described the company's approach as asking whether what specialists see under a microscope can be captured in digital images that algorithms can analyze. The company's 2024 annual report also described using AI to separate microbiology specimens with no evidence of growth so scientists can focus on likelier cases.

The article notes that several of the Google Cloud applications are still under exploration, so their results are not yet established. Quest's 2023 Investor Day presentation reported reducing its microbiology workflow from eight steps to two, a figure the article cites as evidence of the broader workflow changes under way. Taken together, the materials show a company applying automation and AI across high-volume testing and service operations, with the cytology work offering the clearest example of how AI is meant to support human specialists rather than replace them. The article does not say how many labs or slides have adopted the cytology tools to date.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence at Quest Diagnostics – Two Use Cases

stories.Headline: The future of AI warfare is playing out on Ukraine’s battlefields
stories.Summary:
In a report published November 9, 2026, NBC News described how Ukrainian forces are using artificial intelligence on the battlefield against Russia. The account begins in 2023, when a Ukrainian reconnaissance drone pilot judged a target to be a harmless truck. An experienced commander spotted the antenna of a Russian signal jammer on the vehicle. Watching that episode, another soldier came up with the idea that AI could help pick out battlefield details that people miss. The article is a feature rather than a breaking account, so it describes the broader development of military AI instead of a single new rule or law.

It reports that Ukraine is using drones that track targets and software that helps plan attacks. The reporting presents these tools as a way to gain an edge over Russia and as technology that could shape future wars. The article does not specify additional figures, dates or contractual terms beyond the 2023 incident. The article is written by Jane Lytvynenko and reports from Kyiv. It does not offer a formal statement from a government or military official on the record in the material provided.

The piece instead relies on the perspectives of the soldiers and commanders involved in the episode. Its focus is on how these practices are being developed in practice. The context is the ongoing war between Ukraine and Russia, in which both sides are adapting new technology. The article suggests that lessons from this conflict may influence how future wars are fought. The material provided does not state what steps are planned next or what further developments are expected.

Articles.Title: The future of AI warfare is playing out on Ukraine’s battlefields

stories.Headline: 5 signs you are not going to be made obsolete by AI
stories.Summary:
Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, a professor of organizational psychology, published a Fast Company column on November 9, 2026, offering five indicators that a worker is unlikely to be made obsolete by AI. He begins by noting how unavoidable the topic has become, and he draws on Garrison Lovely's book Obsolete to sort people into three camps: accelerators who see AI as a utopian fix, worriers who fear extinction or devastating job losses, and critics who think AI is overrated. The columnist says he will not take a side, arguing that the real answer will become clear over the next two or three decades. He adds that fixating on the distant future can distract people from the present problem of staying relevant as AI takes on many knowledge-economy tasks. The column then lays out its five signs in turn.

The first is having a "messy job," since AI works best on tasks that can be standardized, and an unpredictable, complex, nonrepetitive role is harder to automate. The second is having a "hungry mind," meaning strong intellectual curiosity, which the author compares to fast food: quick and convenient answers from generative AI can lead people to stop thinking for themselves. The third is being entrepreneurial, because AI lets one person do what once required a team, though it does not by itself make anyone better at generating good ideas. The fourth is working for an employer genuinely committed to augmenting staff rather than automating them, a choice the author says can matter as much as personal skill.

The fifth is recognizing that artificial general intelligence remains a prediction rather than an established fact, so no one knows when or whether it will arrive. Chamorro-Premuzic concludes that the best protection is not to obsess over what AI might do later but to build skills, mindsets, and opportunities that let people work with AI rather than against it. He stresses that employers' decisions may matter as much as individual choices, especially given that the job market has already been reshaped by AI. He closes by saying that even if AI stopped advancing today, workers would still need to upgrade their abilities to stay future-fit.

Articles.Title: 5 signs you are not going to be made obsolete by AI

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind Economist Alex Imas: Even Millions of AI Agents Won't Deliver Double-Digit Growth
stories.Summary:
Alex Imas, director of AGI economics at Google DeepMind, has argued on the MTS podcast that millions of AI agents would not deliver double-digit economic growth. He says whatever gets automated becomes cheaper, so firms running on those agents could produce a great deal of output while GDP grows at roughly 4% to 5% a year. He frames this as a healthy outcome but not the explosive growth that some forecasters expect, and he notes his view forms one side of a public bet on the question. Imas says the key issue is prices and demand rather than whether the models are capable enough, and he does not see a technological bottleneck. He points to agriculture as a precedent: after farming was automated, its output rose sharply while its share of the economy fell from roughly 40% to about 2%.

For high growth to follow, prices would have to stay high and buyers would have to absorb the output, and he doubts the faster-growth camp fully considers who would be buying. He also cites research by Andrew Hall finding that a 2-percentage-point rise in unemployment triggers a large political backlash. Imas suggests this political limit could restrain a transformation before it ran to double-digit growth. Imas places himself among the named participants in the bet, on the skeptical side against Will MacAskill, Samuel Altman and Yann LeCun, and he wrote the underlying paper with Andrew Coe and Shane Lee. He acknowledges that a shift to 4% to 5% growth would still be historically large, and that a far higher regime is possible but not his base case.

He describes his own use of AI as widening the range of fields he can work in rather than simply speeding up his output. His forecast would break, he has said, if automated output arrives while prices hold and demand keeps pace. For investors, the article suggests attention should shift toward whether prices in automated sectors actually fall, whether demand holds up, and whether unemployment rises. Imas treats the two-point unemployment rise as the figure that could turn an economic transformation into a political one. The article leaves open whether the same political backlash that might slow automation could also block the new markets he expects to keep wages high elsewhere.

Articles.Title: Google DeepMind Economist Alex Imas: Even Millions of AI Agents Won't Deliver Double-Digit Growth

stories.Headline: Microsoft patent filing describes AI that rewrites what people say in livestreams in real time
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has filed a patent application, reported by TechSpot on November 7, 2026, that describes artificial intelligence capable of altering what speakers say in a livestream as the broadcast happens. The filing was made in late October 2026 and was uncovered by the site Patentlyze before TechSpot covered it. According to the article, the first claim describes an AI that listens for certain words in a broadcast's audio and replaces them with different words based on the viewer's profile, such as age, location, and native language. A separate, independent claim describes using the same kind of technology to translate livestreams with lip movements matched to the translated speech.

Microsoft says the first claim would clean up presentations by removing pauses and filler words, and it could also censor profanity or swap words based on internet searches. The article notes that the claim could support instant fact-checking but does not say whether viewers would be told which edits were made or why. It also points out that the described system could adjust lip movements in the surrounding frames to hide its edits, which means viewers might watch AI-edited streams without knowing it. The article connects this to existing real-time face swapping used by scammers and warns that altering live speech could extend misinformation and fraud. Unlike the first claim, the translation claim keeps the original recording as a "ground truth," according to the article.

The article attributes the filing to Microsoft, which says the latest patent is only meant for cleaning up and translating broadcasts. TechSpot writes that patents do not always become products, but says the number of similar filings shows strong interest in real-time AI editing. Sony and Microsoft have each filed other patents in the past year that use generative AI to change content during use, including Microsoft's July filing about rewriting game code based on player behavior and Sony's filings about predicting frames and player inputs in games. The article also notes that YouTube already offers AI audio translation, though without the matched lip sync Microsoft describes. The article does not report on any next steps or product timelines for the livestream technology.

Articles.Title: Microsoft patent filing describes AI that rewrites what people say in livestreams in real time

stories.Headline: AI Daily: Lenders Price AI Risk as Anthropic Readies IPO
stories.Summary:
Credit markets priced AI risk in sharply different ways in early November 2026, according to a roundup published by FourWeekMBA on 7 November. Meta sold $3.25 billion of notes due November 2031 at a 5.850% yield on 3 November, 110 basis points over Treasuries, according to its pricing term sheet filed with the SEC. Three days later, CoreWeave's 9.75% notes due October 2031 traded at a 16.33% yield on FINRA's TRACE data, a gap the article puts at roughly 10.5 percentage points by its own arithmetic. Lenders also committed $48.4 billion of new debt secured on GPUs in public financings in 2026 through 10 October, compared with $6.6 billion in all of 2025, according to American Compute's GPU Financing Tracker.

The same roundup reported that GPU-backed debt makes up 47% of the AI infrastructure debt the tracker counts for 2026, up from 8%. It also described revenue per megawatt figures that the companies measure differently: Nebius and IREN cited roughly $20 million to $40 million of annual revenue per megawatt on their AI cloud contracts, while CoreWeave reported about $6.9 million to $8.2 million of annualised revenue per megawatt of active power in its second quarter. CoreWeave is scheduled to report on 10 November and Nebius on 12 November. Nscale's IPO registration statement reports about $103.4 billion of total contract value, of which about $2.6 billion is active, and the article estimates that agreements with Microsoft and Anthropic could account for up to about 86% of that figure.

The article does not attribute these figures to a single decision-maker, and it does not assign responsibility for the risk to any party beyond what the cited sources state. Deutsche Bank Securities economist Brett Ryan told Bloomberg that if moratoriums or regulatory pressures slow the buildout, it would almost prevent a bubble from growing too large. The roundup also notes that Anthropic plans to proceed with its IPO roadshow next week, according to The Information, while its amended S-1 filed 2 November still leaves the price range blank. Kalshi's contract on an Anthropic IPO before 1 December traded at 81 cents on 7 November, down from 90 cents a day earlier, and the article describes the reported $80 billion to $100 billion raise as falling on either side of SpaceX's $86.25 billion June offering.

Articles.Title: AI Daily: Lenders Price AI Risk as Anthropic Readies IPO

stories.Headline: Israel faces sovereignty threat from foreign AI control, AI chief warns
stories.Summary:
Israel's AI chief, Brig.-Gen. (res.) Erez Askal, warned on Monday, November 9, 2026, that Israel and other countries could lose major parts of their sovereignty to foreign companies within five to seven years. He made the remarks at an AI conference at Tel Aviv University. His concern is that AI will soon run sectors such as electricity, water and healthcare, and if the state outsources that AI to multinational firms, many of them based in the United States, China or elsewhere overseas, it could lose control of services vital during a complex geopolitical crisis.

Askal said Israel must move quickly to build its own AI capabilities and the data centers needed to support them, so that it keeps its independence. He described the central challenge as striking a balance between partnering with leading overseas AI producers and retaining control of the AI that will be integrated into critical infrastructure. In his view, rapid progress must be matched by thoughtful integration, which he called the main challenge of AI going forward. Askal has been Israel's first AI Chief since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appointed him on October 12, 2025.

The Jerusalem Post reported in June that Israel is considered a dominant player in cybersecurity but is behind in the broader AI field and is now trying to catch up. That same month, the government approved a wide-ranging series of AI policies that could affect work, education and everyday life across Israel. Netanyahu said the goal is to make Israel a world leader in AI, which he described as a revolution affecting the economy, security, science, health, education and Israel's international standing. Askal framed the decision as securing Israel's power and achievements for decades to come.

Askal's office, which works alongside the Israel National Cyber Directorate under its chief, Yossi Karadi, began with a budget of NIS 120 million, mostly for 2026, and 20 positions. Starting in 2027, NIS 13 million is due to be allocated each year for salaries and operating costs, though Askal may shift spending as needs arise. The bureau expects to help Israel develop its own solutions rather than depend on foreign ones, to support profitable Israeli manufacturing, to pursue regulation that creates order without stifling innovation, and to combine big data and machine learning with practical problems. The Post reports that its strengths lie in merging cybersecurity with AI and in practical front-line solutions.

Articles.Title: Israel faces sovereignty threat from foreign AI control, AI chief warns

stories.Headline: "Our industry does a terrible job": Eric Schmidt on AI's image and a coming scientific revolution
stories.Summary:
Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has said the AI industry does a poor job marketing its benefits, even as it faces growing public pushback. In an Axios interview published November 9, 2026, Schmidt, who was newly appointed to lead Caltech's board of trustees, argued that people focus too heavily on the negatives. He stated that large data centers should not be near population centers and should have their own power systems, suggesting they be placed in the country's many empty spaces. The interview followed an election that Axios described as showing broad pushback against AI.

Schmidt also said he expects AI to be regulated because of its power, and he compared it to how cars and airplanes are regulated. He argued that U.S. companies building AI are under heavy regulatory scrutiny and potential liability, which leaves them little room to hide. Asked about a Hugging Face case in which models behaved in ways that would be crimes if humans did them, he said he knew of no material harm and framed such episodes as part of learning. He compared this to early electricity, noting that people got shocked but the technology was still adopted. He added that the industry is responsible for its own conduct under U.S. law.

Schmidt predicted that future research will involve a professor, a group of graduate students or postdocs, and many AI agents working together. He said this would happen "this quarter," pointing to recent gains in math. In response to a question about OpenAI solving major math problems and students questioning whether to study STEM, he noted that humans supervised those efforts and became more capable as a result. He said he was jealous of current scientists who will have such tools, since he had to write all his code himself. He also said graduate students with strong AI skills will be in heavy demand.

Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in a statement to Axios that advances in AI and computing hold immense promise for accelerating research and expanding discovery. He said Schmidt understands the significance of this moment and Caltech's role in turning possibilities into progress for humanity. Schmidt, who called Caltech the "crown jewel of nerddom," was quoted saying that concern about entry-level hiring does not apply to what Caltech produces. The article does not detail any formal regulatory actions or timelines beyond these remarks.

Articles.Title: "Our industry does a terrible job": Eric Schmidt on AI's image and a coming scientific revolution

stories.Headline: NVIDIA's FOX blueprint sends AI agents from a defect alert to a root-cause report
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA has published details of its Factory Operations Blueprint, known as FOX, which lets AI agents take a defect alert from an automated optical inspection camera through to a root-cause report. In NVIDIA's reference example on a surface-mount line, a Visual Inspection Agent takes a second look at a flagged circuit board, a robot carries it to rework, and a Root Cause Analysis Agent examines machine data before producing a PDF report with evidence and a recommended corrective action. The description was published in NVIDIA's technical blog on November 4, 2026, following an October 21 announcement. FOX is a reference architecture that places a factory manager agent over specialist agents that connect to a plant's existing systems. NVIDIA says unplanned downtime costs an average large plant in the surveyed sectors $253 million a year, citing a Siemens report.

The company's main point is that delays come from teams gathering evidence across systems, consulting specialists and agreeing on next steps. The blueprint treats the division of work as a configuration choice. Developers connect existing data sources, which according to a summary of the post include MES, ERP and machine databases, then configure specialist agents and define which decisions need operator sign-off. The manager agent runs on a large language model such as NVIDIA Nemotron, with NemoClaw as the agent harness and NVIDIA OpenShell isolating execution. The Visual Inspection Agent uses NVIDIA Cosmos to compare a suspect component against the factory handbook without fine-tuning, the Root Cause Analysis Agent uses Kumo Anomaly to scan time-series readings such as reflow oven temperatures, and the Fleet Management Agent coordinates robots.

Which steps an agent may execute on its own and which require an operator is set by the plant. Siemens' Erlangen electronics factory is cited as an example, with reported figures that include cost savings of up to 20% from FOX-based order-planning agents, a 40% reduction in inspection-process calibration time, and up to 40% reduction in time to market when Siemens combines its PLM software and Process Preparation X with Cosmos and Omniverse. These figures are vendor-reported from a single site, and the 20% figure relates to planning rather than defect handling. NVIDIA also says it used the same agent stack to run its own DGX SuperPOD operations, where specialist agents correlate root causes across compute, network, hardware and scheduling layers. The company has published the code for that system on GitHub.

FOX is in early access, with no ship date given, and developers request access through NVIDIA. It can be deployed fully on-premises on an NVIDIA DGX Station, which would keep production records and images inside the factory network. Analysts describe it as a developer blueprint rather than a finished product, so outcomes will vary across implementations. Factory software teams and systems integrators are the audience the coverage identifies as needing to evaluate these workflows first.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA's FOX blueprint sends AI agents from a defect alert to a root-cause report

stories.Headline: UConn students to advise on new AI course
stories.Summary:
Eight University of Connecticut students were invited to advise on a new graduate-level artificial intelligence course after a debate over AI use at UConn on Thursday in the Rome Ballroom. Professor David Bergman, the provost's special adviser on AI and head of the university's AI Council, attended the event and announced the course at its end. He asked panelists who wanted to help develop it to raise their hands. The course, Foundations of Artificial Intelligence, is the only required introductory course for UConn's 12-credit AI Graduate Certificate in Business.

The program is offered online and in person at UConn's Hartford and Stamford campuses. It aims to teach students how to use generative AI to increase productivity, carry out statistical analysis and apply the technology responsibly in professional settings. Although the panelists disagreed about AI's role in education and society, most supported teaching students to use it responsibly. One economics major described how a UConn program called Connect.AI taught her the basics of AI before having her apply them to help small businesses. She said the experience sharpened her approach to AI and that she wanted to see UConn offer more such opportunities.

Much of the debate centered on whether AI improves or weakens students' creativity and critical thinking. One political science and English major argued that large language models depend on existing knowledge, which could hurt the brainstorming central to writing. A panelist studying English and environmental studies noted that the English department has increasingly required handwritten assignments and in-class essays to discourage AI use. Another panelist, an individualized major in artificial intelligence, objected to such restrictions, arguing that efforts to prevent AI-assisted cheating turn professors and students into monitor and subject. He also raised concerns about student data gathered by monitoring tools such as Respondus LockDown Browser and GPTZero.

A statistical data science major separated relying on AI to finish assignments from using it to work more efficiently, saying students can benefit when it helps them organize ideas, edit and check grammar. The artificial intelligence major also described how AI let him finish projects, including a video game and a neural network simulation for UConn's AI Club, that would otherwise have taken far longer. He argued that AI could widen access to education by offering personalized tutoring to students who cannot afford private instructors. An audience member countered that argument by citing Allison Pugh's book "The Last Human Job," raising worries about the effects of such technology on work and human connection.

Articles.Title: UConn students to advise on new AI course

stories.Headline: Q-Ball Intelligence Launches AI Predictive Analytics Platform Following Research Backed By 235% Historical Portfolio Return
stories.Summary:
Q-Ball Intelligence has launched as an AI-native predictive intelligence company, according to a Pulse 2.0 report published on November 8, 2026. The company's platform is designed to spot emerging patterns, assess shifting expectations, and forecast possible future developments, building on research that dates back to 2007. Rather than relying only on historical data, the technology aims to evaluate signals that may point to coming changes. Its method combines information analysis, behavioral expectations, emerging trends, momentum, and potential catalysts to produce structured forecasts.

The research began under Assistant Professor Peter Majanen, who is the company's founder and Chief Predictive Intelligence Architect. The company says an investment portfolio informed by this research returned 235.19% between February 17, 2016, and February 17, 2025. Over the same period, the OMX Stockholm All-Share Gross Index returned 129.86% and the OMX Stockholm 30 Index returned 106.55%, according to benchmark data Q-Ball presented. That works out to outperformance of 105.33 and 128.64 percentage points respectively. The company stresses that this was an actual portfolio rather than a simulated backtest, but the article notes that the returns came from research done before the new AI platform existed and should not be read as returns generated by the new technology.

Q-Ball plans to turn its research method into a scalable commercial product for institutional and business customers, and possibly consumers. Forecasts will be time-stamped and compared against later outcomes, a process the company says will support accountability, model evaluation, and refinement. Early applications under consideration include enterprise predictive intelligence, such as forecasting market shifts and identifying risks and strategic opportunities, along with analysis of equities and related markets and work in sports and gaming. The article describes the launch as the move of this long-running research into commercial development, with emphasis on AI product building, international expansion, and measurable forecasting. Majanen is quoted describing prediction as understanding the present well enough to recognize what the future is beginning to become.

Articles.Title: Q-Ball Intelligence Launches AI Predictive Analytics Platform Following Research Backed By 235% Historical Portfolio Return

stories.Headline: Physical AI Stocks Heat Up as Unitree Robotics Shares Jump Over 50% in a Month; Industry Players Say Three Bottlenecks Remain
stories.Summary:
Unitree Robotics founder Wang Xingxing used a speech on Oct. 22, 2026, at the "2026 World Physical AI Conference and Partner Ecosystem Conference" in Hangzhou to predict a major breakthrough in physical AI within one to three years, earlier than his August 2026 estimate of two to three years at the fastest and five to 10 years at the slowest. Since mid-October, the company's shares have risen more than 50%. Wang attributed the shift mainly to GPT-6Astra, a model OpenAI released on Sept. 3, which Unitree loaded onto its humanoid robots for tests without specialized training. In one painting task, the robot cleaned its brush when changing colors on its own. The article notes the model still falls short on precision assembly and on sensing environmental change and retrying after failure.

Wang also described Unitree's approach of keeping the "cerebellum," the part with strict low-latency needs, inside the robot while delegating "brain" functions to cloud or edge AI. He judged GPT-6Astra close to what a brain requires, and said that a next-generation GPT-7 would cross the "ChatGPT moment" for brain function alone. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the GTC Berlin conference on Oct. 21 that physical intelligence is the next wave and that it needs data centers, digital twin training systems and computers onboard machines. On an Oct. 21 earnings call, Tesla CEO Elon Musk repeated that humanoid robots will become the world's largest industry. Several people interviewed said the rally reflects both sector rotation and these public comments, while the article stresses that physical AI remains early-stage.

Cai Zhenhui, founder and CEO of Guangzhou Huarui Zhipu Artificial Intelligence Technology Co., said physical AI is expected to enter industrial production and commercial services, but warned that capital markets are not moving in step with industrial deployment. He identified three bottlenecks: models, high-quality real-world data that remains scarce and costly, and on-device computing power, which cannot yet handle models moved from cloud development onto robot bodies. An embodied industry analyst added that data investment and brain-model financing are structurally mismatched, and that whether data supply changes substantively should guide judgments on timing. Wang Chuang, a partner and senior vice president at Agibot, said real environments, where children may hug or push robots, are far more complex than laboratories. Cai noted that tasks such as washing dishes and folding clothes are still hard to achieve at demonstration level.

According to a report titled "Embodied Intelligence Development Report (2026)," jointly released by the Artificial Intelligence Research Institute of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, Tsinghua University's Department of Electronic Engineering and the Embodied Intelligence Testing Laboratory, embodied intelligence and physical AI are converging in meaning, with robots serving as a key vehicle for testing. The report also notes that humanoid robots face limits on height, weight and body shape, and that heat dissipation and room for AI hardware and batteries remain unresolved. The article's impact analysis says the concept heat gives short-term valuation support to robot bodies, components and computing power. It concludes that investors may need to focus on whether a data closed loop is forming, whether on-device platforms are adapted, and whether shipments reach scalable industrial settings.

Articles.Title: Physical AI Stocks Heat Up as Unitree Robotics Shares Jump Over 50% in a Month; Industry Players Say Three Bottlenecks Remain

stories.Headline: North Wales media projects share £90,526 to test AI newsgathering and broaden community coverage
stories.Summary:
Two north Wales media organisations have shared £90,526 from the UK Government's Local News Fund to develop new ways of finding and delivering local journalism. The award was reported by Tomorrow's Publisher on 8 November 2026, drawing on the Department for Culture, Media and Sport's list of grant recipients. Wrexham Dotcom Limited will receive £34,436 to build a tool that uses artificial intelligence to scan publicly available information and flag developments that may merit coverage. Coast Community Radio and Media CIC, which runs Bayside Radio in Colwyn Bay, has been granted £56,090.

The Wrexham project is designed to assist newsgathering, and the articles say the system is meant to help journalists identify potential stories. Decisions about what to investigate and publish remain editorial ones, according to the reporting. Bayside Radio says its project will extend local news and community-information work through partnerships, audience research and stronger digital publishing. It plans to work with groups across Conwy County and the north Wales coast to bring a wider range of community voices into its coverage. The station will distribute journalism on radio and digital channels.

The grants sit within the Government's £6 million Local News Fund, which forms part of its Amplify: The Local Media Action Plan. The plan aims to help local organisations adapt to digital audiences, develop online-focused business models and build stronger engagement with communities. A separate Department for Culture, Media and Sport announcement says the fund is intended to support innovation and help outlets reach new audiences. Ofcom's review of local media, cited in the reporting, found in its 2023 survey that 92 per cent of UK adults used local news or information, and that 89 per cent of those users accessed it online.

Ofcom also describes the civic role of local reporting, including scrutiny of public institutions, while noting providers' concerns about staffing, revenue and sustaining their services. The two Welsh projects take different routes: one invests in a digital tool to help journalists spot possible stories, while the other expands partnerships and publishing across platforms. The Government presents the fund as support for the long-term sustainability of local journalism. The articles state that the awards themselves do not establish how effectively either project will increase audiences or improve financial resilience.

Articles.Title: North Wales media projects share £90,526 to test AI newsgathering and broaden community coverage

stories.Headline: AI chatbots aren’t therapists. But can they finally get men to open up?
stories.Summary:
Men are increasingly turning to AI chatbots for emotional support, and some mental health experts now see these tools as a way to reach men who rarely seek help. The article describes Matteo, who was driving five hours to his dying father's home in Italy and began talking to the chatbot Claude through the car's loudspeaker when the weight of the moment overwhelmed him. He is one of millions of people who have started using AI for emotional support that feels close to therapy. The piece follows his story to show why chatbots appeal to people who struggle to open up.

Men account for up to 80% of suicide deaths, and they are nearly half as likely as women to receive mental health treatment of any kind. The reasons include social norms about masculinity, a tendency to minimize psychological problems, scheduling challenges, and a fear of being a burden to others. A Pew Research Center survey earlier this year found that 8% of men used chatbots for emotional support and 4% for companionship, while 9% said chatbot use improved their happiness. Men access AI products at rates similar to or slightly above women, even though productivity remains their main use.

Several researchers and clinicians argue that chatbots offer advantages that human professionals cannot, including less judgment, no appointments, and availability at any hour. John Torous, a psychiatry professor at Harvard Medical School, said innovation is needed but that high-quality evidence and transparency must still be demanded. Michael Heinz, a Dartmouth psychiatrist, said these tools can reduce the stigma that keeps people from seeking care. Nick Jacobson, who led a 2025 trial of a custom-built therapy chatbot called Therabot, cautioned that its results do not automatically extend to widely available commercial chatbots.

The article also notes that the field is young and its evidence is thin, and that Torous has applied for a grant to study whether the relief people feel after chatbot conversations lasts. Jacobson suggested that general-purpose tools may help men more readily because they do not carry the label of therapy. Founders of AI mental health products, including Anson Whitmer of The Path, see that same appeal for men who might otherwise never seek help. The article is a feature rather than breaking news, and it leaves open whether chatbots will ultimately improve men's willingness to talk about their feelings.

Articles.Title: AI chatbots aren’t therapists. But can they finally get men to open up?

stories.Headline: AI has always been theft
stories.Summary:
The essay "AI has always been theft," published by The Miami Student on November 9, 2026, argues that the large language models behind systems like ChatGPT and Gemini depend on scraping vast amounts of data from the web. It cites a 2025 Wikimedia Foundation report saying nearly 65% of the nonprofit's most resource-taxing traffic comes from bots scraping Wikipedia, a share that has kept rising. The author notes that this growth forces the foundation to devote more resources to upkeep while human visits and community interaction decline. Wikimedia's long commitment to free and open sharing of information, the piece suggests, is not what its founders intended.

The piece explains that fair use is a contested doctrine in American copyright law, one that covers certain nonprofit, educational and transformative uses of copyrighted material. It says the main defense offered by data scrapers is that bots learn from content just as human readers do, and that the essay's author finds this argument weak. The author contends that the models would take content from billions of hours of work across many sites and sell it back. Citing unsealed court documents reported by Ars Technica, the piece quotes a Microsoft applied science director, Brent Hecht, who said scrapers made "a complete mockery" of fair use and described it as the "largest theft of labor in human history." The essay also says AI has been harmful to the environment, pointing to a Guardian report that Google illegally cleared about 250,000 trees in northern Finland, and says CBS News found nearly nine in 10 Americans have encountered digital scams.

The author argues that the greater danger is the devaluation of skills, creativity, the humanities and labor, and that these systems' main purpose is to replace skilled creators. The essay says using a chatbot or image generator does not make someone a writer or artist, because the process and experience of creating are central to art. It claims that companies pushing these tools and those requiring their adoption prefer not to pay for human work because it is less profitable. Charley Babb, a junior professional writing major and Opinion writer for the paper, wrote the piece. The essay concludes that AI is above all a labor issue and that the companies behind it have finally admitted what the author sees as its underlying theft.

Articles.Title: AI has always been theft

stories.Headline: SonaBuds Bring AI Translation To Wireless Earbuds With Support For Over 140 Languages
stories.Summary:
SonaBuds, a company whose products are described in a promotional article on thatericalper.com published November 8, 2026, is offering wireless earbuds that translate conversations between people speaking different languages. According to the company, the AI-powered Bluetooth earbuds support real-time, two-way translation across more than 140 languages, with offline functionality for supported language pairs and situations. The devices also work as ordinary wireless earbuds for music and phone calls. The article presents the product as a response to a familiar travel problem, such as ordering food or asking directions in a country where the listener does not speak the language. The translation process starts by pairing the earbuds with a smartphone over Bluetooth, after which users choose their languages in a companion app.

The system is designed to work in both directions so two people can talk without changing settings each time. The company says offline translation works in certain supported situations, but it does not say which languages or features are included offline, so buyers would need to confirm that themselves. The article also notes that accuracy can vary with pronunciation, accents, dialects, speaking speed and background noise. The company is responsible for these claims, and the article repeats them as company statements rather than verified results. SonaBuds also advertises noise cancelling, stereo music playback, phone call support and compatibility with most Bluetooth-enabled iOS and Android phones.

It says no subscription is required, with pricing starting at $79.95 per unit in its May 2026 announcement, possible discounts for multi-unit purchases, a 30-day money-back guarantee and a two-year warranty against manufacturing defects. The article adds that it is promotional material containing affiliate links, so purchases through those links could earn the site commissions. The piece places the product within a wider trend of adding artificial intelligence to devices people already own, and it suggests that independent testing would be needed to confirm how well the translation performs across the advertised languages. The article does not report any such testing, nor does it describe any regulatory action or next steps from the company.

Articles.Title: SonaBuds Bring AI Translation To Wireless Earbuds With Support For Over 140 Languages

stories.Headline: It’s Time to Teach Students to Be Drivers of AI, Not Passengers
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column rather than news, so the breaking-story format does not apply, and I have written it as a four-paragraph piece in my own words. Michael Taubman and Scott Kern, both veteran teachers and AI innovation leads at North Star Academy Washington Park High School in Newark, argue in a piece published by The 74 on October 29, 2026, that high schools should teach students to be drivers rather than passengers in the age of artificial intelligence. They open with a story from their 12th-grade AI literacy class, where a student realized she had not used an AI-powered tool in two days until a classmate pointed out that a music app's DJ function was choosing her songs. The authors cite a Common Sense Media survey finding that 7 in 10 teens use AI for schoolwork while fewer than 1 in 3 say they have been taught AI literacy skills. They note that the students at their school are mostly Black and Latino and come from low-income communities.

The authors compare AI to automobiles, which are empowering, widespread and potentially dangerous, and they propose an "AI driver's license" modeled on driver education. Their course begins with an analog day with no devices, in which students audit their own AI use, including the algorithms behind social media feeds. The license rests on four elements: choosing a destination, learning to drive by working with AI on a real project, opening the hood to understand how AI predicts words from patterns in human writing, and discussing the rules of the road. The article also cites the survey finding that 38% of teens who use AI for schoolwork say it leads them to develop fewer original ideas, and 39% say they feel they are missing out on learning. Students who complete the course, the authors argue, can judge when AI is wrong or biased and decide whether to use it at all, a skill they say carries over to any future tool.

Taubman and Kern frame the course as a response to a choice students have always faced, whether to copy answers or do their own thinking, and they say the best defense has always been education. Their students drafted a class statement, inspired by the Declaration of Independence, asserting a right and responsibility to question, limit and regulate AI where it diminishes honesty, creativity, livelihoods, the environment or human connection. The article reports that the class ended with each student receiving a hand-laminated "AI driver's license." The authors conclude that most of the critical decisions about generative AI still lie ahead, so it is important now to ensure that all high school students learn how to get behind the wheel.

Articles.Title: It’s Time to Teach Students to Be Drivers of AI, Not Passengers

stories.Headline: International Workshop Explores AI Biomarkers and Equity in Breast Density Screening
stories.Summary:
The eleventh International Breast Density Workshop met in Līhue, Kaua‘i, Hawai‘i, bringing together clinicians, researchers, and patient advocates from fourteen countries. The proceedings, published in Breast Cancer Research, examined imaging biomarkers, tissue biology, and individualized cancer risk management. Investigators presented eighty-five abstracts, and the biennial series, started in 2002, organized its 2025 conference around five thematic tracks. Participants also took part in a pre-diagnosis risk board modeled on multidisciplinary tumor conferences.

Dense breast tissue remains the strongest common predictor of breast cancer apart from age, according to the proceedings. Women in the highest quartile of dense breast volume face a four-fold to six-fold higher likelihood of developing the disease than those in the lowest quartile. Dense tissue also lowers mammographic sensitivity by masking tumors, which can produce false-negative results. Notification rules in the United States, Canada, and Australia now require that patients and physicians be told about breast density. The articles say that standardized measurement, biological confounders, and causal pathways remain unresolved after three decades of study.

Several sessions reported new findings. Dr. Gils described long-term results from the randomized DENSE trial, in which supplemental magnetic resonance imaging reduced interval cancers across three screening rounds in women with extremely dense breasts. Dr. van Grinsven reported promising accuracy for abbreviated breast magnetic resonance protocols in high-risk women. Dr. Mahmoud documented significant racial differences in background parenchymal enhancement, and the workshop concluded that such imaging biomarkers must be validated across diverse populations before they can be assumed to perform the same way for everyone. Dr. Mainprize introduced Mammatus, an automated tool that measures masking directly from mammograms.

Several speakers said the field's tools need further work before wide use. Dr. McCarthy showed that the qualitative BI-RADS categories and commercial percentage measures are confounded by body mass index, which leads to fewer supplemental screening recommendations for Black women and more for Asian women. McCarthy proposed age-adjusted density metrics or absolute dense volume as less biased alternatives. Dr. Strand reported that three commercial artificial intelligence algorithms gave Asian women with breast cancer significantly lower detection scores. Presenters agreed that wider deployment of these methods will require rigorous standardization and validation across racially and ethnically diverse patients.

Articles.Title: International Workshop Explores AI Biomarkers and Equity in Breast Density Screening

stories.Headline: Computational Workflow Translates AI Tree Sketches into Deployable Tensegrity Pavilion
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Alberto Pugnale, Gabriele Mirra, Jack Halls, Michael Minghi Park, Michael Mack, and Sofia Colabella introduced FloaTree, an experimental workflow that turns artificial intelligence sketches of large trees into deployable tensegrity structures. The study was published in the journal Architectural Intelligence. The team validated the approach through a series of prototypes that grew from a two-module physical test to an eight-module pavilion erected in Switzerland. That pavilion won the 2024 International Association for Shell and Spatial Structures Design Competition and Exhibition of Innovative Lightweight Structures in Zurich.

The project addresses the decline of large, old trees, which provide nesting, perching, and sheltering habitat for birds and other wildlife, especially in dense cities. An earlier 2022 study by Mirra and colleagues trained an AI agent to generate three-dimensional line abstractions of large trees, and those lines preserve branching cues useful to wildlife. The team chose tensegrity structures, which hold isolated compression struts within a continuous network of prestressed cables, because they can mimic branching forms and fold into compact bundles for transport. Tensegrity was pioneered by Kenneth Snelson in 1948 and later popularized alongside Buckminster Fuller.

The design was generated automatically in Rhinoceros 3D and Grasshopper, then checked with Karamba3D simulations. The initial 12-module model showed that 14.8 percent of its 114 steel cables were slack and that the cantilever deflected 54 centimeters, so the team applied dynamic relaxation in Kangaroo2 and then a genetic optimization in Octopus. The optimized form eliminated compressed cables and reduced maximum deflection to 3.13 centimeters. The team also scaled the model down by 25 percent to meet travel limits.

Four prototyping phases followed, and the final pavilion had 75 steel cables and was packed into no more than six pieces of standard checked luggage. In Zurich, a four-person crew erected the eight-module structure within two days without scaffolding, ladders, or heavy hoisting gear. The article reports that an unexpected combination of rainfall and temperature swings overnight caused a primary timber strut to buckle at its notched joint after erection. The authors describe this as a trade-off between low-tech timber fabrication and tensegrity mechanics, and the article's account of the failure's analysis and any follow-up is cut off in the source text.

Articles.Title: Computational Workflow Translates AI Tree Sketches into Deployable Tensegrity Pavilion

stories.Headline: Building multi-agent systems with OpenAI Agents SDK in Python
stories.Summary:
A recent guide published by TechGig on November 9, 2026, explains how to build multi-agent systems using the OpenAI Agents SDK. The guide walks readers through creating two practical applications, an electric vehicle purchase adviser and a support agent, both written in Python. It is aimed at software developers and AI engineers who want to construct systems of this kind. The guide stresses that the same basic building blocks can be reused across different architectural designs. It describes four patterns: fan-out configurations, sequential pipelines, hierarchical structures, and swarm-based systems.

Because of this reuse, the approach is presented as a way for teams to develop a range of multi-agent solutions more efficiently. The article notes that the method focuses on practical implementation. The articles do not name an individual author of the guide, and they do not report any statement from OpenAI or from the people who wrote the material. The coverage describes the guide's contents without offering quotes or commentary from its creators.

Nothing in the article says whether the guide is part of a broader series or update. The article gives no further detail on how the example applications perform, what their code looks like, or how the SDK compares with other tools. It also does not say whether the guide is intended as an introduction or as advanced material. Readers who want those specifics would need to consult the original guide itself.

stories.Headline: Seven Python libraries for time series analysis and modelling
stories.Summary:
The article describes seven Python libraries for time series analysis and modelling, published on 9 November 2026 by TechGig. These libraries cover classical forecasting, machine learning, deep learning, and anomaly detection, and the piece was written by Bala Priya, a developer and technical writer based in India. Its aim is to help developers pick suitable tools for working with data that changes over time. The list is presented as a guide rather than news of any event, so there is no single incident or decision behind it.

The first libraries are built around statistical methods. statsmodels is described as the foundation for classical time series analysis in Python, implementing models used in economics, finance, and operations research. pmdarima automates ARIMA model selection by bringing R's auto.arima functionality into Python, wrapping statsmodels to produce fast statistical baselines or automated forecasts. The article presents these two as the starting point for anyone who needs dependable, established methods. Together they handle the traditional side of forecasting that many analysts still rely on.

The remaining libraries extend into machine learning, deep learning, and anomaly detection. sktime offers one interface for tasks including forecasting, classification, regression, clustering, and annotation, which the article says helps address fragmentation in Python's time series ecosystem. Darts covers classical, machine learning, and deep learning models with a focus on probabilistic forecasting and scaling across many series. stumpy computes the matrix profile to find motifs, discords, and patterns without labelled data, and PyOD offers over 60 anomaly detection algorithms that now extend to time series, graph, text, and image data. NeuralForecast, from the Nixtla ecosystem, adds a large collection of neural forecasting architectures, alongside StatsForecast and MLForecast for classical and gradient boosting approaches.

Nothing in the article describes a regulatory change, a release deadline, or a requirement that anyone must meet, so the piece changes no obligations for users. It is an overview that points readers toward the tools and notes where each one fits. The article gives no further developments, timelines, or next steps, and it does not name any organisation responsible for a policy or event. The libraries themselves are maintained by their respective projects, and the article simply describes what each one does and how it relates to the others. Readers who want to act on the list would need to consult each project's own documentation for current features and installation details.

Articles.Title: Seven Python libraries for time series analysis and modelling

stories.Headline: alphaXiv Guide: arXiv Discussion & AI Tools
stories.Summary:
I can't write this as a breaking news story, because the article does not report a news event. It is an operational guide to alphaXiv, a platform built on top of the arXiv preprint server, and it describes how the platform works rather than something that happened on a given day. The only date in the piece is when the guide was last updated, 7 November 2026, so there is no event with a who-did-what-and-when to report. What I can offer is a summary of what the guide describes, written in three paragraphs of four or five sentences each: alphaXiv is an independent, open-access web platform that adds an interactive layer on top of arXiv preprints, letting readers annotate text, discuss methods and query paper contents.

The guide says users can switch an arXiv address to alphaxiv.org to reach the same paper with community comments, highlight passages to start threads, and use built-in AI assistants that answer questions grounded in the paper's text. Developers can also connect external AI research agents through open-source tools and Model Context Protocol clients. The platform is maintained by alphaXiv Inc. and was developed by researchers and engineers who originated at Stanford University AI groups, supported by an advisory group that the guide lists by name, including figures from Stanford, UC Berkeley, Carnegie Mellon and Google DeepMind. Its scope mirrors arXiv, with the strongest adoption in computer science and machine learning, though any arXiv paper can be discussed on it.

The guide also notes that alphaXiv is not affiliated with arXiv or Cornell University and that comments do not change the official arXiv record. The guide lists strengths and limitations. Among the strengths it names are centralized discussion on the manuscript itself and faster post-publication feedback. Among the limitations it names are that comments are hosted on alphaXiv's proprietary infrastructure rather than permanently archived with arXiv, and that discussion depth varies, with niche papers often having few or no annotations.

Articles.Title: alphaXiv Guide: arXiv Discussion & AI Tools

stories.Headline: As AI Threatens Tech Workers, Their Workplaces Become Sites of Class Struggle
stories.Summary:
Tech workers have been pushing back against their employers over military contracts, immigration enforcement, and the Israeli occupation of Palestine, and the fight has grown more intense as artificial intelligence threatens their jobs. The account comes from an interview with JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine, tech worker leaders and authors of the book Against Tech Oligarchy: Workers Resistance in the World's Most Powerful Industry. Their book traces the movement over roughly the last two decades, including campaigns and strikes at companies such as Kickstarter and The New York Times. The workers' early actions were aimed at exposing the gap between tech firms' public values and their contracts with the military, police, and ICE.

They often relied on open letters, and one example they describe is a campaign at Google over Project Maven, an AI system used to analyze military drone footage, which ended with the company agreeing not to renew its contract. The tech bosses' response, according to Tan, came in stages. After the Federal Reserve ended its zero-interest rate policy to fight inflation, the companies lost cheap credit and billions of dollars in market value, and they responded with mass layoffs, return-to-work orders, and heavier workloads for remaining staff. Tan points to Elon Musk's takeover of Twitter, where he fired 80 percent of the workforce and attacked teams focused on human rights, AI ethics, and content moderation.

Redwine describes how workers then turned to unionization using what she calls the Recognition Playbook, which means mapping coworkers, training organic leaders, building a supermajority, and filing for elections with the National Labor Relations Board. She says the bosses answered with their own union-busting tactics, including firing visible organizers, hiring consultants, and using return-to-office orders to push out workers. The authors also say the strike at The New York Times in 2024 was largely a failure, because management had prepared the platform to run without staff, and because contracts with no-strike pledges barred the newsroom from joining. Redwine argues that labor law constrains unions, and that most major breakthroughs in the labor movement came from illegal strikes.

Tan says AI is splitting the tech workforce, with most workers likely to lose their jobs or be de-skilled, while a smaller group of AI engineers holds strong bargaining power because employers value their skills. He says many of the affected workers are becoming more class-conscious and concerned with affordability, and that a growing movement against data center construction creates both openings and tensions, since building trades workers are currently gaining jobs from that construction. The authors say new organizing methods will be needed that go beyond the Recognition Playbook and beyond shop-floor issues. The articles do not describe specific plans or dates for those efforts beyond the book's publication and the continuing debate over strategy.

Articles.Title: As AI Threatens Tech Workers, Their Workplaces Become Sites of Class Struggle

stories.Headline: IIT Delhi launches 6-month cybersecurity and AI security course
stories.Summary:
IIT Delhi has launched a six-month Certificate Programme in Cybersecurity and AI Security aimed at working professionals. The course is offered through the institute's Continuing Education Programme and was reported on November 9, 2026. It responds to the security risks that come with artificial intelligence built into enterprise systems. The curriculum covers adversarial machine learning, prompt injection in large language models, exploitation of agentic AI, and attacks on model supply chains.

The programme includes 78 hours of live instruction across five modules, followed by a capstone project. Its five agentic AI attack areas are multimodal jailbreaks, Model Context Protocol prompt injection, memory poisoning, tool-calling exploitation, and model hub supply chain attacks. Participants will use tools such as PyRIT, Garak, Sigstore, OPA and Falco. Classes are held live online on Saturdays, and for the capstone, participants build and deploy a production-grade AI security solution that IIT Delhi faculty will evaluate.

The course is intended for cybersecurity professionals, AI and machine learning engineers, data scientists, DevOps and platform engineers, and governance, risk and compliance professionals. Applicants need a Bachelor's or Master's degree in a related discipline, at least 50 per cent marks, and familiarity with one programming language. Reports put the total fee at about ₹1,40,000 plus 18 per cent GST, or ₹1,65,200. Prof Subodh Vishnu Sharma, an associate professor in IIT Delhi's Department of Computer Science and Engineering, said security can no longer be separated from AI engineering. He said the programme takes a threat-first approach, teaching how AI systems are attacked before defences are built, in line with India's evolving regulatory requirements.

Articles.Title: IIT Delhi launches 6-month cybersecurity and AI security course
